A read-only template containing everything needed to run an application: the code, the language runtime, system libraries, and the metadata describing how to start it.

An image is built from layers, one per instruction in the Dockerfile, stacked and presented as a single filesystem. Layers are what make Docker efficient: they are content-addressed and shared, so ten images built on node:22-alpine store that base exactly once on disk and pull it exactly once from a registry.

Two consequences of the layer model worth internalising early. Layers are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space in the image, and is still recoverable, which is why a deleted secret is a leaked secret. And layers are cached, so the order of instructions in a Dockerfile largely determines how fast rebuilds are.

Go deeper: Docker images and image layers.

```bash
docker images
```

## Container

A running instance of an image. If the image is the recipe, the container is the meal.

Technically it is an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, process table, network stack and hostname; cgroups cap what CPU and memory it can consume. There is no virtual machine and no guest operating system. This is why a container starts in milliseconds where a VM takes a minute.

Docker adds one thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers. Every file the container creates or modifies lands there, and it is deleted with the container. That single fact explains most Docker surprises for newcomers: your database is empty again because its data lived in the writable layer of a container that no longer exists.

Containers are ephemeral by design. Treat them as disposable and keep anything that must survive in a volume.

Go deeper: Docker containers and the container lifecycle.

```bash
docker ps
```

## Dockerfile

A plain text file of instructions for building an image, executed top to bottom:

Each instruction produces a layer. The reason the package manifest is copied and installed before the source is that Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so copying source first would reinstall every dependency on every code edit.

Go deeper: Dockerfile basics.

```bash
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

## Registry

Storage and distribution for images. GitHub, but for images rather than source. You push to share and pull to consume.

Docker Hub is the default: if you run docker pull nginx with no registry prefix, that is where it comes from. Most organisations also use a private registry. GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry. For their own images.

A tag such as 1.0 or latest is a mutable pointer to an image, not a permanent name. latest in particular is just a default tag with no special meaning; it does not track the newest version. A digest (@sha256:…) is immutable and is what you pin when reproducibility matters.

Go deeper: Docker Hub and registries.

```bash

docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
```

## Volume

Storage that outlives the container. Since the container's writable layer is destroyed with it, anything that must persist, database files, uploads, goes in a volume.

Three kinds, and the distinction comes up constantly:

Go deeper: Docker volumes.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

## Network

Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by container name, which is Docker's built-in DNS at work:

The API connects to db:5432. No IP addresses, no --link, nothing to update when a container restarts with a different address.

Note that localhost inside a container means that container, not the host and not another container. Expecting localhost:5432 to reach a database in a different container is one of the most common beginner errors.

Go deeper: container networking.

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapp:1.0
```

## Docker Compose

Real applications are several containers. Compose describes them in one file so the whole stack starts together:

Compose creates a network automatically, which is why db resolves as a hostname without any extra configuration.

It is a single-host tool. Excellent for development and small deployments, not a replacement for an orchestrator. Once you need scheduling across machines, rolling updates and self-healing, that is Kubernetes.

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

One more piece, because it explains a whole class of error messages.

The docker command is a client. It does almost nothing itself. It sends requests over a socket to the daemon (dockerd), which builds images, runs containers and manages storage.

So Cannot connect to the Docker daemon means the CLI is installed and working, and nothing is listening. Start the service. And permission denied ... docker.sock means the daemon is running but your user cannot talk to its socket.

It also explains why the build context is sent to the daemon: the daemon may not be on your machine at all.

```bash
docker CLI ──/var/run/docker.sock──▶ dockerd ──▶ containerd ──▶ runc ──▶ your process
```

sections.title: Layers
paragraphs: Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. A set of filesystem changes stacked on the one before. The final image is those layers combined and presented as one filesystem.
docker history is the first command to reach for on any size problem. It shows exactly which instruction added the weight, which is rarely the one people expect.
Three properties follow, and between them they explain most image behaviour.
Ten images built on the same base store that base once. This is why docker images can list ten images at 200 MB each while docker system df reports far less total disk:
A rebuild reuses every layer up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. Instruction order therefore determines build speed:
Reversing those two blocks means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile performance mistake and costs minutes on each build.
A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is still in the image. The later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding it; the bytes remain in the earlier layer and still ship.
This catches nearly everyone once, usually with apt-get caches:

codeBlock.code: docker history nginx:1.27

sections.title: Tags and digests
paragraphs: A tag is a mutable pointer. nginx:1.27 today and nginx:1.27 next month can be different images, because the maintainer can repoint it.
For reproducible builds, and anything security-sensitive, pin the digest.

At minimum, never deploy latest. It is not special, just the default tag name, and it means your deployment depends on whatever was most recently pushed. Two deploys of "latest" can run different code, and a rollback has nothing specific to return to.
Tagging adds a name to an existing image rather than copying it:
Both names now point at one image ID.

codeBlock.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # mutable
docker pull nginx@sha256:a1b2c3...     # immutable content hash

sections.title: Reducing image size
paragraphs: Size affects pull time, registry storage, and cold start on every platform that schedules containers. Three techniques, in order of impact.

Choose a smaller base. node:22 is roughly 1.1 GB; node:22-alpine around 150 MB; distroless smaller still. Alpine uses musl rather than glibc, which occasionally breaks native modules. Test rather than assume.
Use a multi-stage build, so build tooling never reaches the final image:
The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a scratch image is a few megabytes.
Add a .dockerignore. Without one, COPY . . sends node_modules, .git and every local artifact into the build context and often into the image:
This speeds builds too, since the context is uploaded to the daemon before the build starts.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: Dangling images and reclaiming disk
paragraphs: That <none> entry is a dangling image. The previous build of myapp, orphaned when the tag moved to the newer image. It still occupies disk.
Rebuilding the same tag repeatedly produces one every time, which is why disk usage climbs steadily during development and why Docker eventually reports no space left on device.

One thing prune does not touch: container logs. A long-running container using the default json-file driver with no rotation can write tens of gigabytes to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log. If docker system prune frees less than expected, that is usually where the space went:
Put that in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart Docker to cap it.

codeBlock.code: docker images

sections.title: Registries
paragraphs: Docker Hub is the default, so nginx means docker.io/library/nginx. Any other registry must be named explicitly.

Two practical notes. Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls, which a busy CI pipeline hits quickly. Authenticate, or mirror base images into your own registry. And a push only transfers layers the registry does not already hold, so pushing a rebuilt image is usually fast.

codeBlock.code:
docker login registry.example.com
docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker pull registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile downloads a 500 MB archive in one RUN and deletes it in the next. The image is still 500 MB larger than expected. Why?
A server reports "no space left on device". docker system prune -a removes several images but frees little space. What is the likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?

An image is a read-only template made of stacked filesystem layers; a container is a running instance created from it with its own thin writable layer. One image can produce any number of containers, all sharing the same underlying layers, which is why running ten containers from one image consumes very little extra disk. Images are built and pulled; containers are run, stopped and removed.
How do I reduce my Docker image size?

Three things, in order of impact. Switch to a smaller base, node:22-alpine is around 150 MB against roughly 1.1 GB for node:22. Use a multi-stage build so compilers and development dependencies stay in the build stage and never ship. Add a .dockerignore so node_modules, .git and local artifacts are not copied in. Then run docker history to see which instruction is actually adding the weight, because it is often not the one you would guess.
Why doesn't deleting files reduce my Docker image size?

Because layers are additive and all of them ship together. A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is hidden by a whiteout marker, but its bytes remain in the earlier layer and are still part of the image. Anything downloaded and then deleted must be handled within a single RUN instruction chained with &&, so only the net result is committed. The same applies to package manager caches. Clean them in the same RUN that installed the packages.
What are dangling images and is it safe to delete them?

They are the <none> entries in docker images. Previous builds whose tag was reassigned to a newer image, leaving them unreferenced. They are entirely safe to remove, and docker image prune does exactly that. They accumulate quickly during development because every rebuild of the same tag creates one, which is the usual reason disk usage climbs steadily and eventually produces "no space left on device".
Why did docker system prune not free much disk space?

Almost certainly container logs, which prune never touches. With the default json-file log driver and no rotation, a long-running container can write tens of gigabytes to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log. Check that directory's size directly. Fix it by setting "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restarting Docker. Named volumes are the other common culprit, since they are only removed with --volumes.
Should I use the latest tag?

No. latest is not special. It is simply the default tag name, pointing at whatever the maintainer most recently pushed, which can change without warning. Deploying it means two deploys of the same nominal version can run different code, and a rollback has no specific artifact to return to. Pin an explicit version tag, and for anything security-sensitive pin the digest with image@sha256:..., which is a content hash and genuinely immutable.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
docker-images.markdown:
A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process namespace and network interface. Images are templates; containers are what actually runs.

## The lifecycle

```
docker run âââº Running âââº docker stop âââº Exited âââº docker rm âââº gone
                  â            â²
                  ââ pause âââââ
```

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27   # create + start
docker stop web                       # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s
docker start web                      # start it again. Same container
docker rm web                         # delete it
```

The distinction that matters: **`docker run` creates a new container every time.** `docker start` restarts an existing one. Running the same command three times gives three containers, which is why `docker ps -a` fills up unexpectedly.

```bash
docker ps        # running only
docker ps -a     # including exited
```

## Why your container exits immediately

The most common Docker frustration, and it has one root cause.

**A container lives exactly as long as its main process.** When PID 1 exits, the container exits. There is no background mode that keeps it alive.

```bash
docker run ubuntu           # exits instantly
docker run ubuntu bash      # also exits, no TTY, bash has no input and quits
docker run -it ubuntu bash  # stays running. Interactive terminal attached
```

The same applies to your own images. A web server that daemonises itself, forking into the background and returning, makes PID 1 exit, so Docker concludes the work is done:

```dockerfile
# Wrong, nginx forks and the foreground process exits
CMD ["nginx"]

# Right. Stays in the foreground
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
```

Diagnosing it:

```bash
docker ps -a                    # check the STATUS and exit code
docker logs <container>         # what did it print before dying?
```

```
STATUS
Exited (127) 2 seconds ago
```

Exit codes carry information: **0** means clean exit, **1** a general application error, **125** the Docker command itself failed, **126** the command is not executable, **127** command not found, **137** SIGKILL (often out of memory), **143** SIGTERM.

Exit 127 nearly always means a typo in the command or a binary missing from the image.

## Publishing ports

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
#               â    âââ container port
#               âââ host port
```

Host on the left, container on the right. Reversing them is a rite of passage.

```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # bind to localhost only
docker run -d -P nginx                     # publish all EXPOSEd ports randomly
docker port web                            # what is actually mapped?
```

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It is documentation. Only `-p` or `-P` at run time actually maps a port.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash
docker run -d \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \
  --env-file .env \
  myapp:1.0
```

Environment variables are the standard way to configure a container, which is what lets one image serve every environment.

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies

```bash
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped nginx:1.27
```

| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |

**`unless-stopped` is usually the right choice** for a long-running service. `always` will restart a container you deliberately stopped when the daemon next starts, which is rarely what anyone wants.

## Resource limits

```bash
docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp:1.0
```

Without limits, one container can consume the whole host. A memory limit means the container is killed when it exceeds it, exit code 137, rather than the host running out of memory and the kernel choosing a victim arbitrarily.

```bash
docker stats           # live usage
docker stats --no-stream
```

## Working with a running container

```bash
docker logs -f web                 # follow
docker logs --tail 100 web
docker logs --since 10m web

docker exec -it web sh             # shell inside
docker exec web env                # single command

docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./   # copy a file out
docker inspect web                       # full configuration as JSON
docker top web                           # processes
```

`docker exec` attaches to an **already running** container. If the container has exited, `exec` fails. You need `docker run` with a different command, or `--entrypoint` to override what it starts:

```bash
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp:1.0
```

That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately.

## stop vs kill

```bash
docker stop web           # SIGTERM, wait 10s, then SIGKILL
docker stop -t 30 web     # allow 30 seconds
docker kill web           # SIGKILL immediately
```

`docker stop` gives the application a chance to finish in-flight work. Use it. `docker kill` is for a process that is genuinely stuck.

If `docker stop` always takes exactly 10 seconds, your application is not receiving `SIGTERM`, almost always because the Dockerfile used shell-form `CMD`, making `/bin/sh` PID 1 instead of your process.

## Cleaning up

Stopped containers accumulate and hold disk through their writable layers:

```bash
docker container prune          # remove all stopped containers
docker rm -f web                # force-remove a running one
docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f   # remove everything, carefully
```

The best habit is preventing the buildup: **`--rm` deletes the container the moment it exits.**

```bash
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash
```

Use it for anything one-off. Tests, scripts, exploration. Nothing accumulates.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run detached with a port | `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name <n> <image>` |
| Run and auto-delete | `docker run --rm -it <image> <cmd>` |
| List running | `docker ps` |
| List all | `docker ps -a` |
| Logs | `docker logs -f <n>` |
| Shell inside | `docker exec -it <n> sh` |
| Explore an image that exits | `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>` |
| Port mappings | `docker port <n>` |
| Live resource usage | `docker stats` |
| Stop gracefully | `docker stop <n>` |
| Remove stopped containers | `docker container prune` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **A container lives exactly as long as PID 1.** Exit immediately usually means the process daemonised or was not found.
- **`docker run` creates a new container each time**; `docker start` reuses one.
- **Port mapping is `-p host:container`**, and `EXPOSE` publishes nothing.
- **Bind to `127.0.0.1` when you do not want a port on all interfaces**: Docker writes its own iptables rules and can bypass a host firewall.
- **`unless-stopped` is the sensible restart policy** for services.
- **Exit 137 is SIGKILL, usually out of memory; 127 is command not found.**
- **A 10-second `docker stop` every time means `SIGTERM` is not reaching your process.**
- **Use `--rm` for anything one-off** so containers do not accumulate.

---

## Check your understanding

The usual causes are a service that daemonises itself into the background, or an image whose default command simply runs and exits. Fix it by keeping the process in the foreground, such as nginx -g "daemon off;".',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'The container did start. It has an exit status, which only exists once a process has run and finished.',
      c: 'A corrupt image fails at pull or create with an explicit error, not with a clean exit code of 0.',

    },
  }}

<MCQExercise

    options: [

    },
  }}
/>

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

paragraphs: Understand how Docker image names and tags are structured, tag images with docker tag, avoid the latest trap, and pin exact versions using digests.

sections.title: Docker Image Name
paragraphs: A Docker image name is basically an address. It tells Docker three things: where the image lives, what it is, and which version you want.
The full format looks like this:
When you run docker pull nginx, Docker automatically expands it to docker.io/library/nginx:latest. The short name is just a convenient.
Here's a simple analogy: imagine ordering a book. The registry is the bookstore, the repository is the book title, and the tag is the book's edition.

codeBlock.code: registry/repository:tag

sections.title: Breaking Down a Real Docker Image Name
paragraphs: Let's look at some real examples to make this concrete:

codeBlock.code:
# Just the image name - Docker fills in the rest automatically
nginx

# Same image, but with a specific version
nginx:1.25

# Lightweight version of the same image
nginx:1.25-alpine

# Full name written out completely
docker.io/library/nginx:latest

# An image published by a user or organization on Docker Hub
username/myapp:v2.0.0

# An image stored on a private company registry
myregistry.company.com/backend/api:production

# An image hosted on Google's registry
gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0

# An image on GitHub's registry, identified by a commit hash
ghcr.io/owner/repo:sha-abc1234

sections.title: What Is a Docker Tag?
paragraphs: A tag is a label that points to a specific version of an image. The catch? Tags are mutable which means not permanent. They're more like sticky notes: someone can move them to point to a different image at any time. This is why using the latest tag in production is risky:
Bottom line: For anything serious (production apps, CI/CD pipelines, team projects), always pin to a specific version tag. It saves you from mysterious bugs caused by unexpected version changes.

codeBlock.code:
# Today this might download Node.js version 18
# Tomorrow it might download Node.js version 22
docker pull node:latest

# This will ALWAYS download exactly Node.js 20.11.0
docker pull node:20.11.0

sections.title: How to Tag Docker Images Like a Pro
paragraphs: Good tagging habits make your images easier to manage, understand, and reproduce. There are really only four questions a good tag can answer: what version is this, how big/lean is it, where does it go, and what exact code is inside it. Each strategy below answers one of those questions. Once you know which question you're answering, the right tag style becomes obvious.

Semantic versioning follows the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format, and it's the closest thing Docker has to a universal standard. Think of the three numbers as a report card, read left to right from "biggest change" to "smallest change":

Easy way to remember it: the more numbers in the tag, the more "locked in" you are. One number is loose and will silently change under you; three numbers never move. For production, always reach for the full three-number tag. You want to know exactly what you're running, not "whatever the latest patch happens to be today."
Many official images ship in different "flavors" of the same software, built on different base operating systems. The variant name usually shows up after a dash:

Easy way to remember it: picture ordering coffee. bookworm is the large cup with everything included: more room to work, more disk space used. slim is a medium cup with just the essentials trimmed out. alpine is the tiny espresso shot: fast and small, but it's brewed differently (Alpine uses musl instead of glibc), so it doesn't always taste right with every recipe. That's why Alpine images are popular for production (small, fast to pull, smaller attack surface) but are also the most likely to cause a strange compatibility bug, so always test before committing to one.

This kind of tag isn't really describing the code itself; it's a destination label, like a shipping sticker on a box. On its own it doesn't tell you what's inside, only where it's headed, which is why the best environment tags combine the destination with a real version, like staging-v2.1.0 above: now the tag answers both "where" and "what."
Easy way to remember it: if you can answer the question "where is this going?" just by reading the tag, it's an environment tag.

A Git commit SHA is a unique fingerprint for one exact snapshot of your source code. Baking it into the tag means that if something breaks in production six months from now, you can read the tag straight off the running container, paste that SHA into git show, and see the exact lines of code that were live at that moment. No guessing, no "which version was this again?"

Easy way to remember it: SHA tags are your evidence trail. They don't replace a version number (you can have both, like v1.4.2-sha-a3f8c2d) - they just guarantee you can always trace a running container back to one specific commit.

In practice, most real-world tags combine two or three of these in one string - myapp:staging-v2.1.0 and myapp:v1.4.2-sha-a3f8c2d are both already doing that above. Pick the question you most need answered when someone looks at the tag six months from now, and build from there.

codeBlock.code:
myapp:1.0.0   # A specific patch release (most precise)
myapp:1.0     # Floats to the latest 1.0.x release
myapp:1       # Floats to the latest 1.x.x release

sections.title: The Most Permanent Way to Reference an Image: Digests
paragraphs: Every image has a unique fingerprint called a digest, a long hash that looks like this:
Unlike tags (which can change), a digest never changes. It will always refer to the exact same image content, forever.
Use digests when you need 100% reproducibility. For example, in regulated industries, security-sensitive environments, or when debugging a production incident months after the fact.

codeBlock.code: docker pull nginx@sha256:7144f7bab3d4c2648d7e59409f15ec52a18006a128c733fcff20d3a4a54ba44a

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Tag an Image Yourself
paragraphs: The best way to understand tagging is to try it. Here's a quick exercise:
Notice that tagging doesn't create a new copy of the image; it just creates new pointers to the same data. Docker is efficient like that.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Download the official nginx image
docker pull nginx

# Step 2: Give it a new tag called webserver:v1.0
docker tag nginx webserver:v1.0

# Step 3: Give it another tag called webserver:stable
docker tag nginx webserver:stable

# Step 4: Confirm all three tags exist (they all point to the same image)
docker images | grep -E "nginx|webserver"

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What happens if I don't specify a tag?
Docker automatically uses latest. This is fine for quick experiments but risky in production because latest can point to a different image version over time.
Can I create my own tags for someone else's image?
Yes! The docker tag command lets you add your own tags to any image you've pulled. The tags only exist locally on your machine unless you push them to a registry.
What's the difference between a registry and a repository?

A registry is the entire hosting platform (like Docker Hub). A repository is one specific image within that platform (like the nginx repo on Docker Hub). A registry can hold thousands of repositories.
Are Alpine images always better?

Not always. Alpine images are smaller and faster to pull, but they use a different C library (musl instead of glibc), which can cause compatibility issues with some software. Test Alpine images thoroughly before using them in production.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
docker-images-naming-tags.markdown:
## Tagging Images

A tag is just a label that points to an image. The same image can have multiple tags, which is useful for marking the same build as `v1.0`, `latest`, and `production` all at once without duplicating any data.

```bash
# Add a new tag to an existing image
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:latest

# Tag the same image for different environments
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:production
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:staging

# Tag it for a private registry before pushing
docker tag myapp:v1.0 registry.company.com/myteam/myapp:v1.0

# Tag with the Git commit SHA for full traceability
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:sha-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
```

Tagging never copies data, every tag pointing to the same image ID shares the exact same layers on disk. It's just an alias.

---

## Removing Images

When you're done with an image, `docker rmi` removes it:

```bash
# Remove by name and tag
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Remove by image ID (you only need enough characters to make it unique)
docker rmi 605c77

# Remove multiple images in one go
docker rmi nginx:1.24 nginx:1.25 postgres:15

# Force removal even if a stopped container still references it
docker rmi -f myapp:old

# Remove all images (use with caution)
docker rmi $(docker images -q)
```

**Note:** Docker won't remove an image if any container  is stopped. You'll need to remove the container first with `docker rm <container-id>`, or use the `-f` flag to force it.

---

## Cleaning Up Unused Images

As you rebuild images over time, old versions lose their tags but the layers stick around on disk. These tagless leftovers are called **dangling images** and they serve no purpose, they're just taking up space.

```bash
# Remove only dangling (untagged) images
docker image prune

# Remove all images not currently used by any container
docker image prune -a

# Skip the confirmation prompt
docker image prune -f

# Remove images that haven't been used in the last 24 hours
docker image prune -a --filter "until=24h"
```
---

## Pushing Images to a Registry

Once your image is ready, you push it to a registry so other machines like your server, your teammates, your CI pipeline, can pull it down.

**Docker Hub:**
```bash
# Log in with your Docker Hub account
docker login

# Tag the image with your Docker Hub username
docker tag myapp:v1.0 yourusername/myapp:v1.0

# Push it
docker push yourusername/myapp:v1.0
```

**A Private Registry:**
```bash
# Log in to your company's registry
docker login registry.company.com

# Tag the image for that registry
docker tag myapp:v1.0 registry.company.com/team/myapp:v1.0

# Push it
docker push registry.company.com/team/myapp:v1.0
```

The process is the same everywhere: log in, tag the image with the registry address, push. The registry address at the front of the tag is how Docker knows where to send it.

---

## Saving Images as Files

Sometimes you need to move an image without using a registry across a network with no internet access, as a backup, or to share directly with someone.

**Save an image to a file:**
```bash
# Export to a tar archive
docker save nginx:latest > nginx.tar

# Save compressed to reduce file size
docker save nginx:latest | gzip > nginx.tar.gz

# Save multiple images into one archive
docker save nginx:latest postgres:16 alpine:3.18 > images.tar
```

**Load it back on another machine:**
```bash
# Load from a tar file
docker load < nginx.tar

# Load a compressed archive
gunzip -c nginx.tar.gz | docker load

# Alternative syntax if piping feels awkward
docker load --input nginx.tar
```

After loading, the image shows up in `docker images` with its original name and tag, no re-tagging needed.

---

## Hands-On Practice: Tag, Save, and Remove

```bash
# Step 1: Tag the nginx image as webserver:backup
docker tag nginx webserver:backup

# Step 2: Save it to a tar file
docker save webserver:backup > webserver.tar

# Step 3: Remove the original nginx image
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Step 4: Confirm nginx is gone but webserver:backup still exists
docker images
```

After step 3, `nginx:latest` will be gone but `webserver:backup` which points to the same image data, will still be there. And you'll have a `webserver.tar` file you could move to another machine.

---

## save/load vs export/import What's the Difference?

Docker has two pairs of commands that look similar but do very different things:

`docker save` / `docker load` works with **images**: it preserves every layer, all the metadata, environment variables, and the full layer history. This is what you should use almost always.

`docker export` / `docker import` works with a **running or stopped container's filesystem**: it flattens everything into a single layer and discards all history and metadata.

```bash
# Export a container's filesystem (flattened, loses history)
docker export my-container > container-fs.tar

# Import as a new image
docker import container-fs.tar myimage:imported
```

Unless you specifically want to flatten an image's layers, stick with `save` and `load`.

---

## Full Cleanup: Starting Fresh

When your disk is getting full and you want to wipe the slate clean:

```bash
# Remove all stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove all unused images
docker image prune -a

# Remove unused volumes
docker volume prune

# Remove unused networks
docker network prune

# Do all of the above in one command
docker system prune -a --volumes
```

The last command removes everything Docker isn't actively using. Run `docker system df` first to understand what you're about to delete, and make sure anything you want to keep is either running or pushed to a registry.

---

## Key Takeaways

- `docker tag` creates a new label pointing to an existing image, and no data is copied.
- `docker rmi` removes images. If a container (even stopped) still references it, remove the container first or use `-f`.
- Run `docker system df` before pruning to see how much space you'll actually reclaim.
- `docker push` sends your image to a registry. Always tag it with the registry address first.
- `docker save` / `docker load` transfers images as files, useful when you don't have registry access.
- `docker system prune -a --volumes` removes everything unused. It's powerful and destructive.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**If I remove a tag, does it delete the image?**

Only if it was the last tag pointing to that image. If the same image has multiple tags (`latest`, `v1.0`, `production`), removing one tag just removes that label, the image and its layers stay on disk until all tags pointing to it are removed.

**Why can't I remove an image that I'm not using?**

A stopped container still holds a reference to the image it was created from. Run `docker ps -a` to see stopped containers, remove them with `docker rm <id>`, and then try removing the image again.

**What's the difference between `docker image prune` and `docker image prune -a`?**

Without `-a`, it only removes dangling images, untagged leftovers from old builds. With `-a`, it removes any image not currently used by a running or stopped container. The `-a` version reclaims much more space but is more aggressive.

**Do I need to be logged in to push to Docker Hub?**

Yes. Run `docker login` first. For CI/CD pipelines, use a personal access token instead of your password as it's more secure and can be revoked independently.

**Is `docker save` the same as making a backup?**

It's a portable snapshot of your image that can be moved between machines without a registry. It's a reasonable backup approach for small setups, but for production workflows a registry (even a self-hosted one) is much more manageable at scale.

docker-images-hub.markdown:
## What Is Docker Hub?

Docker Hub is the internet's largest public library of container images. Think of it like the App Store but instead of apps, it stores pre-built Docker images that you can download and run instantly.

It's also Docker's **default** registry, which means Docker looks there automatically whenever you pull an image without specifying where it should come from. Docker Hub hosts millions of images, ranging from bare-bones operating systems to fully configured databases, web servers, and developer tools.

---

## What Kind of Images Can You Find There?

Not all Docker Hub images are the same quality. There are three tiers you should know about:

**Official Images** are the gold standard. They're maintained by Docker itself or directly by the software's creators. They have no username prefix in their name (just `nginx`, not `someuser/nginx`), they're updated regularly with security patches, and they come with proper documentation.

Here are some of the most commonly used official images organized by category:

| Category | Popular Images |
|----------|----------------|
| Operating Systems | `ubuntu`, `alpine`, `debian`, `fedora` |
| Programming Languages | `node`, `python`, `golang`, `ruby` |
| Databases | `postgres`, `mysql`, `mongodb`, `redis` |
| Web Servers | `nginx`, `httpd`, `caddy`, `traefik` |
| Utility Tools | `busybox`, `curl`, `git`, `helm` |

**Verified Publisher Images** are published by well-known companies, like Bitnami, Elastic, or HashiCorp. They have a company namespace (e.g. `bitnami/postgresql`) but are still trustworthy.

**Community Images** are published by regular developers and organizations. Quality varies enormously. Before using one, check how many stars it has, how many times it's been pulled, and when it was last updated.

**The safe approach:** start with official images whenever possible, then verified publishers, and treat community images with a healthy dose of skepticism.

---


## How to Use the Docker Hub Website

The Docker Hub website (`hub.docker.com`) is more than just a search engine. For any image, you'll find:

- **Tags tab** - every available version of the image, so you can pick exactly what you need
- **README** - the most important page. It tells you which environment variables the image supports, which ports it uses by default, and how to configure it
- **Digest** - a cryptographic fingerprint for each tag, useful for pinning to an exact image version
- **Vulnerabilities** - for official images, Docker runs automated security scans and shows known CVEs

Make it a habit to read the README before running an unfamiliar image. It'll save you from a lot of head-scratching when things don't work as expected.

---

## Docker Hub Rate Limits (And How to Avoid Hitting Them)

If you're pulling images frequently without logging in, you'll eventually hit Docker Hub's rate limits. Here's what they are:

| Your Status | Pull Limit |
|-------------|------------|
| Not logged in (anonymous) | 100 pulls every 6 hours |
| Free Docker Hub account | 200 pulls every 6 hours |
| Pro or Team account | Unlimited |

For personal use, creating a free account and logging in is usually enough. You can do that from the terminal with:

```bash
docker login
# Enter your Docker Hub username and password (or access token)
```

If you're setting up a CI/CD pipeline (like GitHub Actions), don't use your main password. Instead, generate a **personal access token** from the Docker Hub security settings and use that. It's more secure and you can revoke it without changing your password.

---

## Key Takeaways

Docker Hub is your starting point for almost every Docker project. Here's what to keep in mind:

- It's Docker's default registry, so no setup is needed to start pulling public images.
- Official images are maintained, patched, and documented. Start there.
- The `docker search` command works for quick lookups, but the website gives you much more information.
- Always check a few things before using a community image: star count, pull count, and last updated date.
- Log in with a free account to double your rate limit. Use an access token in automated pipelines.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do I need an account to use Docker Hub?**

No, you can pull public images without logging in. But creating a free account increases your rate limit from 100 to 200 pulls every 6 hours, and lets you push your own images.

**How do I know which tag to use?**

Check the Tags tab on Docker Hub for the image you want. For production, always use a specific version tag (like `redis:7.2`) rather than `latest`, since `latest` can change at any time.

**Are community images safe to use?**

Some are, some aren't. Red flags include: no recent updates, very few stars/pulls, and no documentation. Always prefer official or verified publisher images when they exist.

sections.title: How to Pull Images
paragraphs: Pulling an image just means downloading it to your local machine. Here are the most common ways to do it:

One thing that makes Docker smart: it downloads images in layers, and it caches those layers locally. If two images share the same base OS layer, Docker only downloads it once. This saves both time and disk space as you accumulate more images.

codeBlock.code:
# Download the latest version of nginx (simplest form)
docker pull nginx

# Download a specific version (always safer in production)
docker pull postgres:16

# Download a lightweight Alpine variant
docker pull python:3.12-alpine

# Download from a different registry (not Docker Hub)
docker pull gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0

# Download by digest (the most permanent, unchangeable reference)
docker pull ubuntu@sha256:77906da...

sections.title: What Does the Pull Output Actually Mean?
paragraphs: When you pull an image, you'll see something like this:

Each line represents a layer - a piece of the image stacked on top of the previous one. If you've already pulled another image that shares a layer, you'll see Already exists instead of Pull complete. That's Docker being efficient and reusing what's already on your machine.

codeBlock.code:
7.2: Pulling from library/redis
a480a496ba95: Pull complete      ← downloading the base OS layer
e2677dab5ef2: Pull complete      ← installing packages on top
ca5b0a5ac559: Pull complete      ← adding the Redis binary itself
Digest: sha256:e96c03a6dda7...
Status: Downloaded newer image for redis:7.2

sections.title: How to Search for Images
paragraphs: You can search Docker Hub right from your terminal without opening a browser:
The output looks something like this:
The [OK] in the OFFICIAL column is your signal that this is an officially maintained image. Images without it are community-contributed.
For seeing all available version tags, reading documentation, or checking security scan results, head to hub.docker.com and search there. The web UI gives you a lot more detail than the CLI.

codeBlock.code:
# Search for any image by name
docker search nginx

# Limit results to the top 5
docker search --limit 5 postgres

# Only show images with at least 50 stars
docker search --filter stars=50 redis

# Only show official images
docker search --filter is-official=true python

sections.title: Practice: Search and Pull from Docker Hub
paragraphs: The best way to get comfortable with these commands is to try them yourself. Here's a quick walkthrough:
Notice the [OK] badge in the search results. This confirms Redis is an officially maintained image. And after pulling, docker images should show redis with the 7.2 tag, its image ID, and size.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Search for official Redis images on Docker Hub
docker search --filter is-official=true redis

# Step 2: Pull a specific version - never just "latest" in real projects
docker pull redis:7.2

# Step 3: Confirm the image downloaded successfully
docker images | grep redis

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do I need to run docker pull before docker run?

No - docker run automatically pulls the image if it isn't already on your machine. docker pull is useful when you want to download an image ahead of time, or update a locally cached image to its newest version.
How do I see all the images I've already pulled?
Run docker images (or docker image ls). It lists every image stored locally along with its tag, ID, size, and when it was created.
Why does my pull say Already exists for some layers?
That's Docker reusing a cached layer from a previously pulled image. It's completely normal and actually a good thing: it means Docker is being efficient and not re-downloading data you already have.
What's the difference between a tag and a digest?

A tag (like redis:7.2) is a human-readable label that can be reassigned over time. A digest (like ubuntu@sha256:779...) is a cryptographic fingerprint that is permanently tied to one exact version of an image. Use digests when you need a guarantee that nothing will ever change.
Why do some image names have a slash and others don't?

Images without a slash (like nginx) are official images maintained by Docker or the software vendor. Images with a slash (like bitnami/postgresql) belong to a user or organization. The slash separates the namespace from the image name.
I'm on a Mac with Apple Silicon and the image isn't working. Why?
Some images are only built for linux/amd64 (Intel architecture). Pull with --platform linux/amd64 to explicitly request that version, and Docker Desktop will run it through emulation automatically.

docker-images-pull.markdown:
An image is a read-only template containing a filesystem and the metadata needed to run it. Containers are created from images; images are built from Dockerfiles or pulled from registries.

Nearly everything worth knowing about images comes down to **layers**.

## Layers

Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. A set of filesystem changes stacked on the one before. The final image is those layers combined and presented as one filesystem.

```bash
docker history nginx:1.27
```

```
IMAGE          CREATED BY                                      SIZE
a1b2c3d4e5f6   CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemon off;"]                0B
<missing>      EXPOSE map[80/tcp:{}]                           0B
<missing>      COPY docker-entrypoint.sh / # buildkit          1.62kB
<missing>      RUN /bin/sh -c apt-get update && apt-get insâ¦   61.2MB
<missing>      ADD file:4f4fb700ef54461cfâ¦ in /                 80.5MB
```

`docker history` is the first command to reach for on any size problem. It shows exactly which instruction added the weight, which is rarely the one people expect.

Three properties follow, and between them they explain most image behaviour.

### Layers are shared

Ten images built on the same base store that base **once**. This is why `docker images` can list ten images at 200 MB each while `docker system df` reports far less total disk:

```bash
docker system df
```

```
TYPE          TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images        14      5        4.2GB     2.8GB (66%)
```

### Layers are cached

A rebuild reuses every layer up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. **Instruction order therefore determines build speed:**

```dockerfile
# Dependencies change rarely. Install them first
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Source changes constantly. Copy it last
COPY . .
```

Reversing those two blocks means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile performance mistake and costs minutes on each build.

### Layers are additive: deleting does not shrink

A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is **still in the image**. The later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding it; the bytes remain in the earlier layer and still ship.

```dockerfile
# Wrong. The archive is in the image forever
RUN curl -O https://example.com/big.tar.gz
RUN tar -xzf big.tar.gz && rm big.tar.gz

# Right. One layer, nothing left behind
RUN curl -O https://example.com/big.tar.gz \
 && tar -xzf big.tar.gz \
 && rm big.tar.gz
```

This catches nearly everyone once, usually with `apt-get` caches:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

## Tags and digests

A tag is a **mutable pointer**. `nginx:1.27` today and `nginx:1.27` next month can be different images, because the maintainer can repoint it.

```bash
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # mutable
docker pull nginx@sha256:a1b2c3...     # immutable content hash
```

For reproducible builds, and anything security-sensitive, pin the digest.

At minimum, **never deploy `latest`**. It is not special, just the default tag name, and it means your deployment depends on whatever was most recently pushed. Two deploys of "latest" can run different code, and a rollback has nothing specific to return to.

Tagging adds a name to an existing image rather than copying it:

```bash
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/myapp:stable
```

Both names now point at one image ID.

## Reducing image size

Size affects pull time, registry storage, and cold start on every platform that schedules containers. Three techniques, in order of impact.

**Choose a smaller base.** `node:22` is roughly 1.1 GB; `node:22-alpine` around 150 MB; distroless smaller still. Alpine uses musl rather than glibc, which occasionally breaks native modules. Test rather than assume.

**Use a multi-stage build**, so build tooling never reaches the final image:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a `scratch` image is a few megabytes.

**Add a `.dockerignore`.** Without one, `COPY . .` sends `node_modules`, `.git` and every local artifact into the build context and often into the image:

```
node_modules
.git
.env
dist
*.log
```

This speeds builds too, since the context is uploaded to the daemon before the build starts.

## Dangling images and reclaiming disk

```bash
docker images
```

```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       SIZE
myapp        1.4.2     a1b2c3d4e5f6   142MB
<none>       <none>    f6e5d4c3b2a1   140MB
```

That `<none>` entry is a **dangling image**. The previous build of `myapp`, orphaned when the tag moved to the newer image. It still occupies disk.

Rebuilding the same tag repeatedly produces one every time, which is why disk usage climbs steadily during development and why Docker eventually reports **no space left on device**.

```bash
docker image prune        # dangling only. Safe to run routinely
docker image prune -a     # every image not used by a container
docker system df          # see what is reclaimable first
```

One thing `prune` does **not** touch: **container logs**. A long-running container using the default `json-file` driver with no rotation can write tens of gigabytes to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log`. If `docker system prune` frees less than expected, that is usually where the space went:

```json
{ "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" } }
```

Put that in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restart Docker to cap it.

## Registries

```bash
docker login registry.example.com
docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker pull registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
```

Docker Hub is the default, so `nginx` means `docker.io/library/nginx`. Any other registry must be named explicitly.

Two practical notes. **Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls**, which a busy CI pipeline hits quickly. Authenticate, or mirror base images into your own registry. And a push only transfers layers the registry does not already hold, so pushing a rebuilt image is usually fast.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| List images | `docker images` |
| Pull | `docker pull <image>:<tag>` |
| Build | `docker build -t <name>:<tag> .` |
| Tag | `docker tag <source> <target>` |
| Push | `docker push <registry>/<name>:<tag>` |
| Layer sizes | `docker history <image>` |
| Full metadata | `docker inspect <image>` |
| Remove one | `docker rmi <image>` |
| Remove dangling | `docker image prune` |
| Remove all unused | `docker image prune -a` |
| Disk usage | `docker system df` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Each Dockerfile instruction is a layer**, and layers are shared, cached and additive.
- **Copy dependency manifests before source code** so the install layer stays cached.
- **Deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image**: clean up inside the same `RUN`.
- **Tags are mutable; digests are not.** Never deploy `latest`.
- **Multi-stage builds keep compilers and dev dependencies out of the shipped image.**
- **`<none>` images are dangling**: previous builds of a retagged image. `docker image prune` clears them.
- **`docker system prune` does not touch container logs.** Cap them with `max-size` in `daemon.json`.
- **Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls.** Authenticate or mirror in CI.

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-img-layer-delete',
    title: 'An image that will not shrink',
    description: 'A Dockerfile downloads a 500 MB archive in one RUN and deletes it in the next. The image is still 500 MB larger than expected. Why?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Layers are additive. The file remains in the earlier layer and is only hidden by the later one, so it still ships' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'The rm command needs the -f flag to actually remove the file' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Docker caches deleted files for 24 hours before reclaiming the space' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'The archive is counted twice because it was downloaded and then extracted' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'Each instruction commits a layer recording changes relative to the previous one, and every layer ships with the image. A deletion in a later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding the file rather than removing its bytes from the earlier layer. Download, extract and delete must happen in a single RUN chained with &&, so only the net result is ever committed.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'The file is genuinely deleted from the running container filesystem. The problem is that the earlier layer still contains it.',
      c: 'There is no deferred reclamation. Layer contents are immutable once committed.',
      d: 'The extracted contents do add their own size, but the question is specifically about the archive persisting after deletion.',
    },
  }}

    },

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?**

An image is a read-only template made of stacked filesystem layers; a container is a running instance created from it with its own thin writable layer. One image can produce any number of containers, all sharing the same underlying layers, which is why running ten containers from one image consumes very little extra disk. Images are built and pulled; containers are run, stopped and removed.

**How do I reduce my Docker image size?**

Three things, in order of impact. Switch to a smaller base, `node:22-alpine` is around 150 MB against roughly 1.1 GB for `node:22`. Use a multi-stage build so compilers and development dependencies stay in the build stage and never ship. Add a `.dockerignore` so `node_modules`, `.git` and local artifacts are not copied in. Then run `docker history` to see which instruction is actually adding the weight, because it is often not the one you would guess.

**Why doesn't deleting files reduce my Docker image size?**

Because layers are additive and all of them ship together. A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is hidden by a whiteout marker, but its bytes remain in the earlier layer and are still part of the image. Anything downloaded and then deleted must be handled within a **single** `RUN` instruction chained with `&&`, so only the net result is committed. The same applies to package manager caches. Clean them in the same `RUN` that installed the packages.

**What are dangling images and is it safe to delete them?**

They are the `<none>` entries in `docker images`. Previous builds whose tag was reassigned to a newer image, leaving them unreferenced. They are entirely safe to remove, and `docker image prune` does exactly that. They accumulate quickly during development because every rebuild of the same tag creates one, which is the usual reason disk usage climbs steadily and eventually produces "no space left on device".

**Why did docker system prune not free much disk space?**

Almost certainly container logs, which prune never touches. With the default `json-file` log driver and no rotation, a long-running container can write tens of gigabytes to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log`. Check that directory's size directly. Fix it by setting `"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarting Docker. Named volumes are the other common culprit, since they are only removed with `--volumes`.

**Should I use the `latest` tag?**

No. `latest` is not special. It is simply the default tag name, pointing at whatever the maintainer most recently pushed, which can change without warning. Deploying it means two deploys of the same nominal version can run different code, and a rollback has no specific artifact to return to. Pin an explicit version tag, and for anything security-sensitive pin the digest with `image@sha256:...`, which is a content hash and genuinely immutable.

docker-images-listing.markdown:
## List & Inspect Images

You've pulled a few images. Maybe you've built one too. Now the natural question is "what's actually sitting on my machine, and how do I understand what's inside these images?"

Docker gives you a handful of commands to answer exactly that. This guide walks through all of them in plain English.

## How to See All Your Local Images

The most basic command is `docker images`. Run it and you'll get a table of every image stored on your machine:

```bash
# List all images
docker images

# Identical alternative
docker image ls

# Include intermediate build layers
docker images -a

# Show only image IDs
docker images -q

# Filter by repository name
docker images nginx

# Filter by reference (name + tag)
docker images "nginx:1.25"
```

**Sample output:**
```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
nginx        latest    605c77e624dd   2 weeks ago    141MB
postgres     16        6e52a4f81b47   3 weeks ago    432MB
alpine       3.18      c1aabb73d233   3 weeks ago    7.33MB
node         18-alpine 8cdf5e4fca3f   4 weeks ago    127MB
```

Here's what each column actually means:

| Column | What it tells you |
|--------|-------------------|
| `REPOSITORY` | The image name (registry is omitted if it's from Docker Hub) |
| `TAG` | The version or variant (e.g. `latest`, `16`, `3.18-alpine`) |
| `IMAGE ID` | A short fingerprint of the image (first 12 characters of its full hash) |
| `CREATED` | When the image was *built* |
| `SIZE` | How much disk space it takes up on your machine, uncompressed |

One thing worth knowing about the SIZE column: if two images share layers (for example, both use the same Ubuntu base), that shared layer is only stored once on disk, but it still gets counted in each image's size. So the total disk usage is usually less than the sum of all the sizes you see listed.

---

# Filtering and Formatting the Image List

As you pull more images, the list gets long. These commands help you to filter the images:

```bash
# Show dangling images (untagged leftovers from old builds)
docker images --filter dangling=true

# Show images created before a specific image
docker images --filter before=nginx:latest

# Show images created after a specific image
docker images --filter since=alpine:3.18

# Custom output (show only name, tag, and size)
docker images --format "{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} - {{.Size}}"
```

Dangling images are the most common thing to clean up. They're leftover layers from previous builds that no longer have a name or tag attached to them.

---

## How to Inspect What's Inside an Image

`docker images` tells you *what* you have. `docker inspect` tells you *everything about* a specific image. It returns a detailed JSON document packed with metadata:

```bash
# See the full details of an image
docker inspect nginx:latest

# Extract just the default command the image runs
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Cmd}}' nginx

# See all environment variables baked into the image
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Env}}' nginx

# See which ports the image expects to be open
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.ExposedPorts}}' nginx

# List all the layers that make up the image
docker inspect --format='{{.RootFS.Layers}}' nginx
```

The `--format` flag uses Go templates to pull out just the field you care about, so you don't have to wade through the entire JSON output. Here's a taste of what the full output contains:

```json
{
  "Id": "sha256:605c77e624dd...",
  "RepoTags": ["nginx:latest"],
  "Created": "2022-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "Config": {
    "Env": ["PATH=/usr/local/sbin:...", "NGINX_VERSION=1.23.3"],
    "Cmd": ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"],
    "ExposedPorts": { "80/tcp": {} },
    "WorkingDir": ""
  },
  "RootFS": {
    "Layers": [
      "sha256:ad6562704f37...",
      "sha256:3a6d0e8b2b4c...",
      "sha256:c8f1b15a9c1f..."
    ]
  }
}
```

The most practically useful fields for beginners are `ExposedPorts` (which port your container will listen on), `Env` (what environment variables are pre-configured), and `Cmd` (what command runs when you start the container).

---

## Hands-On Practice: List and Inspect an Image

```bash
# Step 1: See all images currently on your machine
docker images

# Step 2: Inspect the nginx image to find which port it exposes
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.ExposedPorts}}' nginx

# Step 3: Check the default command nginx runs on startup
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Cmd}}' nginx
```

After step 2, you should see `map[80/tcp:{}]` which tells you nginx listens on port 80. That's the port you'll need to map when you run the container.

---

## How to See an Image's Layer History

Every Docker image is built up from layers, one on top of the other, like a stack of transparent sheets. `docker history` shows you every layer, what command created it, and how much space it takes:

```bash
docker history nginx:latest
```

```
IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                                      SIZE
605c77e624dd   2 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop)  CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemoâ¦   0B
<missing>      2 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop)  STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT          0B
<missing>      2 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop)  EXPOSE 80                   0B
<missing>      2 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c apt-get install -y nginx             58.4MB
<missing>      2 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop)  ENV NGINX_VERSION=1.23.3    0B
<missing>      3 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop)  CMD ["bash"]                0B
<missing>      3 weeks ago    /bin/sh -c #(nop) ADD file:abc123... in /      80.4MB
```

A few things to notice here:

Layers showing `0B` are metadata-only, things like setting an environment variable (`ENV`) or declaring a port (`EXPOSE`). They don't add any actual files to the image, so they take up no space.

The big layers (58.4MB, 80.4MB) are where real files were added, like installing nginx, or laying down the base OS filesystem.

`<missing>` in the IMAGE ID column is completely normal. It just means the intermediate layer isn't stored as a standalone image on your machine, only the final result is kept.

---

## How to Check How Much Disk Space Docker Is Using

Docker can quietly eat up a lot of disk space over time because of old images, stopped containers, unused volumes, and build cache all accumulate. This command gives you a clear overview:

```bash
# Quick summary
docker system df

# Full breakdown with details
docker system df -v
```

```
TYPE            TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          8       3        2.1GB     1.4GB (66%)
Containers      2       1        45MB      0B (0%)
Local Volumes   3       2        512MB     156MB (30%)
Build Cache     12      0        890MB     890MB (100%)
```

The `RECLAIMABLE` column is the key one. It shows how much space you could free up by cleaning things out. In this example, 890MB of build cache can be fully reclaimed since none of it is actively in use.

---

## Key Takeaways

- `docker images` is your starting point. It lists everything stored locally with the name, tag, ID, and size.
- The SIZE column can be misleading: shared layers are counted per image but only stored once on disk, so actual usage is lower.
- `docker inspect` gives you deep metadata about an image, especially useful for finding exposed ports, environment variables, and startup commands.
- Use `--format` with `docker inspect` to extract just the field you need instead of reading through pages of JSON.
- `docker history` shows you every layer in an image and what created it. It is important to understand what's actually inside a third-party image.
- `docker system df` shows how much disk space Docker is using across images, containers, volumes, and build cache and how much is safe to clean up.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What's the difference between `docker images` and `docker image ls`?**

They do exactly the same thing. `docker image ls` is the newer, more structured syntax that Docker introduced as part of a broader command reorganization.

**Why does `CREATED` show a date from weeks ago even though I just pulled the image?**

The `CREATED` date is when the image was *built* by whoever published it, not when you downloaded it. If you pulled nginx today but the image was built two weeks ago, you'll see two weeks ago.

**What are dangling images and should I delete them?**

Dangling images are untagged layers left behind from previous builds. For example, when you rebuild an image and the old version loses its tag. They're generally safe to delete with `docker image prune`.

**Why do I see `<missing>` in `docker history` output?**

It means the intermediate layer isn't stored as a separate image on your machine, only the final image is kept locally. This is normal and doesn't indicate anything is broken.

**The sizes in `docker images` add up to way more than my actual disk usage. Why?**

Because shared layers are counted in each image's size but only stored once on disk. Two images that both use the same Alpine base will each show the Alpine layer in their size, but your disk only holds one copy of it. `docker system df` gives a more accurate picture of real disk usage.
