sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how to build a Docker image with a Dockerfile and docker build. Covers core instructions, .dockerignore and a complete Python API example.

sections.title: What Is a Dockerfile?
paragraphs: A Dockerfile is a plain text file that contains step-by-step instructions for building a Docker image. Think of it as a recipe: Docker reads it from top to bottom, follows each instruction in order, and produces a finished image at the end.

Every instruction in a Dockerfile adds a new layer to the image, like stacking transparent sheets on top of each other. This layered system is what makes Docker images so efficient to store and share.
Here's what a complete, real-world Dockerfile looks like for a Node.js app:

codeBlock.code:
# Start from an official Node.js base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the image
WORKDIR /app

# Copy the dependency file first (explained below)
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm install

# Copy the rest of your application code
COPY . .

# Tell Docker your app listens on port 3000
EXPOSE 3000

# The command that runs when someone starts a container from this image
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: The Core Dockerfile Instructions
paragraphs: Every Dockerfile must begin with FROM. It tells Docker which base image to build on top of.
Choosing the right base image matters. Alpine-based images (like node:18-alpine) are much smaller than full OS images, which means faster downloads and a smaller attack surface.
WORKDIR sets the folder that all following instructions will run inside. If the folder doesn't exist yet, Docker creates it automatically.
This is cleaner than writing cd /app && before every command, and it makes your Dockerfile easier to read.
COPY takes files from your computer (the build context) and puts them into the image. The first argument is the source on your machine, the second is the destination inside the image.
RUN runs a shell command at build time. This is how you install software, compile code, create folders, or do anything else that needs to happen before your app runs.
One important thing to know: each RUN instruction creates a new layer. To keep your image lean, combine related commands into a single RUN using &&:
ENV sets environment variables that are available both during the build and when the container is running.
These are a great way to configure your application's behavior without hardcoding values directly into your code.
ARG is similar to ENV, but the variable only exists during the build process which means it won't be available inside the running container.
Use ARG for things like version numbers or build timestamps that you want to pass in at build time but don't need at runtime.

EXPOSE tells Docker which port your application listens on. Important to understand: this is documentation only, it doesn't actually open the port. You still need to use the -p flag when running the container to make it accessible.
Think of it as leaving a note for whoever runs your image: "hey, this app expects traffic on port 3000."
CMD defines what command runs when someone starts a container from your image. It can be overridden by passing a different command to docker run.
Stick with the exec form (the one with square brackets) as it's more explicit and handles signals correctly.
ENTRYPOINT is similar to CMD but harder to override. Use it when your container should always run a specific program, no matter what.
When both ENTRYPOINT and CMD are set, CMD provides the default arguments passed to ENTRYPOINT. Someone running the container can change the arguments (CMD) but not the executable (ENTRYPOINT).

codeBlock.code:
FROM ubuntu:22.04          # Full Ubuntu operating system
FROM node:18-alpine        # Node.js on a tiny Alpine Linux base
FROM python:3.12-slim      # Python with a trimmed-down Debian base
FROM scratch               # Completely empty, for advanced use cases only

sections.title: How to Build an Image
paragraphs: Once you have a Dockerfile, building it is a single command:
The . at the end is called the build context. It is the folder that Docker looks in when processing COPY instructions. It's almost always the current directory.

codeBlock.code:
# Build from the current directory and tag it as myapp:v1.0
docker build -t myapp:v1.0 .

# Use a specific Dockerfile (useful for multiple environments)
docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t myapp:production .

# Pass in a build argument
docker build --build-arg VERSION=2.1.0 -t myapp:2.1.0 .

# Force a full rebuild, ignoring cached layers
docker build --no-cache -t myapp:latest .

# Build for a specific CPU architecture
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t myapp:amd64 .

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Build Your First Image
paragraphs: After step 1, you'll see Docker processing each instruction in your Dockerfile one by one. Each step corresponds to a layer, and if you build again without changes, Docker reuses the cached layers, making rebuilds much faster.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Build the image from the current directory and tag it
docker build -t myapp:v1.0 .

# Step 2: Confirm the image was created
docker images | grep myapp

# Step 3: Run a container from it to verify everything works
docker run myapp:v1.0

sections.title: The .dockerignore File: Don't Skip This
paragraphs: A .dockerignore file works exactly like .gitignore. It tells Docker which files and folders to exclude from the build context. This matters for two reasons: speed and security.
Without it, COPY . . could accidentally copy hundreds of megabytes of node_modules into your image, or copy your .env file containing API keys and passwords.
Create a .dockerignore file in the same directory as your Dockerfile:
Always set this up before your first real build. It's a small step that prevents a lot of headaches.

codeBlock.code:
node_modules/
.git/
.env
*.log
coverage/
dist/
.DS_Store
.vscode/
README.md

sections.title: A Complete Real-World Example: Python API
paragraphs: Here's a production-ready Dockerfile for a Python web API that demonstrates all of the best practices together:

A few things this example does that are worth noting: it installs dependencies before copying the app code (so Docker can cache the dependency layer and skip reinstalling when you only change code), and it switches to a non-root user before running the app, which is a basic but important security practice.

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Install system packages needed to compile some Python dependencies
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Copy and install Python dependencies first (cache optimization)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application source code
COPY ./src ./src

# Don't run as root - create and switch to a regular user
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Does the order of instructions in a Dockerfile matter?

Yes, a lot. Docker processes instructions top to bottom, and each one builds on the previous. Order also affects caching, if an early instruction changes, all layers after it are rebuilt. This is why you copy and install dependencies before copying your app code.
What's the difference between RUN and CMD?

RUN executes during the build. It is how you install software and set things up. CMD executes when someone runs a container from the finished image. A Dockerfile can have many RUN instructions but only one effective CMD.
What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?

CMD is the default command and can be easily overridden at runtime. ENTRYPOINT locks in the executable and if someone running the container can change the arguments but not the program itself. When in doubt, use CMD.
Why does my build take so long the first time but faster after that?

Docker caches each layer. On the first build everything is downloaded and executed fresh. On subsequent builds, Docker reuses cached layers for any instruction that hasn't changed. If you change your app code but not your dependencies, Docker skips reinstalling them entirely.
What does the . mean at the end of docker build?

It's the build context, the folder Docker sends to its build engine. All COPY paths in your Dockerfile are relative to this folder. It's almost always . (the current directory), but you can point it to any folder.
Should I use CMD in exec form or shell form?

Always use exec form: CMD ["node", "server.js"]. Shell form runs your command inside /bin/sh -c, which can cause issues with signal handling (like graceful shutdown) and behaves differently across environments.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
docker-images-building.markdown:
Docker has perhaps eight ideas in it. Most early confusion comes from three of them sounding interchangeable when they are not, image, container and Dockerfile, so this page defines each precisely and shows how they connect.

## The one-line version

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe. Building it produces an **image**, which is a read-only template. Running an image produces a **container**, which is a live process. A **registry** is where images are stored and shared.

```
Dockerfile ââdocker buildâââ¶ Image ââdocker runâââ¶ Container
                              â  â²
                    docker pushâ  âdocker pull
                              â¼  â
                            Registry
```

Everything else, volumes, networks, Compose, exists to make containers useful together.

## Image

A **read-only template** containing everything needed to run an application: the code, the language runtime, system libraries, and the metadata describing how to start it.

An image is built from **layers**, one per instruction in the Dockerfile, stacked and presented as a single filesystem. Layers are what make Docker efficient: they are content-addressed and shared, so ten images built on `node:22-alpine` store that base exactly once on disk and pull it exactly once from a registry.

```bash
docker images
```

```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
myapp        1.0       a3f2c1d4e5b6   2 hours ago    142MB
node         22-alpine 7b8c9d0e1f2a   3 days ago     135MB
```

Two consequences of the layer model worth internalising early. Layers are **immutable**, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space in the image, and is still recoverable, which is why a deleted secret is a leaked secret. And layers are **cached**, so the order of instructions in a Dockerfile largely determines how fast rebuilds are.

Go deeper: [Docker images](/tutorials/docker/docker-images) and [image layers](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-layers).

## Container

A **running instance** of an image. If the image is the recipe, the container is the meal.

Technically it is an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, process table, network stack and hostname; cgroups cap what CPU and memory it can consume. There is no virtual machine and no guest operating system. This is why a container starts in milliseconds where a VM takes a minute.

Docker adds one **thin writable layer** on top of the image's read-only layers. Every file the container creates or modifies lands there, and **it is deleted with the container**. That single fact explains most Docker surprises for newcomers: your database is empty again because its data lived in the writable layer of a container that no longer exists.

```bash
docker ps
```

```
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS         PORTS                    NAMES
9f2c1a4b7e3d   myapp:1.0   Up 4 minutes   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp   api
```

Containers are **ephemeral** by design. Treat them as disposable and keep anything that must survive in a volume.

Go deeper: [Docker containers](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers) and [the container lifecycle](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-lifecycle).

## Dockerfile

A plain text file of instructions for building an image, executed top to bottom:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
```

Each instruction produces a layer. The reason the package manifest is copied and installed *before* the source is that Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so copying source first would reinstall every dependency on every code edit.

Go deeper: [Dockerfile basics](/tutorials/docker/dockerfile-basics).

## Registry

Storage and distribution for images. GitHub, but for images rather than source. You `push` to share and `pull` to consume.

```bash
docker pull postgres:17
docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
```

**Docker Hub** is the default: if you run `docker pull nginx` with no registry prefix, that is where it comes from. Most organisations also use a private registry. GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry. For their own images.

A **tag** such as `1.0` or `latest` is a mutable pointer to an image, not a permanent name. `latest` in particular is just a default tag with no special meaning; it does not track the newest version. A **digest** (`@sha256:â¦`) is immutable and is what you pin when reproducibility matters.

Go deeper: [Docker Hub and registries](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-hub).

## Volume

Storage that outlives the container. Since the container's writable layer is destroyed with it, anything that must persist, database files, uploads, goes in a volume.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

Three kinds, and the distinction comes up constantly:

| Type | Written as | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Named volume** | `-v pgdata:/var/lib/â¦` | Docker manages it; the default for data |
| **Bind mount** | `-v ./src:/app/src` | A host directory; the default for development |
| **tmpfs** | `--tmpfs /tmp` | Memory only; never touches disk |

Go deeper: [Docker volumes](/tutorials/docker/docker-volumes).

## Network

Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other **by container name**, which is Docker's built-in DNS at work:

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapp:1.0
```

The API connects to `db:5432`. No IP addresses, no `--link`, nothing to update when a container restarts with a different address.

Note that `localhost` inside a container means *that container*, not the host and not another container. Expecting `localhost:5432` to reach a database in a different container is one of the most common beginner errors.

Go deeper: [container networking](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-networking).

## Docker Compose

Real applications are several containers. Compose describes them in one file so the whole stack starts together:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down
```

Compose creates a network automatically, which is why `db` resolves as a hostname without any extra configuration.

It is a **single-host** tool. Excellent for development and small deployments, not a replacement for an orchestrator. Once you need scheduling across machines, rolling updates and self-healing, that is [Kubernetes](/tutorials/kubernetes/introduction-to-kubernetes).

## Client and daemon

One more piece, because it explains a whole class of error messages.

The `docker` command is a **client**. It does almost nothing itself. It sends requests over a socket to the **daemon** (`dockerd`), which builds images, runs containers and manages storage.

```
docker CLI ââ/var/run/docker.sockâââ¶ dockerd âââ¶ containerd âââ¶ runc âââ¶ your process
```

So `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon` means the CLI is installed and working, and nothing is listening. Start the service. And `permission denied ... docker.sock` means the daemon is running but your user cannot talk to its socket.

It also explains why the build context is *sent* to the daemon: the daemon may not be on your machine at all.

## The vocabulary, condensed

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Image** | Read-only template built from layers |
| **Layer** | One filesystem diff, produced by one instruction |
| **Container** | A running instance, plus a thin writable layer |
| **Dockerfile** | Build instructions for an image |
| **Build context** | The directory sent to the daemon at build time |
| **Registry** | Where images are stored and shared |
| **Tag** | A mutable pointer to an image |
| **Digest** | An immutable content hash |
| **Volume** | Storage that outlives the container |
| **Bind mount** | A host directory mounted into a container |
| **Network** | Container-to-container connectivity with DNS |
| **Compose** | Multi-container definition for one host |
| **Daemon** | `dockerd`, the process doing the work |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Image is the template, container is the running instance.** Recipe and meal.
- **A container's writable layer dies with it.** Anything that must survive belongs in a volume.
- **Layers are immutable and cached**: which sets both your rebuild speed and why deleted files still ship.
- **Containers are processes, not virtual machines.** Namespaces isolate, cgroups limit.
- **`latest` is just a default tag**, not the newest version. Pin a digest when it matters.
- **Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name**, and `localhost` means that container alone.
- **The CLI only talks to the daemon**, which is why "cannot connect" is a different problem from "not installed".

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-concepts-writable-layer',
    title: 'A database that keeps forgetting',
    description: 'A Postgres container is started with docker run, data is written, then the container is removed and recreated from the same image. The data is gone. Which concept explains this?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Writes go to the container\'s thin writable layer, which is deleted with the container. Persistence requires a volume' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'The image was rebuilt between runs, so the previous data was overwritten' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Postgres containers require --restart always to keep their data' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'Data written by a container is stored in the image and needs docker commit to be saved' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'An image is read-only. Docker gives each container a thin writable layer on top, and every file the container creates or changes lands there, including the entire Postgres data directory. Removing the container removes that layer and everything in it. Mounting a named volume at the data path, such as -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data, keeps the files under Docker\'s management so a new container from the same image picks up exactly where the last one left off.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'No rebuild happened, and rebuilding an image would not touch a running container\'s data anyway.',
      c: '--restart controls whether Docker restarts a container automatically. It has no bearing on storage.',
      d: 'docker commit does snapshot a container into a new image, but treating that as a persistence mechanism is an anti-pattern. Data belongs in a volume, not baked into images.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?**

An image is a read-only template: the application, its runtime, its libraries and the metadata describing how to start it, stored as a stack of layers. A container is a running instance created from that image, with a thin writable layer on top for anything it changes. One image can back any number of containers simultaneously, each with its own writable layer, in the same way one class can have many instances. The practical consequence is that images persist and containers are disposable.

**Where does data written inside a container go?**

Into the container's writable layer, which exists only as long as the container does. Remove the container and every file it created is removed with it, which is why a database restarted from the same image comes back empty. Mount a named volume at the path that matters (`-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) and the data lives outside the container lifecycle. Bind mounts do the same thing with a specific host directory, which is what you usually want in development.

**What is a Docker layer and why does it matter?**

Each Dockerfile instruction produces one layer, a filesystem diff, and the image is those layers stacked into a single view. They matter for three reasons. They are shared, so images built on the same base store and transfer it once. They are cached, so ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing makes rebuilds dramatically faster. And they are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space and remains extractable from the image.

**What is a Docker registry and is Docker Hub the only one?**

A registry stores and distributes images, the way a Git host stores repositories. Docker Hub is the default, `docker pull nginx` with no prefix goes there, and hosts official images for most common software. It is not the only option, and most organisations push their own images to a private registry such as GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry or Azure Container Registry. Prefixing the image name with a hostname selects one: `ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0`.

**Do I need Docker Compose or Kubernetes?**

Compose if you are running several containers on one machine. A local development stack, a small single-server deployment. It defines services, networks and volumes in one file and starts them together, and it is the right tool most of the time. Kubernetes when you need containers scheduled across multiple machines with rolling updates, self-healing and autoscaling. They solve different problems, and starting with Compose costs nothing if you later move: the concepts transfer directly.

**Why can't my container reach another container on localhost?**

Because `localhost` inside a container refers to that container and nothing else. Each one has its own network namespace and its own loopback interface. Put both on the same user-defined network and use the container name as the hostname: `docker network create appnet`, start each with `--network appnet`, then connect to `db:5432`. Compose does this for you automatically, which is why service names work as hostnames there without any configuration.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: See how Docker image layers and the build cache work, why Dockerfile order matters, and how to speed up docker build by avoiding unneeded cache misses.

sections.title: What Are Docker Image Layers?
paragraphs: A Docker image isn't a single big file. It's a stack of thin, read-only snapshots called layers. There is one layer attached to for each instruction in your Dockerfile that makes a change to the filesystem.
Here's a simple Node.js Dockerfile with each layer labeled:
Visually, the final image looks like this:
Docker Image Layers (top = newest)
Image layers are read-only and shared between containers

Each layer only stores the difference from the layer below it, similar to how Git commits work. This means if two different images use node:18-alpine as their base, that base layer is stored only once on your disk and shared between them.

When you run a container, Docker adds one extra thin writable layer on top of the stack. The image layers underneath stay read-only and untouched, which is why multiple containers can run from the same image without interfering with each other.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:18-alpine      # Layer 1: base OS + Node runtime (~127MB)
WORKDIR /app             # Layer 2: metadata only, takes up 0 bytes
COPY package*.json ./    # Layer 3: adds package.json (~2KB)
RUN npm install          # Layer 4: adds node_modules (~40MB)
COPY . .                 # Layer 5: adds your source code (~100KB)
CMD ["node", "app.js"]   # Layer 6: metadata only, takes up 0 bytes

sections.title: How Docker's Build Cache Works
paragraphs: After Docker builds a layer, it caches it. The next time you build, Docker checks each instruction from top to bottom. If nothing has changed in that instruction or the files it touches, Docker skips re-executing it and uses the cached version instead. This is what makes rebuilds so much faster:

There's one critical rule about how cache invalidation works: when a layer is invalidated, every layer that comes after it is also rebuilt, even if those later instructions didn't change. This is the key insight that shapes how you should order your Dockerfile.

codeBlock.code:
First build (nothing cached):
FROM node:18-alpine     ✓ downloaded fresh
WORKDIR /app            ✓ created
COPY package*.json ./   ✓ copied
RUN npm install         ✓ installed, let's say it took 30 seconds
COPY . .                ✓ copied
→ Total: ~35 seconds

Second build (only your app code changed):
FROM node:18-alpine     ✓ CACHED (skipped)
WORKDIR /app            ✓ CACHED (skipped)
COPY package*.json ./   ✓ CACHED (skipped)
RUN npm install         ✓ CACHED (skipped), saves 30 seconds
COPY . .                ✗ REBUILT (source code changed)
→ Total: ~2 seconds

sections.title: Order of Dockerfile Matters
paragraphs: Put instructions that change rarely near the top. Put instructions that change often near the bottom.
The most common mistake beginners make is this:

The problem here: COPY . . copies your source code along with package.json. Every time you change even one line of code, that COPY layer is invalidated, and since RUN npm install comes after it, npm has to reinstall everything from scratch in every single build.
Now npm install is cached as long as package.json and package-lock.json stay the same. Changing your app code only rebuilds the last COPY layer. A 35-second build becomes a 2-second build.
Note: This isn't a Node.js-specific trick; it applies everywhere. The pattern is always the same: copy the dependency file first, install, then copy your source code.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .               # Copies everything, including your source code
RUN npm install        # Invalidated every time ANY file changes
CMD ["node", "app.js"]

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Watch the Cache in Action
paragraphs: The best way to understand caching is to see it yourself:

On the second build, you'll see Using cache next to every step. On the third build after a code change, you'll see Using cache for the dependency steps but REBUILT for the source code step. That's the cache doing exactly what it should.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Build the image for the first time (everything runs fresh)
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .

# Step 2: Build again without changing anything
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .

# Step 3: Make a small change to your app code, then build again
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .

sections.title: When You Need to Skip the Cache
paragraphs: Sometimes you want Docker to ignore the cache, for example, to pick up the latest security patches from apt even though the instruction string hasn't changed:
If you only want to bust the cache from a specific point forward (without rebuilding everything), you can use a build argument as a cache-busting trick:

codeBlock.code:
# Force a completely fresh build (no cached layers)
docker build --no-cache -t myapp:latest .

sections.title: Cleaning Up the Build Cache
paragraphs: The build cache can quietly grow to gigabytes over time. Here's how to manage it:
docker system df is a good habit to run occasionally. It gives you a quick overview of how much space images, containers, volumes, and build cache are each taking up.

codeBlock.code:
# See how much space the cache is using
docker system df

# Remove build cache that's no longer needed
docker builder prune

# Remove all build cache, including layers still referenced by images
docker builder prune -a

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does Docker rebuild everything after I change one file?

Because you're probably copying all your files (including source code) before installing dependencies. When COPY . . comes before RUN npm install, any file change invalidates the install layer. Fix it by copying your dependency manifest first, installing, then copying the rest of your code.
How does Docker know if a layer has changed?

For COPY and ADD instructions, Docker compares the actual file contents, not just timestamps. For RUN instructions, Docker compares the instruction string itself. If the string is identical, Docker assumes the result is the same and uses the cache.
Does the cache work across different machines?

Not by default. The local build cache lives only on your machine. In CI/CD pipelines you can use cache backends (like storing layers in a registry) to share cache across machines, but that's an advanced topic.
Why do some layers show 0B in docker history?
Those are metadata-only instructions like WORKDIR, ENV, EXPOSE, and CMD. They don't add or modify any files in the image, so they take up no space, but they still create a layer.
When should I use --no-cache?

Use it when you need to pull in external updates that Docker can't detect, most commonly when running apt-get update or pip install to get the latest security patches. Since the instruction string hasn't changed, Docker would normally use the cache and miss the new patches.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
docker-images-layers.markdown:
An image is a read-only template containing a filesystem and the metadata needed to run it. Containers are created from images; images are built from Dockerfiles or pulled from registries.

Nearly everything worth knowing about images comes down to **layers**.

## Layers

Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. A set of filesystem changes stacked on the one before. The final image is those layers combined and presented as one filesystem.

```bash
docker history nginx:1.27
```

```
IMAGE          CREATED BY                                      SIZE
a1b2c3d4e5f6   CMD ["nginx" "-g" "daemon off;"]                0B
<missing>      EXPOSE map[80/tcp:{}]                           0B
<missing>      COPY docker-entrypoint.sh / # buildkit          1.62kB
<missing>      RUN /bin/sh -c apt-get update && apt-get insâ¦   61.2MB
<missing>      ADD file:4f4fb700ef54461cfâ¦ in /                 80.5MB
```

`docker history` is the first command to reach for on any size problem. It shows exactly which instruction added the weight, which is rarely the one people expect.

Three properties follow, and between them they explain most image behaviour.

### Layers are shared

Ten images built on the same base store that base **once**. This is why `docker images` can list ten images at 200 MB each while `docker system df` reports far less total disk:

```bash
docker system df
```

```
TYPE          TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images        14      5        4.2GB     2.8GB (66%)
```

### Layers are cached

A rebuild reuses every layer up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. **Instruction order therefore determines build speed:**

```dockerfile
# Dependencies change rarely. Install them first
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Source changes constantly. Copy it last
COPY . .
```

Reversing those two blocks means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile performance mistake and costs minutes on each build.

### Layers are additive: deleting does not shrink

A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is **still in the image**. The later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding it; the bytes remain in the earlier layer and still ship.

```dockerfile
# Wrong. The archive is in the image forever
RUN curl -O https://example.com/big.tar.gz
RUN tar -xzf big.tar.gz && rm big.tar.gz

# Right. One layer, nothing left behind
RUN curl -O https://example.com/big.tar.gz \
 && tar -xzf big.tar.gz \
 && rm big.tar.gz
```

This catches nearly everyone once, usually with `apt-get` caches:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

## Tags and digests

A tag is a **mutable pointer**. `nginx:1.27` today and `nginx:1.27` next month can be different images, because the maintainer can repoint it.

```bash
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # mutable
docker pull nginx@sha256:a1b2c3...     # immutable content hash
```

For reproducible builds, and anything security-sensitive, pin the digest.

At minimum, **never deploy `latest`**. It is not special, just the default tag name, and it means your deployment depends on whatever was most recently pushed. Two deploys of "latest" can run different code, and a rollback has nothing specific to return to.

Tagging adds a name to an existing image rather than copying it:

```bash
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/myapp:stable
```

Both names now point at one image ID.

## Reducing image size

Size affects pull time, registry storage, and cold start on every platform that schedules containers. Three techniques, in order of impact.

**Choose a smaller base.** `node:22` is roughly 1.1 GB; `node:22-alpine` around 150 MB; distroless smaller still. Alpine uses musl rather than glibc, which occasionally breaks native modules. Test rather than assume.

**Use a multi-stage build**, so build tooling never reaches the final image:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a `scratch` image is a few megabytes.

**Add a `.dockerignore`.** Without one, `COPY . .` sends `node_modules`, `.git` and every local artifact into the build context and often into the image:

```
node_modules
.git
.env
dist
*.log
```

This speeds builds too, since the context is uploaded to the daemon before the build starts.

## Dangling images and reclaiming disk

```bash
docker images
```

```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       SIZE
myapp        1.4.2     a1b2c3d4e5f6   142MB
<none>       <none>    f6e5d4c3b2a1   140MB
```

That `<none>` entry is a **dangling image**. The previous build of `myapp`, orphaned when the tag moved to the newer image. It still occupies disk.

Rebuilding the same tag repeatedly produces one every time, which is why disk usage climbs steadily during development and why Docker eventually reports **no space left on device**.

```bash
docker image prune        # dangling only. Safe to run routinely
docker image prune -a     # every image not used by a container
docker system df          # see what is reclaimable first
```

One thing `prune` does **not** touch: **container logs**. A long-running container using the default `json-file` driver with no rotation can write tens of gigabytes to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log`. If `docker system prune` frees less than expected, that is usually where the space went:

```json
{ "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" } }
```

Put that in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restart Docker to cap it.

## Registries

```bash
docker login registry.example.com
docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker pull registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
```

Docker Hub is the default, so `nginx` means `docker.io/library/nginx`. Any other registry must be named explicitly.

Two practical notes. **Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls**, which a busy CI pipeline hits quickly. Authenticate, or mirror base images into your own registry. And a push only transfers layers the registry does not already hold, so pushing a rebuilt image is usually fast.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| List images | `docker images` |
| Pull | `docker pull <image>:<tag>` |
| Build | `docker build -t <name>:<tag> .` |
| Tag | `docker tag <source> <target>` |
| Push | `docker push <registry>/<name>:<tag>` |
| Layer sizes | `docker history <image>` |
| Full metadata | `docker inspect <image>` |
| Remove one | `docker rmi <image>` |
| Remove dangling | `docker image prune` |
| Remove all unused | `docker image prune -a` |
| Disk usage | `docker system df` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Each Dockerfile instruction is a layer**, and layers are shared, cached and additive.
- **Copy dependency manifests before source code** so the install layer stays cached.
- **Deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image**: clean up inside the same `RUN`.
- **Tags are mutable; digests are not.** Never deploy `latest`.
- **Multi-stage builds keep compilers and dev dependencies out of the shipped image.**
- **`<none>` images are dangling**: previous builds of a retagged image. `docker image prune` clears them.
- **`docker system prune` does not touch container logs.** Cap them with `max-size` in `daemon.json`.
- **Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls.** Authenticate or mirror in CI.

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-img-layer-delete',
    title: 'An image that will not shrink',
    description: 'A Dockerfile downloads a 500 MB archive in one RUN and deletes it in the next. The image is still 500 MB larger than expected. Why?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Layers are additive. The file remains in the earlier layer and is only hidden by the later one, so it still ships' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'The rm command needs the -f flag to actually remove the file' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Docker caches deleted files for 24 hours before reclaiming the space' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'The archive is counted twice because it was downloaded and then extracted' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'Each instruction commits a layer recording changes relative to the previous one, and every layer ships with the image. A deletion in a later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding the file rather than removing its bytes from the earlier layer. Download, extract and delete must happen in a single RUN chained with &&, so only the net result is ever committed.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'The file is genuinely deleted from the running container filesystem. The problem is that the earlier layer still contains it.',
      c: 'There is no deferred reclamation. Layer contents are immutable once committed.',
      d: 'The extracted contents do add their own size, but the question is specifically about the archive persisting after deletion.',
    },
  }}
/>

  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-img-prune-logs',

      { id: 'a', text: 'Container logs. Prune does not touch them, and an unrotated json-file log can reach tens of gigabytes' },

With the default json-file driver and no rotation configured, a chatty long-running container writes unbounded output to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log. Check the size of that directory, and set max-size and max-file in /etc/docker/daemon.json to cap it.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'Pruned objects are deleted immediately with no recovery period.',

    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?**

An image is a read-only template made of stacked filesystem layers; a container is a running instance created from it with its own thin writable layer. One image can produce any number of containers, all sharing the same underlying layers, which is why running ten containers from one image consumes very little extra disk. Images are built and pulled; containers are run, stopped and removed.

**How do I reduce my Docker image size?**

Three things, in order of impact. Switch to a smaller base, `node:22-alpine` is around 150 MB against roughly 1.1 GB for `node:22`. Use a multi-stage build so compilers and development dependencies stay in the build stage and never ship. Add a `.dockerignore` so `node_modules`, `.git` and local artifacts are not copied in. Then run `docker history` to see which instruction is actually adding the weight, because it is often not the one you would guess.

**Why doesn't deleting files reduce my Docker image size?**

Because layers are additive and all of them ship together. A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is hidden by a whiteout marker, but its bytes remain in the earlier layer and are still part of the image. Anything downloaded and then deleted must be handled within a **single** `RUN` instruction chained with `&&`, so only the net result is committed. The same applies to package manager caches. Clean them in the same `RUN` that installed the packages.

**What are dangling images and is it safe to delete them?**

They are the `<none>` entries in `docker images`. Previous builds whose tag was reassigned to a newer image, leaving them unreferenced. They are entirely safe to remove, and `docker image prune` does exactly that. They accumulate quickly during development because every rebuild of the same tag creates one, which is the usual reason disk usage climbs steadily and eventually produces "no space left on device".

**Why did docker system prune not free much disk space?**

Almost certainly container logs, which prune never touches. With the default `json-file` log driver and no rotation, a long-running container can write tens of gigabytes to `/var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log`. Check that directory's size directly. Fix it by setting `"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}` in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` and restarting Docker. Named volumes are the other common culprit, since they are only removed with `--volumes`.

**Should I use the `latest` tag?**

No. `latest` is not special. It is simply the default tag name, pointing at whatever the maintainer most recently pushed, which can change without warning. Deploying it means two deploys of the same nominal version can run different code, and a rollback has no specific artifact to return to. Pin an explicit version tag, and for anything security-sensitive pin the digest with `image@sha256:...`, which is a content hash and genuinely immutable.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Shrink your Docker image with multi-stage builds. See how COPY --from works, follow real examples, and target a single stage with docker build --target.

sections.title: Why Single-Stage Builds Are a Problem
paragraphs: Here's what a typical single-stage Node.js Dockerfile looks like:
It works, but the resulting image carries a lot of unnecessary weight:
End result: a ~700MB image that's slow to push and pull, and has a much larger attack surface than it needs.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:18
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: What Multi-Stage Builds Do
paragraphs: A multi-stage build lets you use multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a new stage. When Docker builds the final image, it only includes the last stage, and earlier stages exist purely to produce files that get copied forward.
Here's the same Node.js app rewritten with two stages:
End result: a ~180MB image with no compiler, no dev dependencies, no source code. That one change cuts the image size by 75%.

codeBlock.code:
# ── Stage 1: Build ─────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install                       # Install everything, including dev deps
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                     # Compile TypeScript → /app/dist

# ── Stage 2: Production ────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --omit=dev            # Production dependencies only
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist  # Grab only the compiled output
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: How COPY --from Works
paragraphs: The line COPY --from=builder is the magic that makes this possible. It copies files from an earlier stage (identified by its AS name) into the current stage, like picking exactly what you want to keep and leaving the rest behind.
Always name your stages with AS, it makes your Dockerfile much easier to read and maintain.

codeBlock.code:
# Copy from a named stage in your Dockerfile
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

# Copy from an external image directly (no build needed)
COPY --from=nginx:alpine /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# Copy using a stage number instead of a name (works, but harder to read)
COPY --from=0 /app/dist ./dist

sections.title: Real-World Examples
paragraphs: For a React app, the build stage runs Node.js and npm to produce static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files. The production stage just needs a web server to serve them:
The production image contains nginx and your static files which means no Node.js, no npm, no TypeScript, no source code.
Some Python packages (like numpy or Pillow) need compilers to install from source. You can pre-build them in a stage that has the build tools, then install the finished packages in a clean stage:

codeBlock.code:
# Stage 1: Build the React app
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                            # Outputs to /app/dist

# Stage 2: Serve the static files with nginx
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Build a Multi-Stage Image
paragraphs: Multi-stage builds use the exact same docker build command you already know as Docker handles the stages automatically:
During the build you'll see each stage labeled in the output (e.g. [builder 1/5], [stage-2 1/3]). Only the final stage ends up in your tagged image, and the builder stage is discarded automatically.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Build the multi-stage image
docker build -t myapp:slim .

# Step 2: Compare the size to a single-stage build
docker images | grep myapp

sections.title: Targeting a Specific Stage
paragraphs: You can stop the build at any named stage using --target. This is especially useful in CI/CD pipelines where you want to run tests before building the production image:
This way your CI pipeline can fail fast if tests don't pass, without wasting time on the full production build.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:18-alpine AS deps
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install

FROM deps AS test
COPY . .
RUN npm test

FROM deps AS builder
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:18-alpine AS production
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: When Should You Use Multi-Stage Builds?
paragraphs: A good rule of thumb: if your build process requires tools that your running app doesn't need, multi-stage builds are worth it. That covers most real-world projects.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do multi-stage builds make the build slower?

The total build time may be slightly longer because Docker runs more steps. But the resulting image is much smaller, which means faster pushes to your registry, faster pulls on your servers, and faster deployments overall. The tradeoff is almost always worth it.
Does --target skip earlier stages?
No, Docker still processes all stages up to the target in order, because later stages may depend on earlier ones. It just stops after the stage you specified instead of continuing to the end.
Can I have more than two stages?
Absolutely. You can have as many stages as you need. A typical setup might have separate stages for dependencies, testing, building, and production. Each stage can copy from any previous stage.
What happens to the intermediate build stages?

They're used during the build and then discarded. They don't become part of the final image. Docker may keep them in its build cache to speed up future builds, but they won't show up in docker images.
Can I copy files from an external image, not just my own stages?

Yes. COPY --from=nginx:alpine /etc/nginx/nginx.conf . pulls a file directly from the official nginx image without you needing to build it yourself. This is useful for grabbing configuration files or binaries from well-known images.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

## Tagging Images

A tag is just a label that points to an image. The same image can have multiple tags, which is useful for marking the same build as `v1.0`, `latest`, and `production` all at once without duplicating any data.

```bash
# Add a new tag to an existing image
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:latest

# Tag the same image for different environments
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:production
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:staging

# Tag it for a private registry before pushing
docker tag myapp:v1.0 registry.company.com/myteam/myapp:v1.0

# Tag with the Git commit SHA for full traceability
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:sha-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
```

Tagging never copies data, every tag pointing to the same image ID shares the exact same layers on disk. It's just an alias.

---

## Removing Images

When you're done with an image, `docker rmi` removes it:

```bash
# Remove by name and tag
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Remove by image ID (you only need enough characters to make it unique)
docker rmi 605c77

# Remove multiple images in one go
docker rmi nginx:1.24 nginx:1.25 postgres:15

# Force removal even if a stopped container still references it
docker rmi -f myapp:old

# Remove all images (use with caution)
docker rmi $(docker images -q)
```

**Note:** Docker won't remove an image if any container  is stopped. You'll need to remove the container first with `docker rm <container-id>`, or use the `-f` flag to force it.

---

## Cleaning Up Unused Images

As you rebuild images over time, old versions lose their tags but the layers stick around on disk. These tagless leftovers are called **dangling images** and they serve no purpose, they're just taking up space.

```bash
# Remove only dangling (untagged) images
docker image prune

# Remove all images not currently used by any container
docker image prune -a

# Skip the confirmation prompt
docker image prune -f

# Remove images that haven't been used in the last 24 hours
docker image prune -a --filter "until=24h"
```
---

## Pushing Images to a Registry

Once your image is ready, you push it to a registry so other machines like your server, your teammates, your CI pipeline, can pull it down.

**Docker Hub:**
```bash
# Log in with your Docker Hub account
docker login

# Tag the image with your Docker Hub username
docker tag myapp:v1.0 yourusername/myapp:v1.0

# Push it
docker push yourusername/myapp:v1.0
```

**A Private Registry:**
```bash
# Log in to your company's registry
docker login registry.company.com

# Tag the image for that registry
docker tag myapp:v1.0 registry.company.com/team/myapp:v1.0

# Push it
docker push registry.company.com/team/myapp:v1.0
```

The process is the same everywhere: log in, tag the image with the registry address, push. The registry address at the front of the tag is how Docker knows where to send it.

---

## Saving Images as Files

Sometimes you need to move an image without using a registry across a network with no internet access, as a backup, or to share directly with someone.

**Save an image to a file:**
```bash
# Export to a tar archive
docker save nginx:latest > nginx.tar

# Save compressed to reduce file size
docker save nginx:latest | gzip > nginx.tar.gz

# Save multiple images into one archive
docker save nginx:latest postgres:16 alpine:3.18 > images.tar
```

**Load it back on another machine:**
```bash
# Load from a tar file
docker load < nginx.tar

# Load a compressed archive
gunzip -c nginx.tar.gz | docker load

# Alternative syntax if piping feels awkward
docker load --input nginx.tar
```

After loading, the image shows up in `docker images` with its original name and tag, no re-tagging needed.

---

## Hands-On Practice: Tag, Save, and Remove

```bash
# Step 1: Tag the nginx image as webserver:backup
docker tag nginx webserver:backup

# Step 2: Save it to a tar file
docker save webserver:backup > webserver.tar

# Step 3: Remove the original nginx image
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Step 4: Confirm nginx is gone but webserver:backup still exists
docker images
```

After step 3, `nginx:latest` will be gone but `webserver:backup` which points to the same image data, will still be there. And you'll have a `webserver.tar` file you could move to another machine.

---

## save/load vs export/import What's the Difference?

Docker has two pairs of commands that look similar but do very different things:

`docker save` / `docker load` works with **images**: it preserves every layer, all the metadata, environment variables, and the full layer history. This is what you should use almost always.

`docker export` / `docker import` works with a **running or stopped container's filesystem**: it flattens everything into a single layer and discards all history and metadata.

```bash
# Export a container's filesystem (flattened, loses history)
docker export my-container > container-fs.tar

# Import as a new image
docker import container-fs.tar myimage:imported
```

Unless you specifically want to flatten an image's layers, stick with `save` and `load`.

---

## Full Cleanup: Starting Fresh

When your disk is getting full and you want to wipe the slate clean:

```bash
# Remove all stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove all unused images
docker image prune -a

# Remove unused volumes
docker volume prune

# Remove unused networks
docker network prune

# Do all of the above in one command
docker system prune -a --volumes
```

The last command removes everything Docker isn't actively using. Run `docker system df` first to understand what you're about to delete, and make sure anything you want to keep is either running or pushed to a registry.

---

## Key Takeaways

- `docker tag` creates a new label pointing to an existing image, and no data is copied.
- `docker rmi` removes images. If a container (even stopped) still references it, remove the container first or use `-f`.
- Run `docker system df` before pruning to see how much space you'll actually reclaim.
- `docker push` sends your image to a registry. Always tag it with the registry address first.
- `docker save` / `docker load` transfers images as files, useful when you don't have registry access.
- `docker system prune -a --volumes` removes everything unused. It's powerful and destructive.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**If I remove a tag, does it delete the image?**

Only if it was the last tag pointing to that image. If the same image has multiple tags (`latest`, `v1.0`, `production`), removing one tag just removes that label, the image and its layers stay on disk until all tags pointing to it are removed.

**Why can't I remove an image that I'm not using?**

A stopped container still holds a reference to the image it was created from. Run `docker ps -a` to see stopped containers, remove them with `docker rm <id>`, and then try removing the image again.

**What's the difference between `docker image prune` and `docker image prune -a`?**

Without `-a`, it only removes dangling images, untagged leftovers from old builds. With `-a`, it removes any image not currently used by a running or stopped container. The `-a` version reclaims much more space but is more aggressive.

**Do I need to be logged in to push to Docker Hub?**

Yes. Run `docker login` first. For CI/CD pipelines, use a personal access token instead of your password as it's more secure and can be revoked independently.

**Is `docker save` the same as making a backup?**

It's a portable snapshot of your image that can be moved between machines without a registry. It's a reasonable backup approach for small setups, but for production workflows a registry (even a self-hosted one) is much more manageable at scale.

docker-images-optimization.subtitle: Reduce Docker image size with slim base images, merged RUN layers, a .dockerignore file and non-root users. Eight practical steps with examples.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing Optimization must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Docker documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Docker in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Reduce Docker image size with slim base images, merged RUN layers, a .dockerignore file and non-root users. Eight practical steps with examples.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Docker.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Reduce Docker image size with slim base images, merged RUN layers, a .dockerignore file and non-root users. Eight practical steps with examples.

sections.title: 1. Choose the Right Base Image
paragraphs: Your base image has the single biggest impact on final image size. Most people just grab node:20 or python:3.12 without realizing there are much leaner alternatives:

Alpine Linux is the most popular minimal base. At roughly 5MB, it's tiny, but it uses a different C library (musl libc instead of glibc), which occasionally causes compatibility issues with some pre-compiled software. It's worth testing before committing to Alpine for complex applications.
That one-line change can save nearly a gigabyte.

codeBlock.code:
# Before
FROM node:20         # ~1.1GB

# After
FROM node:20-alpine  # ~135MB

sections.title: 2. Combine Related RUN Commands
paragraphs: Every RUN instruction creates a new layer. If you install packages in one layer and delete the cache in a separate layer, the cache files still exist in the earlier layer, they're just hidden. The image size doesn't shrink. Therfore, it's a best practice to combine the RUN statement like:
The --no-install-recommends flag is worth adding too. It tells apt to skip suggested packages that aren't strictly required, which can save a surprising amount of space.

codeBlock.code:
# Install and clean up in one layer, nothing left behind
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl git && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: 3. Set Up a .dockerignore File
paragraphs: Before Docker builds your image, it sends your project folder to the build engine. If that folder contains node_modules, build artifacts, or your .env file, all of that gets included, even if your Dockerfile never explicitly copies it. A .dockerignore file works exactly like .gitignore and prevents this. Create one in the same directory as your Dockerfile:
Without this file, the build context could be hundreds of megabytes. With it, it often drops to just a few kilobytes. It also prevents secrets from accidentally leaking into your image.

codeBlock.code:
node_modules/
.git/
.env
__pycache__/
tests/

sections.title: 4. Don't Install Tools You Don't Need at Runtime
paragraphs: Every package you add increases image size and introduces more potential vulnerabilities, so try not to include this.
If you need to debug a running container, you can install tools temporarily with docker exec without it affecting the image itself:

codeBlock.code:
# Install only what the app actually needs to run
RUN apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5

sections.title: 5. Clean Up in the Same Layer
paragraphs: If you need build tools to compile something (like gcc for a Python package with native extensions), install them, use them, and remove them all in the same RUN instruction:
If you remove tools in a separate RUN, the files are hidden from the final image but still physically present in an earlier layer, which means they still take up space.

codeBlock.code:
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc python3-dev && \
    pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && \
    apt-get purge -y --auto-remove gcc python3-dev && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: 6. Pin Package Versions
paragraphs: Installing packages without specifying a version means your image might build differently tomorrow than it does today. That's a debugging nightmare in production.
For production images especially, pinning versions ensures your builds are reproducible and you're always aware of exactly what's in your image.

codeBlock.code:
# Always installs this exact version
RUN apt-get install -y curl=7.88.1-10+deb12u5

sections.title: 7. Never Run as Root
paragraphs: By default, containers run as the root user. This is a real security risk, if an attacker finds a vulnerability in your application, running as root gives them far more power than they should have.
Always create a dedicated non-root user and switch to it before the final CMD:

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .

# Create a non-root user and group
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

# Give the user ownership of the app directory
RUN chown -R appuser:appgroup /app

# Switch to the non-root user
USER appuser

CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: 8. Use COPY Instead of ADD
paragraphs: ADD and COPY both bring files into your image, but ADD has extra hidden behaviors as it automatically extracts .tar.gz archives and can even download files from URLs. These implicit behaviors are easy to misuse.
Unless you specifically need those features, always use COPY. It does exactly one thing and does it predictably:

codeBlock.code:
# Don't use this
ADD ./archive.tar.gz /app/          # Auto-extracts the archive
ADD https://example.com/file /app/  # Downloads from a URL

# Better Option
COPY ./archive.tar.gz /app/         # Copies the file as-is

sections.title: 9. Use Multi-Stage Builds
paragraphs: If your application has a build step, like compiling TypeScript, building a React app, compiling a Go binary then multi-stage builds are by far the biggest size optimization available to you.

The idea is simple: use a fully-equipped build stage to produce your artifacts, then copy only those artifacts into a clean, minimal final stage. The build tools never make it into the production image.
For a full walkthrough of multi-stage builds, see the Multi-Stage Builds page.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci && npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: 10. Scan Your Images for Vulnerabilities
paragraphs: Even a well-optimized image built from an official base can contain known security vulnerabilities (CVEs) in its packages. Make scanning part of your routine:
The best time to catch vulnerabilities is before they reach production. Add a scan step to your CI pipeline so every image gets checked automatically before it's deployed.

codeBlock.code:
# Docker Scout: built into Docker Desktop and Docker Hub
docker scout cves myapp:latest

# Trivy: popular open source scanner, very fast
trivy image myapp:latest

# Grype: another solid open source option
grype myapp:latest

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do I need to apply all of these techniques to every image?

No, prioritize based on impact. The biggest wins in order are: choosing a smaller base image, using multi-stage builds (if you have a build step), setting up .dockerignore, and combining RUN commands. The others are good habits worth building over time.
Is Alpine always the best base image choice?

It's usually the smallest option, but not always the right one. Some packages behave differently under Alpine's musl libc vs the standard glibc. If you run into strange errors with an Alpine-based image, try the -slim variant instead as it is a Debian-based and much more compatible, while still being significantly smaller than the full image.
My image is still large after switching to Alpine. Why?

The base image is just the starting point. If you're copying in node_modules or running apt-get install without cleaning up, those layers add to the total size regardless of the base. Check your layer sizes with docker history myimage to see where the bulk is coming from.
How often should I scan my images?

At minimum, scan every time you build a new image in CI before deploying. For long-running production images, set up a scheduled scan (weekly is common) since new CVEs are discovered constantly even if your image hasn't changed.
Is it safe to use scratch as a base image?

For statically compiled binaries like Go or Rust programs, yes, scratch is an empty image with nothing in it at all, which is as minimal as it gets. But it means no shell, no package manager, and no OS utilities, so debugging becomes much harder. It's best suited for simple, self-contained services in well-understood production environments.

quickReference.command: docker exec -it my-container sh -c "apk add --no-cache curl"


```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27   # create + start
docker stop web                       # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s
docker start web                      # start it again. Same container
docker rm web                         # delete it
```

The distinction that matters: **`docker run` creates a new container every time.** `docker start` restarts an existing one. Running the same command three times gives three containers, which is why `docker ps -a` fills up unexpectedly.

```bash
docker ps        # running only
docker ps -a     # including exited
```

## Why your container exits immediately

The most common Docker frustration, and it has one root cause.

**A container lives exactly as long as its main process.** When PID 1 exits, the container exits. There is no background mode that keeps it alive.

```bash
docker run ubuntu           # exits instantly
docker run ubuntu bash      # also exits, no TTY, bash has no input and quits
docker run -it ubuntu bash  # stays running. Interactive terminal attached
```

The same applies to your own images. A web server that daemonises itself, forking into the background and returning, makes PID 1 exit, so Docker concludes the work is done:

```dockerfile
# Wrong, nginx forks and the foreground process exits

# Right. Stays in the foreground

```

Diagnosing it:

```bash
docker ps -a                    # check the STATUS and exit code
docker logs <container>         # what did it print before dying?
```

```
STATUS
Exited (127) 2 seconds ago
```

Exit codes carry information: **0** means clean exit, **1** a general application error, **125** the Docker command itself failed, **126** the command is not executable, **127** command not found, **137** SIGKILL (often out of memory), **143** SIGTERM.

Exit 127 nearly always means a typo in the command or a binary missing from the image.

## Publishing ports

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
#               â    âââ container port
#               âââ host port
```

Host on the left, container on the right. Reversing them is a rite of passage.

```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # bind to localhost only
docker run -d -P nginx                     # publish all EXPOSEd ports randomly
docker port web                            # what is actually mapped?
```

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It is documentation. Only `-p` or `-P` at run time actually maps a port.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash
docker run -d \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \
  --env-file .env \
  myapp:1.0
```

Environment variables are the standard way to configure a container, which is what lets one image serve every environment.

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies


| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |



## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.
