sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Manage local images with docker tag, docker rmi, docker push and docker save/load. Includes cleanup with docker image prune and the export vs save difference.

sections.title: Tagging Images
paragraphs: A tag is just a label that points to an image. The same image can have multiple tags, which is useful for marking the same build as v1.0, latest, and production all at once without duplicating any data.
Tagging never copies data, every tag pointing to the same image ID shares the exact same layers on disk. It's just an alias.

codeBlock.code:
# Add a new tag to an existing image
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:latest

# Tag the same image for different environments
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:production
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:staging

# Tag it for a private registry before pushing
docker tag myapp:v1.0 registry.company.com/myteam/myapp:v1.0

# Tag with the Git commit SHA for full traceability
docker tag myapp:v1.0 myapp:sha-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

sections.title: Removing Images
paragraphs: When you're done with an image, docker rmi removes it:
Note: Docker won't remove an image if any container is stopped. You'll need to remove the container first with docker rm <container-id>, or use the -f flag to force it.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove by name and tag
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Remove by image ID (you only need enough characters to make it unique)
docker rmi 605c77

# Remove multiple images in one go
docker rmi nginx:1.24 nginx:1.25 postgres:15

# Force removal even if a stopped container still references it
docker rmi -f myapp:old

# Remove all images (use with caution)
docker rmi $(docker images -q)

sections.title: Cleaning Up Unused Images
paragraphs: As you rebuild images over time, old versions lose their tags but the layers stick around on disk. These tagless leftovers are called dangling images and they serve no purpose, they're just taking up space.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove only dangling (untagged) images
docker image prune

# Remove all images not currently used by any container
docker image prune -a

# Skip the confirmation prompt
docker image prune -f

# Remove images that haven't been used in the last 24 hours
docker image prune -a --filter "until=24h"

sections.title: Pushing Images to a Registry
paragraphs: Once your image is ready, you push it to a registry so other machines like your server, your teammates, your CI pipeline, can pull it down.
The process is the same everywhere: log in, tag the image with the registry address, push. The registry address at the front of the tag is how Docker knows where to send it.

codeBlock.code:
# Log in with your Docker Hub account
docker login

# Tag the image with your Docker Hub username
docker tag myapp:v1.0 yourusername/myapp:v1.0

# Push it
docker push yourusername/myapp:v1.0

sections.title: Saving Images as Files
paragraphs: Sometimes you need to move an image without using a registry across a network with no internet access, as a backup, or to share directly with someone.
Save an image to a file:
Load it back on another machine:
After loading, the image shows up in docker images with its original name and tag, no re-tagging needed.

codeBlock.code:
# Export to a tar archive
docker save nginx:latest > nginx.tar

# Save compressed to reduce file size
docker save nginx:latest | gzip > nginx.tar.gz

# Save multiple images into one archive
docker save nginx:latest postgres:16 alpine:3.18 > images.tar

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Tag, Save, and Remove
paragraphs: After step 3, nginx:latest will be gone but webserver:backup which points to the same image data, will still be there. And you'll have a webserver.tar file you could move to another machine.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Tag the nginx image as webserver:backup
docker tag nginx webserver:backup

# Step 2: Save it to a tar file
docker save webserver:backup > webserver.tar

# Step 3: Remove the original nginx image
docker rmi nginx:latest

# Step 4: Confirm nginx is gone but webserver:backup still exists
docker images

sections.title: save/load vs export/import What's the Difference?
paragraphs: Docker has two pairs of commands that look similar but do very different things:
docker save / docker load works with images: it preserves every layer, all the metadata, environment variables, and the full layer history. This is what you should use almost always.
docker export / docker import works with a running or stopped container's filesystem: it flattens everything into a single layer and discards all history and metadata.
Unless you specifically want to flatten an image's layers, stick with save and load.

codeBlock.code:
# Export a container's filesystem (flattened, loses history)
docker export my-container > container-fs.tar

# Import as a new image
docker import container-fs.tar myimage:imported

sections.title: Full Cleanup: Starting Fresh
paragraphs: When your disk is getting full and you want to wipe the slate clean:

The last command removes everything Docker isn't actively using. Run docker system df first to understand what you're about to delete, and make sure anything you want to keep is either running or pushed to a registry.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove all stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove all unused images
docker image prune -a

# Remove unused volumes
docker volume prune

# Remove unused networks
docker network prune

# Do all of the above in one command
docker system prune -a --volumes

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: If I remove a tag, does it delete the image?

Only if it was the last tag pointing to that image. If the same image has multiple tags (latest, v1.0, production), removing one tag just removes that label, the image and its layers stay on disk until all tags pointing to it are removed.
Why can't I remove an image that I'm not using?
A stopped container still holds a reference to the image it was created from. Run docker ps -a to see stopped containers, remove them with docker rm <id>, and then try removing the image again.
What's the difference between docker image prune and docker image prune -a?

Without -a, it only removes dangling images, untagged leftovers from old builds. With -a, it removes any image not currently used by a running or stopped container. The -a version reclaims much more space but is more aggressive.
Do I need to be logged in to push to Docker Hub?
Yes. Run docker login first. For CI/CD pipelines, use a personal access token instead of your password as it's more secure and can be revoked independently.
Is docker save the same as making a backup?

It's a portable snapshot of your image that can be moved between machines without a registry. It's a reasonable backup approach for small setups, but for production workflows a registry (even a self-hosted one) is much more manageable at scale.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

docker-containers.markdown:
A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process namespace and network interface. Images are templates; containers are what actually runs.

## The lifecycle

```
docker run âââº Running âââº docker stop âââº Exited âââº docker rm âââº gone
                  â            â²
                  ââ pause âââââ
```

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27   # create + start
docker stop web                       # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s
docker start web                      # start it again. Same container
docker rm web                         # delete it
```

The distinction that matters: **`docker run` creates a new container every time.** `docker start` restarts an existing one. Running the same command three times gives three containers, which is why `docker ps -a` fills up unexpectedly.

```bash
docker ps        # running only
docker ps -a     # including exited
```

## Why your container exits immediately

The most common Docker frustration, and it has one root cause.

**A container lives exactly as long as its main process.** When PID 1 exits, the container exits. There is no background mode that keeps it alive.

```bash
docker run ubuntu           # exits instantly
docker run ubuntu bash      # also exits, no TTY, bash has no input and quits
docker run -it ubuntu bash  # stays running. Interactive terminal attached
```

The same applies to your own images. A web server that daemonises itself, forking into the background and returning, makes PID 1 exit, so Docker concludes the work is done:

```dockerfile
# Wrong, nginx forks and the foreground process exits
CMD ["nginx"]

# Right. Stays in the foreground
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
```

Diagnosing it:

```bash
docker ps -a                    # check the STATUS and exit code
docker logs <container>         # what did it print before dying?
```

```
STATUS
Exited (127) 2 seconds ago
```

Exit codes carry information: **0** means clean exit, **1** a general application error, **125** the Docker command itself failed, **126** the command is not executable, **127** command not found, **137** SIGKILL (often out of memory), **143** SIGTERM.

Exit 127 nearly always means a typo in the command or a binary missing from the image.

## Publishing ports

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
#               â    âââ container port
#               âââ host port
```

Host on the left, container on the right. Reversing them is a rite of passage.

```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # bind to localhost only
docker run -d -P nginx                     # publish all EXPOSEd ports randomly
docker port web                            # what is actually mapped?
```

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It is documentation. Only `-p` or `-P` at run time actually maps a port.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash
docker run -d \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \
  --env-file .env \
  myapp:1.0
```

Environment variables are the standard way to configure a container, which is what lets one image serve every environment.

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies

```bash
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped nginx:1.27
```

| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |

**`unless-stopped` is usually the right choice** for a long-running service. `always` will restart a container you deliberately stopped when the daemon next starts, which is rarely what anyone wants.

## Resource limits

```bash
docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp:1.0
```

Without limits, one container can consume the whole host. A memory limit means the container is killed when it exceeds it, exit code 137, rather than the host running out of memory and the kernel choosing a victim arbitrarily.

```bash
docker stats           # live usage
docker stats --no-stream
```

## Working with a running container

```bash
docker logs -f web                 # follow
docker logs --tail 100 web
docker logs --since 10m web

docker exec -it web sh             # shell inside
docker exec web env                # single command

docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./   # copy a file out
docker inspect web                       # full configuration as JSON
docker top web                           # processes
```

`docker exec` attaches to an **already running** container. If the container has exited, `exec` fails. You need `docker run` with a different command, or `--entrypoint` to override what it starts:

```bash
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp:1.0
```

That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately.

## stop vs kill

```bash
docker stop web           # SIGTERM, wait 10s, then SIGKILL
docker stop -t 30 web     # allow 30 seconds
docker kill web           # SIGKILL immediately
```

`docker stop` gives the application a chance to finish in-flight work. Use it. `docker kill` is for a process that is genuinely stuck.

If `docker stop` always takes exactly 10 seconds, your application is not receiving `SIGTERM`, almost always because the Dockerfile used shell-form `CMD`, making `/bin/sh` PID 1 instead of your process.

## Cleaning up

Stopped containers accumulate and hold disk through their writable layers:

```bash
docker container prune          # remove all stopped containers
docker rm -f web                # force-remove a running one
docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f   # remove everything, carefully
```

The best habit is preventing the buildup: **`--rm` deletes the container the moment it exits.**

```bash
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash
```

Use it for anything one-off. Tests, scripts, exploration. Nothing accumulates.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run detached with a port | `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name <n> <image>` |
| Run and auto-delete | `docker run --rm -it <image> <cmd>` |
| List running | `docker ps` |
| List all | `docker ps -a` |
| Logs | `docker logs -f <n>` |
| Shell inside | `docker exec -it <n> sh` |
| Explore an image that exits | `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>` |
| Port mappings | `docker port <n>` |
| Live resource usage | `docker stats` |
| Stop gracefully | `docker stop <n>` |
| Remove stopped containers | `docker container prune` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **A container lives exactly as long as PID 1.** Exit immediately usually means the process daemonised or was not found.
- **`docker run` creates a new container each time**; `docker start` reuses one.
- **Port mapping is `-p host:container`**, and `EXPOSE` publishes nothing.
- **Bind to `127.0.0.1` when you do not want a port on all interfaces**: Docker writes its own iptables rules and can bypass a host firewall.
- **`unless-stopped` is the sensible restart policy** for services.
- **Exit 137 is SIGKILL, usually out of memory; 127 is command not found.**
- **A 10-second `docker stop` every time means `SIGTERM` is not reaching your process.**
- **Use `--rm` for anything one-off** so containers do not accumulate.

paragraphs: After creating image, we run the image and make container out of it.

sections.title: The Basic Syntax
paragraphs: This one command does a lot: it checks if the hello-world image exists locally, if doesn't exists then pulls it from Docker Hub, creates a container from it, runs it, prints a message, and exits. That's the magic of docker run. It handles the entire lifecycle in one step.

codeBlock.code: docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND] [ARGS...]

sections.title: Detached vs. Interactive Mode
paragraphs: The first decision you make with almost every docker run is whether you want to interact with the container or let it run in the background.
Most services like web servers, databases, APIs, should run detached so they don't tie up your terminal:
The container starts and keeps running after the command returns. You get your terminal back immediately. Check that it's running with docker ps.
When you want to explore a container, run commands inside it, or debug something, use -it to open an interactive session:
-i keeps the input stream open so you can type commands. -t allocates a terminal so things like prompts and colors work properly. You almost always use them together as -it.
For one-off tasks like running a script, checking a tool's version, quick tests, you don't want the container sitting around as a stopped container afterward. --rm takes care of that automatically:
Without --rm, every container you run sticks around in a stopped state until you manually clean it up. Over time this clutters your system with dozens of stopped containers you'll never use again.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d nginx
# Returns: a3f8c2d1b4e9...  (the container ID)

sections.title: Naming Your Container
paragraphs: By default, Docker makes up a random two-word name like admiring_lovelace or jolly_tesla. These are fun but useless when you need to manage the container later.
Use --name to give your container a meaningful name:
One rule: names must be unique. If a container named my-db already exists (even if stopped), Docker will refuse to create another one with the same name.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d --name web-server nginx
docker run -d --name my-db postgres:16

sections.title: Port Mapping
paragraphs: Containers run in their own isolated network. If you run nginx inside a container, you can't just visit localhost:80 on your host machine, the ports aren't connected yet.
Port mapping is how you bridge that gap. The format is -p hostPort:containerPort:
Now http://localhost:8080 on your machine sends traffic to port 80 inside the container.
More examples to cover common scenarios:
A common beginner mistake: mapping ports backwards. Remember: host port first, container port second. -p 8080:80 means "my machine's port 8080 goes to the container's port 80."

codeBlock.code:
# Forward host port 8080 to container port 80
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx

sections.title: Overriding the Default Command
paragraphs: Every image has a default command baked in (set by CMD in the Dockerfile). You can replace it by adding a command at the end of docker run:
This is useful for exploring what's inside an image, running one-off scripts, or testing different startup configurations.

codeBlock.code:
# Default: nginx runs its web server
docker run nginx

# Override: open a shell instead
docker run -it nginx bash

# Run a specific Python script
docker run python:3.12 python my_script.py

# Pass flags to the application
docker run redis:7 redis-server --maxmemory 256mb

sections.title: Setting a Working Directory
paragraphs: Use -w to set which directory the container starts in:

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it -w /app node:20-alpine sh
# You'll land directly in /app instead of the root directory

sections.title: Resource Limits
paragraphs: On a shared machine or in production, you don't want a single container consuming all available memory or CPU. Set limits explicitly:
Without limits, a memory leak or traffic spike in one container can starve every other process on the host. It's a good habit to always set these for services running in production.

codeBlock.code:
# Cap memory at 512MB
docker run -d --memory 512m nginx

# Limit to half a CPU core
docker run -d --cpus 0.5 nginx

# Both limits together
docker run -d --memory 256m --cpus 0.25 --name limited-app myapp:latest

sections.title: Restart Policies
paragraphs: What should Docker do if your container crashes, or if the host machine reboots? That's what --restart controls:
unless-stopped is the right choice for most production services. It means your container survives host reboots automatically, but respects it when you intentionally stop it with docker stop.

codeBlock.code:
# Do nothing on exit (the default)
docker run --restart no nginx

# Restart only if the container crashes (exits with a non-zero code)
docker run --restart on-failure nginx

# Restart unless you explicitly stop it
docker run --restart unless-stopped nginx

# Always restart, even after a manual docker stop
docker run --restart always nginx

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Run a Named Container with Port Mapping
paragraphs: After step 1, you should see a container ID printed. After step 2, you'll see my-web listed as running with 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp in the ports column. That confirms the port mapping is active.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Run nginx in the background, named, with port mapping
docker run -d --name my-web -p 8080:80 nginx

# Step 2: Confirm it's running
docker ps

# Step 3: Visit it in your browser or test with curl
curl http://localhost:8080

sections.title: Listing Containers
paragraphs: Once containers are running, these are the commands you'll use to check on them:

codeBlock.code:
# Show currently running containers
docker ps

# Show all containers including stopped ones
docker ps -a

# Show only container IDs (useful for scripting)
docker ps -q

# Custom formatted output
docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What's the difference between docker run and docker start?

docker run creates a brand new container from an image and starts it. docker start restarts an existing container that was previously stopped. You use docker run the first time, and docker start to resume it later.
If I use -d, how do I see what the container is doing?
Use docker logs <container-name> to see its output. Add -f to follow the logs in real time, just like tail -f. For example: docker logs -f my-web.
What happens to a container when it finishes running?

By default it stops and sits in a "stopped" state, and you can see it with docker ps -a. It stays there until you remove it with docker rm. If you used --rm, it's deleted automatically the moment it exits.
Can two containers use the same host port?
No. Only one process on your machine can listen on a given port at a time. If you try to run two containers both mapped to port 8080, the second one will fail with a "port already in use" error.
What does -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 do differently from -p 5432:5432?

-p 5432:5432 binds to all network interfaces, and anyone on your network could potentially reach it. -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 binds only to your loopback interface, meaning only your own machine can connect. For databases, always use the 127.0.0.1 form unless you specifically need network access.
What's the difference between --restart always and --restart unless-stopped?

Both restart automatically after a host reboot. The difference is what happens after a manual docker stop. With unless-stopped, a manual stop is respected, and the container stays stopped. With always, Docker will restart it again even after you stop it manually, which can be surprising and hard to control.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
docker-containers-running.markdown:
A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process namespace and network interface. Images are templates; containers are what actually runs.

## The lifecycle

```
docker run âââº Running âââº docker stop âââº Exited âââº docker rm âââº gone
                  â            â²
                  ââ pause âââââ
```

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27   # create + start
docker stop web                       # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s
docker start web                      # start it again. Same container
docker rm web                         # delete it
```

The distinction that matters: **`docker run` creates a new container every time.** `docker start` restarts an existing one. Running the same command three times gives three containers, which is why `docker ps -a` fills up unexpectedly.

```bash
docker ps        # running only
docker ps -a     # including exited
```

## Why your container exits immediately

The most common Docker frustration, and it has one root cause.

**A container lives exactly as long as its main process.** When PID 1 exits, the container exits. There is no background mode that keeps it alive.

```bash
docker run ubuntu           # exits instantly
docker run ubuntu bash      # also exits, no TTY, bash has no input and quits
docker run -it ubuntu bash  # stays running. Interactive terminal attached
```

The same applies to your own images. A web server that daemonises itself, forking into the background and returning, makes PID 1 exit, so Docker concludes the work is done:

```dockerfile
# Wrong, nginx forks and the foreground process exits
CMD ["nginx"]

# Right. Stays in the foreground
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
```

Diagnosing it:

```bash
docker ps -a                    # check the STATUS and exit code
docker logs <container>         # what did it print before dying?
```

```
STATUS
Exited (127) 2 seconds ago
```

Exit codes carry information: **0** means clean exit, **1** a general application error, **125** the Docker command itself failed, **126** the command is not executable, **127** command not found, **137** SIGKILL (often out of memory), **143** SIGTERM.

Exit 127 nearly always means a typo in the command or a binary missing from the image.

## Publishing ports

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
#               â    âââ container port
#               âââ host port
```

Host on the left, container on the right. Reversing them is a rite of passage.

```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # bind to localhost only
docker run -d -P nginx                     # publish all EXPOSEd ports randomly
docker port web                            # what is actually mapped?
```

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It is documentation. Only `-p` or `-P` at run time actually maps a port.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash
docker run -d \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \
  --env-file .env \
  myapp:1.0
```

Environment variables are the standard way to configure a container, which is what lets one image serve every environment.

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies

```bash
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped nginx:1.27
```

| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |

**`unless-stopped` is usually the right choice** for a long-running service. `always` will restart a container you deliberately stopped when the daemon next starts, which is rarely what anyone wants.

## Resource limits

```bash
docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp:1.0
```

Without limits, one container can consume the whole host. A memory limit means the container is killed when it exceeds it, exit code 137, rather than the host running out of memory and the kernel choosing a victim arbitrarily.

```bash
docker stats           # live usage
docker stats --no-stream
```

## Working with a running container

```bash
docker logs -f web                 # follow
docker logs --tail 100 web
docker logs --since 10m web

docker exec -it web sh             # shell inside
docker exec web env                # single command

docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./   # copy a file out
docker inspect web                       # full configuration as JSON
docker top web                           # processes
```

`docker exec` attaches to an **already running** container. If the container has exited, `exec` fails. You need `docker run` with a different command, or `--entrypoint` to override what it starts:

```bash
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp:1.0
```

That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately.

## stop vs kill

```bash
docker stop web           # SIGTERM, wait 10s, then SIGKILL
docker stop -t 30 web     # allow 30 seconds
docker kill web           # SIGKILL immediately
```

`docker stop` gives the application a chance to finish in-flight work. Use it. `docker kill` is for a process that is genuinely stuck.

If `docker stop` always takes exactly 10 seconds, your application is not receiving `SIGTERM`, almost always because the Dockerfile used shell-form `CMD`, making `/bin/sh` PID 1 instead of your process.

## Cleaning up

Stopped containers accumulate and hold disk through their writable layers:

```bash
docker container prune          # remove all stopped containers
docker rm -f web                # force-remove a running one
docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f   # remove everything, carefully
```

The best habit is preventing the buildup: **`--rm` deletes the container the moment it exits.**

```bash
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash
```

Use it for anything one-off. Tests, scripts, exploration. Nothing accumulates.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run detached with a port | `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name <n> <image>` |
| Run and auto-delete | `docker run --rm -it <image> <cmd>` |
| List running | `docker ps` |
| List all | `docker ps -a` |
| Logs | `docker logs -f <n>` |
| Shell inside | `docker exec -it <n> sh` |
| Explore an image that exits | `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>` |
| Port mappings | `docker port <n>` |
| Live resource usage | `docker stats` |
| Stop gracefully | `docker stop <n>` |
| Remove stopped containers | `docker container prune` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **A container lives exactly as long as PID 1.** Exit immediately usually means the process daemonised or was not found.
- **`docker run` creates a new container each time**; `docker start` reuses one.
- **Port mapping is `-p host:container`**, and `EXPOSE` publishes nothing.
- **Bind to `127.0.0.1` when you do not want a port on all interfaces**: Docker writes its own iptables rules and can bypass a host firewall.
- **`unless-stopped` is the sensible restart policy** for services.
- **Exit 137 is SIGKILL, usually out of memory; 127 is command not found.**
- **A 10-second `docker stop` every time means `SIGTERM` is not reaching your process.**
- **Use `--rm` for anything one-off** so containers do not accumulate.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Understand docker stop vs kill and every container state. Start, restart, pause and rename containers, and read exit codes to see why one stopped.

sections.title: Docker Container Lifecycle
paragraphs: Creating a container with docker run is just the beginning. Once it's running, you need to know how to stop it safely, bring it back up, pause it temporarily, and understand what happened when it exits unexpectedly.
The most important thing to get right here is the difference between docker stop and docker kill, getting this wrong with a database can corrupt your data.

sections.title: Container States at a Glance
paragraphs: A container moves through different states during its lifetime. Here's the full picture:
Docker Container Lifecycle
Both stop and kill lead to stopped, but stop sends SIGTERM first
Understanding this diagram saves a lot of confusion. The key insight is that stop and kill both lead to the same "stopped" state, but they take very different paths to get there.

sections.title: Stopping a Container: stop vs kill
paragraphs: docker stop sends a SIGTERM signal to the main process inside the container. This is like a polite request to shut down, and it gives your application time to finish what it's doing, save its state, flush any data to disk, and close open connections cleanly.
If the application doesn't exit within 10 seconds, Docker then sends SIGKILL to force it closed.
Always use docker stop for databases, message queues, or anything writing to disk. A graceful shutdown means no corrupted files, no partial transactions, no lost messages.
docker kill sends SIGKILL directly. The process is terminated instantly which means there is no cleanup, no flushing, no graceful anything. It's the equivalent of yanking the power cord.
Use docker kill only when a container is completely unresponsive to docker stop, or when you're running a stateless service where data loss doesn't matter.

codeBlock.code:
# Graceful stop with default 10-second timeout
docker stop my-container

# Give it more time (important for databases doing a clean shutdown)
docker stop --time 30 my-container

# Stop multiple containers at once
docker stop web-server db-server cache-server

sections.title: Starting a Stopped Container
paragraphs: Once a container is stopped, you don't need to recreate it from scratch. docker start brings it back using the exact same configuration, volumes, and network settings it had before:

One important distinction that confuses: docker start and docker run are not the same thing. docker run creates a brand new container from an image. docker start resumes an existing container that was previously stopped. Think of it like the difference between installing an app and reopening one you already had.

codeBlock.code:
# Start a stopped container
docker start my-container

# Start it and attach to its output at the same time
docker start -a my-container

# Start several containers at once
docker start web db cache

sections.title: Restarting a Container
paragraphs: docker restart is simply docker stop followed by docker start in one command. It's useful when you've changed a config file or environment variable and need the container to pick up the change:

codeBlock.code:
# Restart with the default stop timeout
docker restart my-container

# Give it more time to stop cleanly before restarting
docker restart --time 15 my-container

# Restart multiple containers
docker restart web db

sections.title: Pausing a Container (Without Stopping It)
paragraphs: docker pause is a lesser-known but useful command. It freezes all processes inside the container. All processes stop executing completely, using no CPU, but everything stays in memory exactly as it was. No shutdown, no cleanup.

This is useful in a few specific scenarios: taking a consistent snapshot of a running container, temporarily freeing up CPU during a maintenance window, or freezing a container mid-execution to inspect its state. Unlike stop, when you unpause there's no re-initialization, the container resumes as if no time passed.

codeBlock.code:
# Freeze the container
docker pause my-container

# Resume it exactly where it left off
docker unpause my-container

sections.title: Renaming a Container
paragraphs: You can rename any container irrespective of it's state, and at any time:
Useful when you realize your container's name doesn't match what it actually does, or when you're reorganizing a project.

codeBlock.code: docker rename old-name new-name

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Stop, Check, and Restart

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Gracefully stop the container
docker stop my-web

# Step 2: Check its status (it should show "Exited")
docker ps -a

# Step 3: Bring it back up
docker restart my-web

# Step 4: Confirm it's running again
docker ps

sections.title: Understanding Exit Codes
paragraphs: When a container stops, it leaves behind an exit code that tells you why it stopped. These are the ones you'll see most often:
Check the exit code of any stopped container with:
If a container keeps restarting and you're not sure why, the exit code is the first thing to check.

codeBlock.code: docker inspect my-container --format='{{.State.ExitCode}}'

sections.title: Waiting for a Container to Finish
paragraphs: In scripts, you sometimes need to wait for a container to complete before moving on. docker wait does exactly that. It blocks until the container exits and then prints the exit code:
This is handy for running containers that do batch jobs, and then checking whether they succeeded before the next step in your script.

codeBlock.code:
docker wait my-task-container
# Prints: 0

sections.title: Keeping Containers Running Automatically
paragraphs: Instead of manually restarting containers after a crash or host reboot, set a restart policy when you first create the container:
unless-stopped is the right choice for most long-running services, it survives host reboots but respects when you intentionally stop a container.

codeBlock.code:
# Restart automatically, but respect manual stops
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped nginx

# Restart only after a crash, up to 5 times
docker run -d --restart on-failure:5 my-worker

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: If I docker stop a container and then docker start it, does it lose its data?

It depends on where the data is stored. Data inside the container's writable layer (files created inside the container) persists across stop/start cycles, the container is just paused, not deleted. But that data is lost if you delete the container with docker rm. For important data, always use volumes.
Why does docker stop wait 10 seconds before force-killing?

That's the default grace period. The window of your application gets to shut down cleanly. If 10 seconds isn't enough (for example, a database doing a large flush), use docker stop --time 30 or more. You can also change the default in your Compose file.
What's the difference between exit code 137 and 143?

Code 137 means SIGKILL was sent (force kill: either docker kill, an OOM event, or the OS terminating the process). Code 143 means SIGTERM was sent (docker stop), and the application exited in response to the polite request. If you see 137 on a container that should have been gracefully stopped, something went wrong during shutdown.
Can I stop a container from inside it?
Yes, running exit in an interactive shell, or any command that causes the main process to exit, will stop the container. The exit code will reflect whether it exited cleanly or with an error.
What happens to a paused container if the host restarts?
The container's in-memory state is lost as a host restart doesn't preserve RAM. The container will be in a stopped state when Docker starts back up, not a paused state.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash

  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \

```

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies

```bash

```

| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |

**`unless-stopped` is usually the right choice** for a long-running service. `always` will restart a container you deliberately stopped when the daemon next starts, which is rarely what anyone wants.

## Resource limits

```bash
docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp:1.0
```

Without limits, one container can consume the whole host. A memory limit means the container is killed when it exceeds it, exit code 137, rather than the host running out of memory and the kernel choosing a victim arbitrarily.

```bash

docker stats --no-stream
```

## Working with a running container

```bash

docker logs --tail 100 web
docker logs --since 10m web
```


Stopped containers accumulate and hold disk through their writable layers:


Use it for anything one-off. Tests, scripts, exploration. Nothing accumulates.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

sections.title: docker exec

sections.title: docker cp
paragraphs: docker cp lets you move files between your host machine and a container, with this option you don't need shell, or mount the volume.

paragraphs: docker attach connects your terminal directly to the container's main process (PID 1), rather than spawning a new one like exec does.

codeBlock.code: docker attach my-container

sections.title: docker inspect
paragraphs: docker inspect gives you a complete JSON dump of everything Docker knows about a container like its config, network settings, mounts, environment variables, and more.

sections.title: docker top

sections.title: A Practical Debugging Workflow
paragraphs: Here's a step-by-step approach when a container is misbehaving:

codeBlock.code:
# 1. Check if it's running and its status
docker ps -a --filter name=my-app

# 2. Stream the most recent logs

# 3. Check the container config

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What's the difference between docker exec and docker attach?

docker exec creates a brand new process inside the container and your container keeps running normally when you exit. docker attach connects you to the container's main process (PID 1), so exiting or pressing Ctrl+C can stop the entire container.
What if bash isn't available in my container?

Many lightweight images (especially Alpine-based ones) don't include bash. Try sh instead: docker exec -it my-container sh. If even sh isn't available, your image is likely a distroless image with no shell at all, and in that case, copy files out with docker cp or add a debug sidecar container.
Can I docker cp from a stopped container?
Yes. docker cp works even when the container isn't running, which makes it useful for recovering logs or files from a crashed container.
How do I exit a container shell without stopping it?
Type exit or press Ctrl+D. Since you opened the shell with docker exec, exiting only closes that shell process; the container and its main process keep running.
Can I run multiple docker exec sessions at the same time?
Yes. Each docker exec call creates an independent process. You can have multiple terminal windows all exec'd into the same container simultaneously.
Why can't I see some files when I exec into my container?

The container only has access to its own filesystem layer. Files that live on your host (outside of mounted volumes) won't appear inside the container. If you need to get a file in, use docker cp or mount a volume when starting the container.

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

paragraphs: Read container output with docker logs -f and --tail, filter it with grep, and monitor resource use with docker stats, events and health checks.

sections.title: docker logs
paragraphs: Docker automatically captures everything your container writes to stdout and stderr. You can retrieve it anytime with docker logs, even after the container has stopped.

codeBlock.code:
# Print all logs
docker logs my-container

# Stream logs in real time (like tail -f)
docker logs -f my-container

# Show only the last N lines
docker logs --tail 100 my-container

# Stream from the last 50 lines onward
docker logs --tail 50 -f my-container

# Show logs from the last 10 minutes
docker logs --since 10m my-container

# Show logs older than 5 minutes ago
docker logs --until 5m my-container

sections.title: Filtering Docker Logs with grep
paragraphs: docker logs outputs plain text, so you can pipe it through any Unix tool:
The 2>&1 part merges stderr into stdout before piping, Docker sends some output to stderr, so without it your grep might miss lines.

codeBlock.code:
# Find all error lines
docker logs my-app 2>&1 | grep -i error

# Find lines matching a specific request path
docker logs my-nginx 2>&1 | grep "POST /api"

# Count how many times an error appears
docker logs my-app 2>&1 | grep -c "ERROR"

sections.title: Log Drivers
paragraphs: By default, Docker uses the json-file driver, which stores logs as JSON files on your host machine. For production environments, you can swap this out to ship logs directly to a central logging system:
Available drivers include json-file, syslog, journald, fluentd, awslogs, splunk, gcplogs, and local.
Heads up: If you switch to a non-json-file driver, docker logs will stop working and logs will go directly to the external system instead.

codeBlock.code:
# Limit log file size and rotation
docker run --log-driver json-file --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 nginx

# Send to syslog
docker run --log-driver syslog nginx

sections.title: docker stats
paragraphs: docker stats gives you a live dashboard of CPU, memory, network, and disk I/O for every running container:
Keep an eye on the MEM % column. When a container hits 100% of its memory limit, Docker kills it with exit code 137 (OOM kill). If you're seeing unexpected container restarts, this is often why.

codeBlock.code:
# Live stats for all running containers
docker stats

# Stats for specific containers only
docker stats my-web my-db

sections.title: docker events
paragraphs: docker events streams a live feed of every action Docker takes like containers starting, stopping, crashing, images being pulled, and more. It's the closest thing Docker has to an audit log. This is especially useful when a container keeps restarting unexpectedly. docker events shows you exactly when and why it died.

codeBlock.code:
# Stream all events live
docker events

# Filter to container events only
docker events --filter type=container

# Filter by a specific event
docker events --filter event=start

# Filter by container name
docker events --filter container=my-app

# Events from the last 10 minutes
docker events --since 10m

sections.title: Container Health Checks
paragraphs: If your Dockerfile defines a HEALTHCHECK, Docker will periodically run it and mark the container as healthy or unhealthy. This is useful for load balancers, orchestration tools, and catching silent failures.
Add a health check to your Dockerfile:
Check health status from the host:

codeBlock.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why do my docker logs show nothing even though the container is running?

Your application might be writing logs to a file inside the container instead of to stdout/stderr. Docker only captures output sent to those two streams. Check where your app writes its logs. You may need to symlink the log file to /dev/stdout, or configure the app to log to stdout.
What's the difference between docker logs -f and docker attach?

docker logs -f streams the captured log output, it's read-only and safe. docker attach connects directly to the container's main process, which means pressing Ctrl+C can stop your container. Use docker logs -f for monitoring.
What does exit code 137 mean?

Exit code 137 means the container was killed by the OS. It's almost always because it exceeded its memory limit (OOM kill). Check docker stats to see if your container is approaching its memory limit, and consider increasing it with --memory or optimizing your app's memory usage.
Can I view logs from a stopped or crashed container?

Yes. docker logs works on stopped containers as long as they haven't been removed. Once you run docker rm, the logs are gone. If you need persistent logs beyond a container's lifecycle, configure a log driver like fluentd or awslogs.
How do I stop docker logs -f without closing my terminal?
Press Ctrl+C. Unlike docker attach, this only stops the log stream and does not affect the container in any way.
How often does HEALTHCHECK run?
By default every 30 seconds, with a 30-second timeout and 3 retries before marking the container unhealthy. You can customize all three with --interval, --timeout, and --retries in your Dockerfile.

docker-containers-logs.markdown:
A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, process namespace and network interface. Images are templates; containers are what actually runs.

## The lifecycle

```
docker run âââº Running âââº docker stop âââº Exited âââº docker rm âââº gone
                  â            â²
                  ââ pause âââââ
```

```bash
docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27   # create + start
docker stop web                       # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10s
docker start web                      # start it again. Same container
docker rm web                         # delete it
```

The distinction that matters: **`docker run` creates a new container every time.** `docker start` restarts an existing one. Running the same command three times gives three containers, which is why `docker ps -a` fills up unexpectedly.

```bash
docker ps        # running only
docker ps -a     # including exited
```

## Why your container exits immediately

The most common Docker frustration, and it has one root cause.

**A container lives exactly as long as its main process.** When PID 1 exits, the container exits. There is no background mode that keeps it alive.

```bash
docker run ubuntu           # exits instantly
docker run ubuntu bash      # also exits, no TTY, bash has no input and quits
docker run -it ubuntu bash  # stays running. Interactive terminal attached
```

The same applies to your own images. A web server that daemonises itself, forking into the background and returning, makes PID 1 exit, so Docker concludes the work is done:

```dockerfile
# Wrong, nginx forks and the foreground process exits
CMD ["nginx"]

# Right. Stays in the foreground
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
```

Diagnosing it:

```bash
docker ps -a                    # check the STATUS and exit code
docker logs <container>         # what did it print before dying?
```

```
STATUS
Exited (127) 2 seconds ago
```

Exit codes carry information: **0** means clean exit, **1** a general application error, **125** the Docker command itself failed, **126** the command is not executable, **127** command not found, **137** SIGKILL (often out of memory), **143** SIGTERM.

Exit 127 nearly always means a typo in the command or a binary missing from the image.

## Publishing ports

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
#               â    âââ container port
#               âââ host port
```

Host on the left, container on the right. Reversing them is a rite of passage.

```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx   # bind to localhost only
docker run -d -P nginx                     # publish all EXPOSEd ports randomly
docker port web                            # what is actually mapped?
```

`EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing. It is documentation. Only `-p` or `-P` at run time actually maps a port.

Binding to `127.0.0.1` is worth knowing: without it, `-p 8080:80` binds all interfaces, and on a cloud VM that can bypass your firewall, because Docker writes its own iptables rules.

## Environment and configuration

```bash
docker run -d \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e DATABASE_URL="postgres://db:5432/app" \
  --env-file .env \
  myapp:1.0
```

Environment variables are the standard way to configure a container, which is what lets one image serve every environment.

Avoid passing secrets with `-e` where you can. They appear in `docker inspect` and in the process list on the host. A mounted file or a secrets manager is better.

## Restart policies

```bash
docker run -d --restart unless-stopped nginx:1.27
```

| Policy | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `no` | Default (never restart) |
| `on-failure[:n]` | Restart on non-zero exit, optionally capped |
| `always` | Always restart, including after daemon restart |
| `unless-stopped` | Like `always`, but stays stopped if you stopped it deliberately |

**`unless-stopped` is usually the right choice** for a long-running service. `always` will restart a container you deliberately stopped when the daemon next starts, which is rarely what anyone wants.

## Resource limits

```bash
docker run -d --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 myapp:1.0
```

Without limits, one container can consume the whole host. A memory limit means the container is killed when it exceeds it, exit code 137, rather than the host running out of memory and the kernel choosing a victim arbitrarily.

```bash
docker stats           # live usage
docker stats --no-stream
```

## Working with a running container

```bash
docker logs -f web                 # follow
docker logs --tail 100 web
docker logs --since 10m web

docker exec -it web sh             # shell inside
docker exec web env                # single command

docker cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./   # copy a file out
docker inspect web                       # full configuration as JSON
docker top web                           # processes
```

`docker exec` attaches to an **already running** container. If the container has exited, `exec` fails. You need `docker run` with a different command, or `--entrypoint` to override what it starts:

```bash
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myapp:1.0
```

That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately.

## stop vs kill

```bash
docker stop web           # SIGTERM, wait 10s, then SIGKILL
docker stop -t 30 web     # allow 30 seconds
docker kill web           # SIGKILL immediately
```

`docker stop` gives the application a chance to finish in-flight work. Use it. `docker kill` is for a process that is genuinely stuck.

If `docker stop` always takes exactly 10 seconds, your application is not receiving `SIGTERM`, almost always because the Dockerfile used shell-form `CMD`, making `/bin/sh` PID 1 instead of your process.

## Cleaning up

Stopped containers accumulate and hold disk through their writable layers:

```bash
docker container prune          # remove all stopped containers
docker rm -f web                # force-remove a running one
docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f   # remove everything, carefully
```

The best habit is preventing the buildup: **`--rm` deletes the container the moment it exits.**

```bash
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run --rm -it ubuntu bash
```

Use it for anything one-off. Tests, scripts, exploration. Nothing accumulates.

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Run detached with a port | `docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name <n> <image>` |
| Run and auto-delete | `docker run --rm -it <image> <cmd>` |
| List running | `docker ps` |
| List all | `docker ps -a` |
| Logs | `docker logs -f <n>` |
| Shell inside | `docker exec -it <n> sh` |
| Explore an image that exits | `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>` |
| Port mappings | `docker port <n>` |
| Live resource usage | `docker stats` |
| Stop gracefully | `docker stop <n>` |
| Remove stopped containers | `docker container prune` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **A container lives exactly as long as PID 1.** Exit immediately usually means the process daemonised or was not found.
- **`docker run` creates a new container each time**; `docker start` reuses one.
- **Port mapping is `-p host:container`**, and `EXPOSE` publishes nothing.
- **Bind to `127.0.0.1` when you do not want a port on all interfaces**: Docker writes its own iptables rules and can bypass a host firewall.
- **`unless-stopped` is the sensible restart policy** for services.
- **Exit 137 is SIGKILL, usually out of memory; 127 is command not found.**
- **A 10-second `docker stop` every time means `SIGTERM` is not reaching your process.**
- **Use `--rm` for anything one-off** so containers do not accumulate.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my Docker container exit immediately?**

Because its main process finished. A container runs exactly as long as PID 1, so anything that completes, or daemonises itself into the background, ends the container. Check `docker ps -a` for the exit code and `docker logs <container>` for output. Exit 0 means a clean finish, so the command simply ran and stopped; exit 127 means command not found, usually a typo or a binary missing from the image. For servers, keep the process in the foreground, such as `nginx -g "daemon off;"`.

**What is the difference between docker run and docker start?**

`docker run` creates a **new** container from an image and starts it, so running the same command three times produces three containers. `docker start` restarts an existing, stopped container by name or ID, preserving its writable layer and configuration. If `docker ps -a` is filling up with stopped containers, that is `run` being used where `start` was intended, or a missing `--rm` flag on one-off commands.

**How does Docker port mapping work?**

`-p hostPort:containerPort`. Host on the left, container on the right. So `-p 8080:80` makes a container listening on 80 reachable at `localhost:8080`. Reversing them is extremely common and produces a mapping that silently forwards to a port nothing is listening on. Note that `EXPOSE` in a Dockerfile publishes nothing; it only documents the port. Use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` to bind to localhost only, since a plain `-p` binds all interfaces and Docker's own iptables rules can bypass a host firewall.

**How do I get a shell inside a Docker container?**

`docker exec -it <container> sh` for a running container, using `bash` if the image has it. Many slim images do not. If the container has already exited, `exec` will not work; start a new one with an overridden command instead: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>`. That is the standard way to explore an image whose normal command exits immediately or crashes on start.

**Which restart policy should I use?**

`unless-stopped` for most long-running services. It restarts the container after a crash or a Docker daemon restart, but respects a deliberate `docker stop`, whereas `always` will bring back a container you intentionally stopped the next time the daemon starts, which is rarely wanted. Use `on-failure` for batch work that should retry on error but not after a successful run, and leave the default `no` for one-off commands.

**How do I remove all stopped Docker containers?**

`docker container prune` removes every stopped container in one command and reports how much space was reclaimed. To remove absolutely everything including running containers, `docker ps -aq | xargs docker rm -f` works but should be used carefully. The better habit is prevention: add `--rm` to any one-off `docker run` so the container deletes itself on exit, which stops the buildup entirely.

paragraphs: Learn how Docker networking works: bridge, host and user-defined networks, port publishing with -p, container DNS, and how EXPOSE differs from -p.

sections.title: Docker Network Types
paragraphs: Docker ships with several built-in network drivers, each suited to a different scenario:

sections.title: The Default Bridge Network
paragraphs: When you run a container without specifying a network, it automatically joins Docker's built-in bridge network:

Containers on the default bridge can reach the internet and each other, but only by IP address. There's no automatic DNS, which means you'd need to hardcode IP addresses to connect containers together. That's fragile and error-prone. That's why user-defined networks exist.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d nginx
docker inspect bridge   # See all containers on the default bridge

sections.title: User-Defined Bridge Networks
paragraphs: Creating your own network unlocks automatic DNS between containers, and they can find each other by name instead of IP:
Now from inside the web container, you can reach the others by their container name:
Docker's embedded DNS server handles name resolution automatically. No IP addresses needed, no manual config. This is why user-defined networks are always recommended over the default bridge.

codeBlock.code:
# Create a network
docker network create my-app-network

# Run containers on it
docker run -d --name web   --network my-app-network nginx
docker run -d --name db    --network my-app-network postgres:16
docker run -d --name cache --network my-app-network redis:7

sections.title: Port Publishing
paragraphs: Containers are isolated from your host machine by default. To make a service accessible from your browser, another machine, or a CI pipeline, you need to publish a port. The format is -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT.
A key rule: Only publish ports that need to be reached from outside. Container-to-container traffic on the same network works without any port publishing at all.

codeBlock.code:
# Map host port 8080 to container port 80
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx

# Bind to localhost only (more secure as it is not accessible from other machines)
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 postgres:16

# Publish multiple ports
docker run -d -p 80:80 -p 443:443 nginx

# Let Docker pick a random available host port
docker run -d -p 80 nginx
docker port <container-id>   # Check what port was assigned

sections.title: Managing Networks
paragraphs: A container can belong to multiple networks at the same time, it is useful when you need one container to bridge two separate networks.

codeBlock.code:
# List all networks
docker network ls

# Inspect a network (see connected containers, subnet, gateway)
docker network inspect my-app-network

# See which network(s) a container is on
docker inspect my-container --format='{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' | python3 -m json.tool

# Connect a running container to a network (no restart needed)
docker network connect my-app-network my-container

# Disconnect a container from a network
docker network disconnect my-app-network my-container

# Connect with an alias (extra DNS name)
docker network connect --alias api my-app-network backend-v2

sections.title: EXPOSE vs -p
paragraphs: These two things sound similar but do very different things:
EXPOSE is just metadata, a note to developers (and tools like Docker Compose) saying "this container listens on this port." It doesn't open anything. Only -p actually publishes a port.

sections.title: Host Networking
paragraphs: With --network host, the container skips network isolation entirely and shares the host's network stack directly. The upside is maximum throughput with no NAT overhead. The downside is zero isolation, the container can bind to any host port, which means port conflicts become your problem. Use it sparingly, typically only for performance-critical tools or network monitoring utilities.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d --network host nginx
# nginx now listens on host port 80, so no -p needed

sections.title: Custom DNS Options
paragraphs: Within a user-defined network, DNS works automatically. But you can also customize it:

codeBlock.code:
# Use a specific DNS server
docker run --dns 8.8.8.8 --dns 8.8.4.4 my-app

# Add a custom /etc/hosts entry
docker run --add-host db.internal:192.168.1.50 my-app

# Set a DNS search domain
docker run --dns-search company.internal my-app

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why can't my two containers talk to each other even though they're both running?

They're probably both on the default bridge network, where containers can only communicate by IP address, not by name. Create a user-defined network with docker network create, add both containers to it with --network, and they'll be able to reach each other by container name automatically.
What's the difference between -p 8080:80 and -p 80?

-p 8080:80 maps host port 8080 to container port 80, and you choose the host port. -p 80 tells Docker to map container port 80 to a random available port on the host. Use docker port <container> to see what port was assigned.
Do I need to publish a port for containers on the same network to communicate?

No. Containers on the same user-defined network can reach each other freely without any port publishing. Port publishing is only needed to make a service accessible from outside Docker which means from your browser, another machine, or the host itself.
What does EXPOSE actually do if it doesn't open ports?

It's documentation. It tells anyone reading the Dockerfile what port the application listens on. Some tools (like Docker Compose and Docker Desktop) use it to suggest port mappings. But it has zero effect on actual network accessibility, only -p does that.
Can a container be on more than one network?

Yes. You can connect a running container to additional networks with docker network connect. This is useful when you have a gateway or proxy container that needs to reach services on two separate isolated networks.
What's the difference between bridge and host networking?

Bridge networking gives each container its own isolated network namespace. It has its own IP, and you control what's exposed via port publishing. Host networking removes that isolation completely; the container shares the host's network interfaces and ports directly. Bridge is safer and more flexible; host is faster but requires careful port management.
