Docker has perhaps eight ideas in it. Most early confusion comes from three of them sounding interchangeable when they are not, image, container and Dockerfile, so this page defines each precisely and shows how they connect.

## The one-line version

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe. Building it produces an **image**, which is a read-only template. Running an image produces a **container**, which is a live process. A **registry** is where images are stored and shared.

```
Dockerfile ââdocker buildâââ¶ Image ââdocker runâââ¶ Container
                              â  â²
                    docker pushâ  âdocker pull
                              â¼  â
                            Registry
```

Everything else, volumes, networks, Compose, exists to make containers useful together.

## Image

A **read-only template** containing everything needed to run an application: the code, the language runtime, system libraries, and the metadata describing how to start it.

An image is built from **layers**, one per instruction in the Dockerfile, stacked and presented as a single filesystem. Layers are what make Docker efficient: they are content-addressed and shared, so ten images built on `node:22-alpine` store that base exactly once on disk and pull it exactly once from a registry.

```bash
docker images
```

```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
myapp        1.0       a3f2c1d4e5b6   2 hours ago    142MB
node         22-alpine 7b8c9d0e1f2a   3 days ago     135MB
```

Two consequences of the layer model worth internalising early. Layers are **immutable**, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space in the image, and is still recoverable, which is why a deleted secret is a leaked secret. And layers are **cached**, so the order of instructions in a Dockerfile largely determines how fast rebuilds are.

Go deeper: [Docker images](/tutorials/docker/docker-images) and [image layers](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-layers).

## Container

A **running instance** of an image. If the image is the recipe, the container is the meal.

Technically it is an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, process table, network stack and hostname; cgroups cap what CPU and memory it can consume. There is no virtual machine and no guest operating system. This is why a container starts in milliseconds where a VM takes a minute.

Docker adds one **thin writable layer** on top of the image's read-only layers. Every file the container creates or modifies lands there, and **it is deleted with the container**. That single fact explains most Docker surprises for newcomers: your database is empty again because its data lived in the writable layer of a container that no longer exists.

```bash
docker ps
```

```
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS         PORTS                    NAMES
9f2c1a4b7e3d   myapp:1.0   Up 4 minutes   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp   api
```

Containers are **ephemeral** by design. Treat them as disposable and keep anything that must survive in a volume.

Go deeper: [Docker containers](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers) and [the container lifecycle](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-lifecycle).

## Dockerfile

A plain text file of instructions for building an image, executed top to bottom:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
```

Each instruction produces a layer. The reason the package manifest is copied and installed *before* the source is that Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so copying source first would reinstall every dependency on every code edit.

Go deeper: [Dockerfile basics](/tutorials/docker/dockerfile-basics).

## Registry

Storage and distribution for images. GitHub, but for images rather than source. You `push` to share and `pull` to consume.

```bash
docker pull postgres:17
docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
```

**Docker Hub** is the default: if you run `docker pull nginx` with no registry prefix, that is where it comes from. Most organisations also use a private registry. GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry. For their own images.

A **tag** such as `1.0` or `latest` is a mutable pointer to an image, not a permanent name. `latest` in particular is just a default tag with no special meaning; it does not track the newest version. A **digest** (`@sha256:â¦`) is immutable and is what you pin when reproducibility matters.

Go deeper: [Docker Hub and registries](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-hub).

## Volume

Storage that outlives the container. Since the container's writable layer is destroyed with it, anything that must persist, database files, uploads, goes in a volume.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

Three kinds, and the distinction comes up constantly:

| Type | Written as | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Named volume** | `-v pgdata:/var/lib/â¦` | Docker manages it; the default for data |
| **Bind mount** | `-v ./src:/app/src` | A host directory; the default for development |
| **tmpfs** | `--tmpfs /tmp` | Memory only; never touches disk |

Go deeper: [Docker volumes](/tutorials/docker/docker-volumes).

## Network

Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other **by container name**, which is Docker's built-in DNS at work:

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapp:1.0
```

The API connects to `db:5432`. No IP addresses, no `--link`, nothing to update when a container restarts with a different address.

Note that `localhost` inside a container means *that container*, not the host and not another container. Expecting `localhost:5432` to reach a database in a different container is one of the most common beginner errors.

Go deeper: [container networking](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-networking).

## Docker Compose

Real applications are several containers. Compose describes them in one file so the whole stack starts together:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down
```

Compose creates a network automatically, which is why `db` resolves as a hostname without any extra configuration.

It is a **single-host** tool. Excellent for development and small deployments, not a replacement for an orchestrator. Once you need scheduling across machines, rolling updates and self-healing, that is [Kubernetes](/tutorials/kubernetes/introduction-to-kubernetes).

## Client and daemon

One more piece, because it explains a whole class of error messages.

The `docker` command is a **client**. It does almost nothing itself. It sends requests over a socket to the **daemon** (`dockerd`), which builds images, runs containers and manages storage.

```
docker CLI ââ/var/run/docker.sockâââ¶ dockerd âââ¶ containerd âââ¶ runc âââ¶ your process
```

So `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon` means the CLI is installed and working, and nothing is listening. Start the service. And `permission denied ... docker.sock` means the daemon is running but your user cannot talk to its socket.

It also explains why the build context is *sent* to the daemon: the daemon may not be on your machine at all.

## The vocabulary, condensed

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Image** | Read-only template built from layers |
| **Layer** | One filesystem diff, produced by one instruction |
| **Container** | A running instance, plus a thin writable layer |
| **Dockerfile** | Build instructions for an image |
| **Build context** | The directory sent to the daemon at build time |
| **Registry** | Where images are stored and shared |
| **Tag** | A mutable pointer to an image |
| **Digest** | An immutable content hash |
| **Volume** | Storage that outlives the container |
| **Bind mount** | A host directory mounted into a container |
| **Network** | Container-to-container connectivity with DNS |
| **Compose** | Multi-container definition for one host |
| **Daemon** | `dockerd`, the process doing the work |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Image is the template, container is the running instance.** Recipe and meal.
- **A container's writable layer dies with it.** Anything that must survive belongs in a volume.
- **Layers are immutable and cached**: which sets both your rebuild speed and why deleted files still ship.
- **Containers are processes, not virtual machines.** Namespaces isolate, cgroups limit.
- **`latest` is just a default tag**, not the newest version. Pin a digest when it matters.
- **Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name**, and `localhost` means that container alone.
- **The CLI only talks to the daemon**, which is why "cannot connect" is a different problem from "not installed".

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?**

An image is a read-only template: the application, its runtime, its libraries and the metadata describing how to start it, stored as a stack of layers. A container is a running instance created from that image, with a thin writable layer on top for anything it changes. One image can back any number of containers simultaneously, each with its own writable layer, in the same way one class can have many instances. The practical consequence is that images persist and containers are disposable.

**Where does data written inside a container go?**

Into the container's writable layer, which exists only as long as the container does. Remove the container and every file it created is removed with it, which is why a database restarted from the same image comes back empty. Mount a named volume at the path that matters (`-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) and the data lives outside the container lifecycle. Bind mounts do the same thing with a specific host directory, which is what you usually want in development.

**What is a Docker layer and why does it matter?**

Each Dockerfile instruction produces one layer, a filesystem diff, and the image is those layers stacked into a single view. They matter for three reasons. They are shared, so images built on the same base store and transfer it once. They are cached, so ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing makes rebuilds dramatically faster. And they are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space and remains extractable from the image.

**What is a Docker registry and is Docker Hub the only one?**

A registry stores and distributes images, the way a Git host stores repositories. Docker Hub is the default, `docker pull nginx` with no prefix goes there, and hosts official images for most common software. It is not the only option, and most organisations push their own images to a private registry such as GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry or Azure Container Registry. Prefixing the image name with a hostname selects one: `ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0`.

**Do I need Docker Compose or Kubernetes?**

Compose if you are running several containers on one machine. A local development stack, a small single-server deployment. It defines services, networks and volumes in one file and starts them together, and it is the right tool most of the time. Kubernetes when you need containers scheduled across multiple machines with rolling updates, self-healing and autoscaling. They solve different problems, and starting with Compose costs nothing if you later move: the concepts transfer directly.

**Why can't my container reach another container on localhost?**

Because `localhost` inside a container refers to that container and nothing else. Each one has its own network namespace and its own loopback interface. Put both on the same user-defined network and use the container name as the hostname: `docker network create appnet`, start each with `--network appnet`, then connect to `db:5432`. Compose does this for you automatically, which is why service names work as hostnames there without any configuration.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn when to use COPY vs ADD in a Dockerfile. Covers build context, --chown and --chmod, COPY --from, the dependency-manifest pattern and .dockerignore.

COPY and ADD both bring files from the build context into the image. The short answer is use COPY, but the long answer is worth knowing, because ADD has picked up genuinely useful features recently and the old advice to never touch it is now slightly out of date.

sections.title: The build context decides what is copyable
paragraphs: Before either instruction runs, Docker packages a directory and sends it to the daemon. That directory is the build context, the . at the end of docker build -t myapp ., and it is the only thing COPY can read from.
That transferring context line is worth watching. If it reports hundreds of megabytes, you are shipping node_modules and .git to the daemon on every single build before any instruction executes.
This is also why the most confusing COPY error exists:

Nothing outside the context is reachable, no matter how valid the path looks on your machine. The fix is to build from a directory that contains everything you need and point at the Dockerfile explicitly:

codeBlock.code: docker build -t myapp .

sections.title: COPY: the default choice
paragraphs: Source paths are relative to the build context. Destination paths are absolute, or relative to WORKDIR.
If /app does not already exist, this creates a file named /app containing your server code. The next instruction that expects /app to be a directory then fails with something that looks unrelated:
Two safe habits: always write a trailing slash on directory destinations, or set WORKDIR /app first and copy to ..
COPY copies the contents of a source directory, not the directory itself:
Getting this backwards produces a /app/src/src nesting that is easy to miss until something 404s at runtime.

codeBlock.code:
# Single file
COPY server.js /app/server.js

# Into a directory. The trailing slash matters
COPY server.js /app/

# Multiple sources always need a directory destination
COPY package.json package-lock.json /app/

# Wildcard
COPY *.json /app/

# Entire directory
COPY ./src /app/src

sections.title: COPY --chown
paragraphs: Copied files are owned by root by default. If your container runs as a non-root user, and it should, that user may not be able to write to its own application directory:
--chown sets ownership as part of the same layer, which costs nothing. A separate RUN chown -R duplicates every file into a new layer and can double your image size:
Numeric IDs are more portable, since a named user has to exist in the image already:
Referencing a user that does not exist yet fails the build:
Create the user with RUN adduser before the COPY that references it.

codeBlock.code: Error: EACCES: permission denied, open '/app/logs/app.log'

sections.title: COPY --chmod
paragraphs: This saves a RUN chmod layer and, more usefully, works regardless of the permissions the file had on the machine that built it, which is what makes a Windows checkout produce a working entrypoint script.
--chmod needs BuildKit, the default builder in current Docker. On an older engine, add the syntax directive at the very top of the Dockerfile:

codeBlock.code:
COPY --chmod=755 entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
COPY --chmod=644 config.yaml /app/config.yaml

sections.title: COPY --from
paragraphs: --from reads from another build stage, or from an entirely separate image, instead of the build context:
Pulling a single binary out of a published image is the other common use, and it beats a curl and checksum dance:

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: The dependency-manifest pattern
paragraphs: The highest-value COPY pattern in any Dockerfile. Copy the manifest, install, then copy source:
Reverse those and every one-character source edit reinstalls every dependency, because the COPY . . layer is invalidated and everything after it rebuilds. The same shape applies in every ecosystem:

You are writing a Dockerfile based on node:20-alpine with WORKDIR /app. You want to copy package.json into the image owned by the "node" user, install dependencies, and then copy the rest of the source, also owned by "node". Which snippet is correct?

codeBlock.code:
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .

sections.title: ADD: what it actually does
paragraphs: ADD is COPY plus three behaviours.
Auto-extracts local tar archives. This is the one legitimate reason to reach for it:
It is also the behaviour that bites people. A .tar.gz you meant to ship verbatim gets unpacked instead, and nothing warns you. Note the asymmetry. A local archive is extracted, a remote one is not.
Fetches URLs, now with checksum verification. The long-standing objection to ADD <url> was that you could not verify what you downloaded. Modern Dockerfile syntax fixes that:
Clones a Git repository:
ADD <url> still cannot clean up after itself. The downloaded file is in that layer permanently. When you need to download, use, and discard something, one RUN does all three in a single layer:
The rule: COPY by default. ADD for local tar extraction, or for a URL when the file is genuinely meant to stay in the image and you pin a --checksum.

codeBlock.code: ADD rootfs.tar.gz /

sections.title: .dockerignore
paragraphs: COPY . . takes everything in the context unless you exclude it. The syntax mirrors .gitignore:
Three things it buys you: local secrets never get baked into a layer, the context shrinks so builds start faster, and irrelevant file changes stop invalidating your cache.
Negation works, which is how you ship one file out of an excluded directory:
The classic .dockerignore failure is over-excluding. A blanket * or an overly broad pattern silently hides a file COPY needs, and the error names the file rather than the ignore rule:
If a COPY cannot find a file that plainly exists, check .dockerignore before anything else.

codeBlock.code:
# Dependencies. Reinstalled inside the image anyway
node_modules/
vendor/
__pycache__/
.venv/

# Version control
.git/
.gitignore

# Secrets and local config
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.key

# Build artifacts
dist/
build/
target/

# IDE and OS noise
.vscode/
.idea/
.DS_Store

# Tests and docs
tests/
coverage/
*.md

paragraphs: A Dockerfile at services/api/Dockerfile has COPY ../../shared/config.json /app/. The file definitely exists on disk, but the build fails with "not found". Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?

COPY copies files and directories from the build context into the image and does nothing else. ADD does the same, and additionally extracts local tar archives automatically, downloads remote URLs, and clones Git repositories. The extras are why the default advice is COPY. An archive you meant to ship intact gets silently unpacked. Use ADD deliberately, for local tar extraction or a URL download you pin with --checksum, and COPY for everything else.
Why does my COPY fail with "forbidden path outside the build context"?

Because the source path climbs above the directory you passed to docker build. Docker packages that directory and sends it to the daemon before any instruction runs, so anything outside it simply does not exist as far as COPY is concerned. Regardless of how valid the path looks in your shell. Build from a directory that contains everything you need and point at the Dockerfile with -f, for example docker build -f services/api/Dockerfile -t api . from the repository root.
How do I fix "permission denied" after adding USER to my Dockerfile?

The copied files are still owned by root, and your non-root user cannot write to them. Add --chown to the COPY instructions, COPY --chown=node:node . ., which sets ownership as part of that layer at no cost. Avoid fixing it with a separate RUN chown -R, because that rewrites every file into a brand new layer and can roughly double the image size. If the user does not exist in the base image, create it with RUN adduser before the COPY that references it.
Why is COPY saying a file is not found when it clearly exists?

Check .dockerignore first. An over-broad exclusion pattern removes the file from the build context, and the resulting error names the file rather than the rule that hid it, typically failed to compute cache key: "/package.json": not found. The other cause is the source path pointing outside the build context. Both mean the same thing: the daemon never received that file.
Do I need a .dockerignore file?

Effectively yes, before your first COPY . .. Without one the entire directory is sent to the daemon on every build, so node_modules and .git slow the build before an instruction runs, local .env files and private keys get baked into layers where anyone with the image can read them, and unrelated file changes invalidate your layer cache. At minimum exclude node_modules/, .git/, .env* and your build output directory.
What does COPY --from do?

It reads from somewhere other than the build context. Either an earlier stage in the same Dockerfile (COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist) or a completely separate image (COPY --from=hashicorp/terraform:1.9 /bin/terraform /usr/local/bin/). The first is what makes multi-stage builds work, letting compilers and dev dependencies stay behind in the build stage. The second is often a cleaner way to obtain a binary than downloading and verifying it yourself, since the image is already versioned and pinnable.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
dockerfile-copy-add.markdown:
## What Are Docker Image Layers?

A Docker image isn't a single big file. It's a stack of thin, read-only snapshots called **layers**. There is one layer attached to for each instruction in your Dockerfile that makes a change to the filesystem.

Here's a simple Node.js Dockerfile with each layer labeled:

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine      # Layer 1: base OS + Node runtime (~127MB)
WORKDIR /app             # Layer 2: metadata only, takes up 0 bytes
COPY package*.json ./    # Layer 3: adds package.json (~2KB)
RUN npm install          # Layer 4: adds node_modules (~40MB)
COPY . .                 # Layer 5: adds your source code (~100KB)
CMD ["node", "app.js"]   # Layer 6: metadata only, takes up 0 bytes
```

Visually, the final image looks like this:

<DockerDiagram type="image-layers" />

Each layer only stores the *difference* from the layer below it, similar to how Git commits work. This means if two different images use `node:18-alpine` as their base, that base layer is stored only once on your disk and shared between them.

When you run a container, Docker adds one extra thin **writable layer** on top of the stack. The image layers underneath stay read-only and untouched, which is why multiple containers can run from the same image without interfering with each other.

---

## How Docker's Build Cache Works

After Docker builds a layer, it caches it. The next time you build, Docker checks each instruction from top to bottom. If nothing has changed in that instruction or the files it touches, Docker skips re-executing it and uses the cached version instead. This is what makes rebuilds so much faster:

```
First build (nothing cached):
FROM node:18-alpine     â downloaded fresh
WORKDIR /app            â created
COPY package*.json ./   â copied
RUN npm install         â installed, let's say it took 30 seconds
COPY . .                â copied
â Total: ~35 seconds

Second build (only your app code changed):
FROM node:18-alpine     â CACHED (skipped)
WORKDIR /app            â CACHED (skipped)
COPY package*.json ./   â CACHED (skipped)
RUN npm install         â CACHED (skipped), saves 30 seconds
COPY . .                â REBUILT (source code changed)
â Total: ~2 seconds
```

There's one critical rule about how cache invalidation works: **when a layer is invalidated, every layer that comes after it is also rebuilt**, even if those later instructions didn't change. This is the key insight that shapes how you should order your Dockerfile.

---

## Order of Dockerfile Matters

Put instructions that change rarely near the **top**. Put instructions that change often near the **bottom**.

The most common mistake beginners make is this:

### The wrong way, rebuilds dependencies every single time

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .               # Copies everything, including your source code
RUN npm install        # Invalidated every time ANY file changes
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

The problem here: `COPY . .` copies your source code along with `package.json`. Every time you change even one line of code, that `COPY` layer is invalidated, and since `RUN npm install` comes after it, npm has to reinstall everything from scratch in every single build.

### The right way, reuses the dependency cache unless packages change

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./  # Copy ONLY the dependency manifest first
RUN npm install        # This only reruns when package.json changes
COPY . .               # Copy your source code after dependencies are installed
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

Now `npm install` is cached as long as `package.json` and `package-lock.json` stay the same. Changing your app code only rebuilds the last `COPY` layer. A 35-second build becomes a 2-second build.

**Note:** This isn't a Node.js-specific trick; it applies everywhere. The pattern is always the same: copy the dependency file first, install, then copy your source code.

---

## Hands-On Practice: Watch the Cache in Action

The best way to understand caching is to see it yourself:

```bash
# Step 1: Build the image for the first time (everything runs fresh)
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .

# Step 2: Build again without changing anything
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .

# Step 3: Make a small change to your app code, then build again
docker build -t cachetest:v1 .
```

On the second build, you'll see `Using cache` next to every step. On the third build after a code change, you'll see `Using cache` for the dependency steps but `REBUILT` for the source code step. That's the cache doing exactly what it should.

---

## When You Need to Skip the Cache

Sometimes you *want* Docker to ignore the cache, for example, to pick up the latest security patches from `apt` even though the instruction string hasn't changed:

```bash
# Force a completely fresh build (no cached layers)
docker build --no-cache -t myapp:latest .
```

If you only want to bust the cache from a specific point forward (without rebuilding everything), you can use a build argument as a cache-busting trick:

```dockerfile
ARG CACHE_BUST=1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y
```

```bash
# Pass a new value to force this layer and everything after it to rebuild
docker build --build-arg CACHE_BUST=$(date +%s) -t myapp:latest .
```

---

## Cleaning Up the Build Cache

The build cache can quietly grow to gigabytes over time. Here's how to manage it:

```bash
# See how much space the cache is using
docker system df

# Remove build cache that's no longer needed
docker builder prune

# Remove all build cache, including layers still referenced by images
docker builder prune -a
```

`docker system df` is a good habit to run occasionally. It gives you a quick overview of how much space images, containers, volumes, and build cache are each taking up.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Docker images are stacks of read-only layers, and each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem creates a new one.
- Layers are cached after the first build. If nothing changed, Docker reuses the cached layer and skips re-executing it.
- When a layer is invalidated, **all layers below it are rebuilt too**, this is the most important caching rule to internalize.
- Always copy your dependency manifest (`package.json`, `requirements.txt`, etc.) and run your install command *before* copying your source code. This one change can turn a 30-second build into a 2-second build.
- Use `docker build --no-cache` when you need a guaranteed fresh build, such as picking up security patches.
- Run `docker builder prune` periodically to reclaim disk space from accumulated build cache.

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does Docker rebuild everything after I change one file?**

Because you're probably copying all your files (including source code) before installing dependencies. When `COPY . .` comes before `RUN npm install`, any file change invalidates the install layer. Fix it by copying your dependency manifest first, installing, then copying the rest of your code.

**How does Docker know if a layer has changed?**

For `COPY` and `ADD` instructions, Docker compares the actual file contents, not just timestamps. For `RUN` instructions, Docker compares the instruction string itself. If the string is identical, Docker assumes the result is the same and uses the cache.

**Does the cache work across different machines?**

Not by default. The local build cache lives only on your machine. In CI/CD pipelines you can use cache backends (like storing layers in a registry) to share cache across machines, but that's an advanced topic.

**Why do some layers show `0B` in `docker history`?**

Those are metadata-only instructions like `WORKDIR`, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, and `CMD`. They don't add or modify any files in the image, so they take up no space, but they still create a layer.

**When should I use `--no-cache`?**

Use it when you need to pull in external updates that Docker can't detect, most commonly when running `apt-get update` or `pip install` to get the latest security patches. Since the instruction string hasn't changed, Docker would normally use the cache and miss the new patches.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how the Dockerfile RUN instruction works, including shell vs exec form, apt-get best practices, same-layer cleanup, cache mounts, secrets and heredocs.

RUN executes a command during the build and commits the result as a layer. It installs packages, compiles code, creates users and sets permissions. How you write it is most of the difference between a 50 MB image and a 500 MB one.
The single fact that explains nearly every RUN mistake: layers are additive and immutable. Anything a RUN creates is permanent, and a later RUN that deletes it only hides it.

sections.title: Shell form and exec form
paragraphs: Shell form is the normal choice for RUN, because &&, pipes, redirects and variable expansion all need a shell. Exec form matters when the base image has no shell at all.
Variable expansion is the trap:
(This is the opposite of the advice for CMD and ENTRYPOINT, where exec form is what you want so the process receives signals.)

codeBlock.code:
# Shell form. Runs via /bin/sh -c "..."
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

# Exec form. Runs the binary directly, no shell
RUN ["apt-get", "install", "-y", "curl"]

sections.title: Installing packages
paragraphs: Three non-negotiables here:
If an install hangs waiting for input, you have hit a package with an interactive prompt:
Prefer setting it inline on the one RUN that needs it, as a persistent ENV it also affects anyone who later docker execs into the container.
--no-cache skips storing the index entirely, so there is no cleanup step.

codeBlock.code:
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      curl \
      git \
      ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: Why cleanup must be in the same layer
paragraphs: A layer is a filesystem diff. Deleting a file in a later layer records a whiteout entry. The file disappears from the container's view while still occupying space in the layer below, and still being readable by anyone who pulls the image and inspects it layer by layer.
That last part matters for more than size. A secret written and then deleted in a later RUN is still extractable from the image.
The fat instruction names itself. Here build-essential is 178 MB that almost certainly belongs in a build stage rather than the shipped image.

codeBlock.code:
# Wrong. The apt lists are permanently in layer 1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Right. Created and removed inside one layer
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: Cache mounts make rebuilds fast
paragraphs: The upgrade most Dockerfiles are missing. A BuildKit cache mount keeps a package or compiler cache on the builder between builds, without putting a single byte in the image:
Note that with a cache mount you deliberately stop deleting the lists. The mount is not part of the image, so there is nothing to clean up.
The same pattern pays off everywhere dependency resolution is slow:
A cold install that took 90 seconds typically drops to a few. The caveat is that the cache lives on whichever builder ran the build, so CI needs a persistent or exported cache to see the benefit.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl

sections.title: Secrets belong in a mount, not a layer
paragraphs: The value exists for the duration of that one instruction and is written to no layer. Passing the same token as an ARG records it in docker history for anyone who pulls the image.

codeBlock.code:
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npmtoken) npm ci

sections.title: Pipes hide failures
paragraphs: Shell form runs under /bin/sh -c, and in a pipeline only the last command's exit status counts. This build succeeds even when the download 404s:
curl fails, sh receives empty input and exits 0, the layer commits, and the missing tool surfaces at runtime instead. Fix it for the whole file:
On Alpine, where bash may be absent, do it per instruction:

codeBlock.code: RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh

sections.title: Heredocs for multi-command blocks
paragraphs: Much easier to read than a wall of && \, and set -eux gives you fail-fast behaviour plus an echo of each command in the build log. Requires BuildKit, which is the default in current Docker.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN <<EOF
set -eux
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
EOF

sections.title: Creating users and directories
paragraphs: Prefer COPY --chown over a trailing RUN chown -R wherever you can, chown on copied files rewrites every one of them into a new layer.

You want a single RUN instruction in a Dockerfile based on ubuntu:24.04 that updates apt, installs curl and wget without recommended packages, and cleans up the package lists afterward, all in one layer. Which instruction is correct?

codeBlock.code:
# Debian
RUN groupadd -r appgroup \
 && useradd -r -g appgroup -d /app -s /sbin/nologin appuser

# Alpine
RUN addgroup -S appgroup \
 && adduser -S -G appgroup appuser

RUN mkdir -p /app/logs && chown -R appuser:appgroup /app

sections.title: Cache-friendly ordering
paragraphs: RUN layers are cached on the instruction string, not on what the command produces. Order from least to most frequently changing:
When you genuinely need to bust the cache:

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

# System packages. Change rarely
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Changes only when requirements.txt does
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt

# Changes on every commit
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile downloads a 400 MB SDK in one RUN and deletes it in the next RUN. The final image is still around 400 MB larger than expected. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?

RUN executes during docker build and commits the result as an image layer, so its effects are baked in permanently. This is where you install packages and compile code. CMD sets the default command executed when a container starts from the finished image, and it produces no layer content. A Dockerfile normally has several RUN instructions and exactly one CMD. If you find yourself wanting to "run something when the container starts", that is CMD or ENTRYPOINT, not RUN.
Why doesn't deleting files in a later RUN reduce my image size?

Because each instruction commits an immutable filesystem diff. A delete in a later layer writes a whiteout marker, which makes the file invisible inside the container while the actual bytes stay in the layer that created them and still travel with the image. Put the creation and the deletion in one RUN joined with &&, or move the whole step into a build stage that never ships. The same mechanism is why a secret written and later deleted is still recoverable from the published image.
Why should apt-get update and apt-get install be in the same RUN?

Docker caches a RUN layer on its command string, not on what the command actually produced. As a separate instruction, RUN apt-get update keeps its cached layer indefinitely, so a later install runs against a package index that may be months old. Producing Version '…' for '…' was not found or silently installing outdated packages. Chaining them means any change to the install list re-runs the update too.
How do I make Docker builds faster without making the image bigger?

Use BuildKit cache mounts. RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci keeps the package cache on the builder between builds while writing nothing into the image, and the same works for pip, Go module and build caches, and apt. Combine that with ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing, and copying dependency manifests before source code. In CI you will also need a persistent or exported cache, since the mount lives on whichever builder ran the build.
Why does my build succeed even though a command inside RUN failed?

Shell form runs under /bin/sh -c, and in a pipeline only the final command's exit status is reported. So RUN curl -fsSL https://… | sh succeeds even when curl 404s, because sh reads empty input and exits cleanly. Add SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"] near the top of the Dockerfile, or prefix the individual instruction with set -o pipefail &&. Using set -eux inside a heredoc block gives the same protection plus a readable build log.
How do I find which instruction made my image so large?

docker history <image> --no-trunc lists every layer with its size and the instruction that created it, largest offenders usually being obvious at a glance. docker image inspect and tools like dive go further if you need to see individual files. Once you have identified it, the fix is normally one of three things: clean up inside the same RUN, add --no-install-recommends, or move the whole step into a build stage and copy only the artefact forward with COPY --from.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
dockerfile-run.markdown:
Docker has perhaps eight ideas in it. Most early confusion comes from three of them sounding interchangeable when they are not, image, container and Dockerfile, so this page defines each precisely and shows how they connect.

## The one-line version

A **Dockerfile** is a recipe. Building it produces an **image**, which is a read-only template. Running an image produces a **container**, which is a live process. A **registry** is where images are stored and shared.

```
Dockerfile ââdocker buildâââ¶ Image ââdocker runâââ¶ Container
                              â  â²
                    docker pushâ  âdocker pull
                              â¼  â
                            Registry
```

Everything else, volumes, networks, Compose, exists to make containers useful together.

## Image

A **read-only template** containing everything needed to run an application: the code, the language runtime, system libraries, and the metadata describing how to start it.

An image is built from **layers**, one per instruction in the Dockerfile, stacked and presented as a single filesystem. Layers are what make Docker efficient: they are content-addressed and shared, so ten images built on `node:22-alpine` store that base exactly once on disk and pull it exactly once from a registry.

```bash
docker images
```

```
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
myapp        1.0       a3f2c1d4e5b6   2 hours ago    142MB
node         22-alpine 7b8c9d0e1f2a   3 days ago     135MB
```

Two consequences of the layer model worth internalising early. Layers are **immutable**, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space in the image, and is still recoverable, which is why a deleted secret is a leaked secret. And layers are **cached**, so the order of instructions in a Dockerfile largely determines how fast rebuilds are.

Go deeper: [Docker images](/tutorials/docker/docker-images) and [image layers](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-layers).

## Container

A **running instance** of an image. If the image is the recipe, the container is the meal.

Technically it is an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, process table, network stack and hostname; cgroups cap what CPU and memory it can consume. There is no virtual machine and no guest operating system. This is why a container starts in milliseconds where a VM takes a minute.

Docker adds one **thin writable layer** on top of the image's read-only layers. Every file the container creates or modifies lands there, and **it is deleted with the container**. That single fact explains most Docker surprises for newcomers: your database is empty again because its data lived in the writable layer of a container that no longer exists.

```bash
docker ps
```

```
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS         PORTS                    NAMES
9f2c1a4b7e3d   myapp:1.0   Up 4 minutes   0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp   api
```

Containers are **ephemeral** by design. Treat them as disposable and keep anything that must survive in a volume.

Go deeper: [Docker containers](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers) and [the container lifecycle](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-lifecycle).

## Dockerfile

A plain text file of instructions for building an image, executed top to bottom:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
```

Each instruction produces a layer. The reason the package manifest is copied and installed *before* the source is that Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so copying source first would reinstall every dependency on every code edit.

Go deeper: [Dockerfile basics](/tutorials/docker/dockerfile-basics).

## Registry

Storage and distribution for images. GitHub, but for images rather than source. You `push` to share and `pull` to consume.

```bash
docker pull postgres:17
docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
```

**Docker Hub** is the default: if you run `docker pull nginx` with no registry prefix, that is where it comes from. Most organisations also use a private registry. GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry. For their own images.

A **tag** such as `1.0` or `latest` is a mutable pointer to an image, not a permanent name. `latest` in particular is just a default tag with no special meaning; it does not track the newest version. A **digest** (`@sha256:â¦`) is immutable and is what you pin when reproducibility matters.

Go deeper: [Docker Hub and registries](/tutorials/docker/docker-images-hub).

## Volume

Storage that outlives the container. Since the container's writable layer is destroyed with it, anything that must persist, database files, uploads, goes in a volume.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

Three kinds, and the distinction comes up constantly:

| Type | Written as | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Named volume** | `-v pgdata:/var/lib/â¦` | Docker manages it; the default for data |
| **Bind mount** | `-v ./src:/app/src` | A host directory; the default for development |
| **tmpfs** | `--tmpfs /tmp` | Memory only; never touches disk |

Go deeper: [Docker volumes](/tutorials/docker/docker-volumes).

## Network

Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other **by container name**, which is Docker's built-in DNS at work:

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapp:1.0
```

The API connects to `db:5432`. No IP addresses, no `--link`, nothing to update when a container restarts with a different address.

Note that `localhost` inside a container means *that container*, not the host and not another container. Expecting `localhost:5432` to reach a database in a different container is one of the most common beginner errors.

Go deeper: [container networking](/tutorials/docker/docker-containers-networking).

## Docker Compose

Real applications are several containers. Compose describes them in one file so the whole stack starts together:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down
```

Compose creates a network automatically, which is why `db` resolves as a hostname without any extra configuration.

It is a **single-host** tool. Excellent for development and small deployments, not a replacement for an orchestrator. Once you need scheduling across machines, rolling updates and self-healing, that is [Kubernetes](/tutorials/kubernetes/introduction-to-kubernetes).

## Client and daemon

One more piece, because it explains a whole class of error messages.

The `docker` command is a **client**. It does almost nothing itself. It sends requests over a socket to the **daemon** (`dockerd`), which builds images, runs containers and manages storage.

```
docker CLI ââ/var/run/docker.sockâââ¶ dockerd âââ¶ containerd âââ¶ runc âââ¶ your process
```

So `Cannot connect to the Docker daemon` means the CLI is installed and working, and nothing is listening. Start the service. And `permission denied ... docker.sock` means the daemon is running but your user cannot talk to its socket.

It also explains why the build context is *sent* to the daemon: the daemon may not be on your machine at all.

## The vocabulary, condensed

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Image** | Read-only template built from layers |
| **Layer** | One filesystem diff, produced by one instruction |
| **Container** | A running instance, plus a thin writable layer |
| **Dockerfile** | Build instructions for an image |
| **Build context** | The directory sent to the daemon at build time |
| **Registry** | Where images are stored and shared |
| **Tag** | A mutable pointer to an image |
| **Digest** | An immutable content hash |
| **Volume** | Storage that outlives the container |
| **Bind mount** | A host directory mounted into a container |
| **Network** | Container-to-container connectivity with DNS |
| **Compose** | Multi-container definition for one host |
| **Daemon** | `dockerd`, the process doing the work |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Image is the template, container is the running instance.** Recipe and meal.
- **A container's writable layer dies with it.** Anything that must survive belongs in a volume.
- **Layers are immutable and cached**: which sets both your rebuild speed and why deleted files still ship.
- **Containers are processes, not virtual machines.** Namespaces isolate, cgroups limit.
- **`latest` is just a default tag**, not the newest version. Pin a digest when it matters.
- **Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name**, and `localhost` means that container alone.
- **The CLI only talks to the daemon**, which is why "cannot connect" is a different problem from "not installed".

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-concepts-writable-layer',
    title: 'A database that keeps forgetting',
    description: 'A Postgres container is started with docker run, data is written, then the container is removed and recreated from the same image. The data is gone. Which concept explains this?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Writes go to the container\'s thin writable layer, which is deleted with the container. Persistence requires a volume' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'The image was rebuilt between runs, so the previous data was overwritten' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Postgres containers require --restart always to keep their data' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'Data written by a container is stored in the image and needs docker commit to be saved' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'An image is read-only. Docker gives each container a thin writable layer on top, and every file the container creates or changes lands there, including the entire Postgres data directory. Removing the container removes that layer and everything in it. Mounting a named volume at the data path, such as -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data, keeps the files under Docker\'s management so a new container from the same image picks up exactly where the last one left off.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'No rebuild happened, and rebuilding an image would not touch a running container\'s data anyway.',
      c: '--restart controls whether Docker restarts a container automatically. It has no bearing on storage.',
      d: 'docker commit does snapshot a container into a new image, but treating that as a persistence mechanism is an anti-pattern. Data belongs in a volume, not baked into images.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?**

An image is a read-only template: the application, its runtime, its libraries and the metadata describing how to start it, stored as a stack of layers. A container is a running instance created from that image, with a thin writable layer on top for anything it changes. One image can back any number of containers simultaneously, each with its own writable layer, in the same way one class can have many instances. The practical consequence is that images persist and containers are disposable.

**Where does data written inside a container go?**

Into the container's writable layer, which exists only as long as the container does. Remove the container and every file it created is removed with it, which is why a database restarted from the same image comes back empty. Mount a named volume at the path that matters (`-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) and the data lives outside the container lifecycle. Bind mounts do the same thing with a specific host directory, which is what you usually want in development.

**What is a Docker layer and why does it matter?**

Each Dockerfile instruction produces one layer, a filesystem diff, and the image is those layers stacked into a single view. They matter for three reasons. They are shared, so images built on the same base store and transfer it once. They are cached, so ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing makes rebuilds dramatically faster. And they are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space and remains extractable from the image.

**What is a Docker registry and is Docker Hub the only one?**

A registry stores and distributes images, the way a Git host stores repositories. Docker Hub is the default, `docker pull nginx` with no prefix goes there, and hosts official images for most common software. It is not the only option, and most organisations push their own images to a private registry such as GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry or Azure Container Registry. Prefixing the image name with a hostname selects one: `ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0`.

**Do I need Docker Compose or Kubernetes?**

Compose if you are running several containers on one machine. A local development stack, a small single-server deployment. It defines services, networks and volumes in one file and starts them together, and it is the right tool most of the time. Kubernetes when you need containers scheduled across multiple machines with rolling updates, self-healing and autoscaling. They solve different problems, and starting with Compose costs nothing if you later move: the concepts transfer directly.

**Why can't my container reach another container on localhost?**

Because `localhost` inside a container refers to that container and nothing else. Each one has its own network namespace and its own loopback interface. Put both on the same user-defined network and use the container name as the hostname: `docker network create appnet`, start each with `--network appnet`, then connect to `db:5432`. Compose does this for you automatically, which is why service names work as hostnames there without any configuration.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile, how to combine them, when to use exec vs shell form, and how to override both at runtime.
Both define what runs when a container starts, and the difference between them is one of the most frequently asked Docker questions.
ENTRYPOINT defines what runs. CMD defines the default arguments.
Everything else follows from how each behaves when you pass arguments to docker run.

sections.title: The behavioural difference
paragraphs: That is the whole distinction. A worked example:

codeBlock.code:
FROM alpine
CMD ["echo", "hello"]

sections.title: Using them together
paragraphs: This is the idiomatic pattern, and it is what most well-built images do:
ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD supplies a default argument the user can override. The container always runs Python, but which script is up to the caller.
Another common shape. A tool with a sensible default subcommand:

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
CMD ["app.py"]

sections.title: Exec form vs shell form
paragraphs: Both instructions accept two syntaxes, and choosing wrongly causes a real and confusing bug.
Use exec form. The signal behaviour is the reason, and it is not a small detail.
With shell form, /bin/sh is PID 1 and your application is a child process. docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1, the shell, which does not forward it. Your application never learns it should shut down.
Docker waits 10 seconds, then SIGKILLs everything.

The symptoms are recognisable: containers always take exactly 10 seconds to stop, in-flight requests are cut off, and graceful shutdown code never runs. On Kubernetes the same problem makes every rolling deploy drop connections.
Variable expansion and shell operators only work in shell form:
The fix that gives you both is exec, which replaces the shell rather than spawning a child:
exec means the shell process is replaced by node, so node becomes PID 1 and receives signals normally.

codeBlock.code:
CMD ["node", "server.js"]      # exec form. JSON array
CMD node server.js             # shell form

sections.title: Entrypoint scripts
paragraphs: The standard pattern for images needing setup before the main process:

Two details make this work. exec "$@" runs whatever CMD supplied, replacing the script so the application ends up as PID 1 with working signal handling. And because CMD is still overridable, docker run myimage sh drops you into a shell while still running the setup first.
Omitting exec, writing just "$@", is the single most common bug in entrypoint scripts. The script stays PID 1, signals go to it, and graceful shutdown breaks.

codeBlock.code:
#!/bin/sh
set -e

# Setup: wait for dependencies, run migrations, render config
until nc -z "$DB_HOST" 5432; do
  echo "waiting for database"
  sleep 1
done

# Hand over. Exec replaces this script, so the app becomes PID 1
exec "$@"

sections.title: Overriding at runtime
paragraphs: --entrypoint is how you get a shell in an image whose entrypoint immediately runs something else. Invaluable for debugging a container that exits instantly.
Note the asymmetry: --entrypoint takes only the executable. Arguments to it go after the image name.

codeBlock.code:
docker run myimage other-arg              # overrides CMD
docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh myimage   # overrides ENTRYPOINT

sections.title: Inheritance
paragraphs: A child image's ENTRYPOINT resets the inherited CMD to null. If you set ENTRYPOINT in a derived image and rely on the base image's CMD, you get nothing:

codeBlock.code:
FROM someimage        # has ENTRYPOINT ["app"] and CMD ["--serve"]
ENTRYPOINT ["wrapper"]
# CMD is now empty. You must restate it
CMD ["--serve"]

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile uses CMD node server.js in shell form. Every docker stop takes exactly 10 seconds and the application's shutdown handler never runs. Why?
An image has ENTRYPOINT ["python"] and CMD ["app.py"]. What runs for docker run myimage other.py?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in Docker?

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD defines the default arguments passed to it. The practical difference shows at runtime: arguments given to docker run replace CMD entirely but are appended to ENTRYPOINT. So an image with ENTRYPOINT ["python"] and CMD ["app.py"] runs python app.py by default and python other.py when you pass other.py. The executable is fixed and the caller controls the arguments.
Should I use CMD or ENTRYPOINT?

Use both together for an image that is one specific tool: ENTRYPOINT fixes the binary, CMD provides overridable defaults. Use CMD alone for a general-purpose image where users may want to run arbitrary commands, such as a language runtime image. Use an ENTRYPOINT script ending in exec "$@" when setup must happen before the main process. Waiting for a dependency, rendering configuration, running migrations.
What is the difference between exec form and shell form?

Exec form is the JSON array syntax, CMD ["node", "server.js"], and runs the binary directly as PID 1. Shell form, CMD node server.js, runs it via /bin/sh -c, making the shell PID 1 with your application as a child. Exec form is strongly preferred because only PID 1 receives signals, with shell form your application never sees SIGTERM and graceful shutdown silently never happens. Shell form does allow variable expansion and pipes, which exec form does not.
Why does my container take 10 seconds to stop?

Because your application is not receiving SIGTERM, so docker stop waits the full grace period and then SIGKILLs it. The usual cause is shell form: /bin/sh is PID 1 and does not forward signals to its child. Switch to exec form so your process is PID 1. If you have an entrypoint script, make sure it ends with exec "$@" rather than plain "$@", since without exec the script remains PID 1 and absorbs the signal.
How do I use an environment variable in CMD?

Exec form does not expand variables, CMD ["node", "app.js", "--port", "$PORT"] passes the literal string $PORT. The safe way to get expansion without losing signal handling is CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec node app.js --port $PORT"]. The exec is essential: it replaces the shell process with your application so it becomes PID 1. Plain shell form expands the variable but leaves the shell as PID 1 and breaks shutdown.
How do I override ENTRYPOINT to debug a container?

docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it myimage replaces the entrypoint and drops you into a shell, which is the standard way to inspect an image whose entrypoint exits immediately or crashes. Note that --entrypoint accepts only the executable. Any arguments go after the image name. For a distroless image with no shell at all, copy the filesystem out with docker create and docker cp instead.

dockerfile-cmd-entrypoint.markdown:
These are the instructions that turn a Dockerfile that builds into one you would put in production. Two of them do considerably less than their names suggest, which is where most of the confusion lives.

## WORKDIR

`WORKDIR` sets the directory for every `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`, `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` that follows, and it is where you land when you `docker exec` into the container.

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json .        # â /app/package.json
RUN npm ci                 # runs in /app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]  # runs /app/server.js
```

It **creates the directory** if it does not exist, so `RUN mkdir -p /app` before it is redundant.

### Never use RUN cd

```dockerfile
RUN cd /app && npm ci      # the cd dies with the shell
WORKDIR /app               # persists for every later instruction
RUN npm ci
```

Each `RUN` starts a fresh shell, so a `cd` inside one has no effect on the next. This is a common source of files landing in `/` when the author was certain they were in `/app`.

### Always use an absolute path

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app        # unambiguous
WORKDIR app         # relative to whatever WORKDIR came before
```

Relative `WORKDIR` stacks, which works until someone inserts a `WORKDIR` above it.

### The permission gotcha

`WORKDIR` creates directories owned by **root**, even when a `USER` instruction came earlier:

```dockerfile
USER node
WORKDIR /app/cache     # created as root, and node cannot write to it
```

```
Error: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/cache/tmp'
```

Create and chown the directory before dropping privileges:

```dockerfile
RUN mkdir -p /app/cache && chown node:node /app/cache
USER node
WORKDIR /app
```

## EXPOSE publishes nothing

This is the single most misunderstood instruction in Docker.

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 3000          # TCP by default
EXPOSE 8080/tcp
EXPOSE 53/udp
EXPOSE 80 443
```

`EXPOSE` is **metadata**. It opens no port, maps nothing, and changes no networking behaviour. A container with `EXPOSE 3000` is not reachable from your host:

```bash
docker run myapp
curl localhost:3000
```

```
curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 3000: Connection refused
```

Publishing is a runtime decision:

```bash
docker run -p 8080:3000 myapp     # host 8080 â container 3000
```

Equally: a container **without** `EXPOSE` is still reachable by other containers on the same Docker network, and still publishable with `-p`. The instruction genuinely changes nothing about connectivity.

So why write it? Three real reasons: it documents the interface for whoever runs the image, `docker run -P` uses it to auto-publish every exposed port to a random host port, and Compose and other tooling read it when wiring services.

If a published port still refuses connections, the usual cause is the application binding to `127.0.0.1` inside the container rather than `0.0.0.0`. Localhost inside a container is that container alone.

## USER

Containers run as **root** by default. That is unnecessary for nearly every application and materially worse when combined with a mounted host path.

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .

USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Many official images already ship a non-root user: `node`, `nginx`, `postgres`. For your own:

```dockerfile
# Alpine
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

# Debian / Ubuntu
RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup appuser
USER appuser
```

Place `USER` after anything that needs root, and step back up briefly when you must:

```dockerfile
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini
USER appuser
```

### Use a numeric UID if you deploy to Kubernetes

```dockerfile
USER 1000
```

Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot: true` check runs before the image's user database is consulted, so a *named* user cannot be verified and the Pod fails to start:

```
Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image has non-numeric user (appuser),
cannot verify user is non-root
```

A numeric `USER` avoids it. `USER 1000:1000` sets the group too.

## LABEL

Key-value metadata, visible in `docker inspect` and filterable with `docker images --filter`.

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
```

Use the OCI standard keys rather than inventing your own. Tooling reads them, and `org.opencontainers.image.source` in particular is what makes GitHub link a published package back to its repository automatically.

Combine labels into one instruction; each `LABEL` is a layer.

```bash
docker inspect myapp --format='{{json .Config.Labels}}'
```

## VOLUME is usually a mistake

```dockerfile
VOLUME /app/data
```

This declares that a path should be backed by a volume, and Docker creates an **anonymous volume** for it whenever the container starts without an explicit `-v`.

That sounds helpful and mostly is not:

- **Anonymous volumes accumulate.** Every `docker run` without `-v` leaves another one behind after the container is removed, quietly filling the disk until someone runs `docker volume prune`.
- **The path becomes effectively frozen.** Any `COPY` or `RUN` that writes to a declared `VOLUME` path in a *later* instruction is discarded, because the volume is mounted over it at container start. Seeding a database image with data this way silently does nothing.
- **The decision is not the image's to make.** Whoever runs the container knows whether they want a named volume, a bind mount or nothing at all.

Declare the path in your documentation and let `docker run -v` or a Compose `volumes:` entry do the work. `VOLUME` earns its place mainly in database images, where accidentally running without persistence is the worse failure.

## HEALTHCHECK

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
```

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `--interval` | 30s | How often the check runs |
| `--timeout` | 30s | Check is a failure if it exceeds this |
| `--start-period` | 0s | Failures here do not count toward `--retries` |
| `--retries` | 3 | Consecutive failures before `unhealthy` |

`--start-period` is the one that matters most. Without enough of it, a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

```bash
docker ps
```

```
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS
9f2c1a4b7e3d   myapp:1.0   Up 2 minutes (healthy)
```

### Kubernetes ignores this entirely

Worth being blunt about, because it is widely assumed otherwise: **Kubernetes does not read a Dockerfile's `HEALTHCHECK`.** It uses its own `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe`, and an image's healthcheck has no effect on scheduling, restarts or traffic routing.

`HEALTHCHECK` is useful for plain `docker run`, Docker Compose (`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`) and Docker Swarm. On Kubernetes, define probes in the Pod spec instead:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
```

---

## Knowledge Check

After installing dependencies and copying the source (owned by node:node), you need to: document that the app listens on port 3000, switch to the non-root "node" user, and start the app with "node server.js" using exec form. Which set of instructions, in order, is correct?',
    options: [
      {
        id: 'a',
        text: 'EXPOSE 3000\nUSER node\nCMD ["node", "server.js"]',
      },
      {
        id: 'b',
        text: 'USER node\nEXPOSE 3000\nCMD node server.js',
      },
      {
        id: 'c',
        text: 'PORT 3000\nUSER node\nCMD ["node", "server.js"]',
      },
      {
        id: 'd',
        text: 'EXPOSE 3000\nUSER root\nCMD ["node", "server.js"]',
      },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: '"EXPOSE 3000" documents that the container listens on port 3000 (a hint for users running the image, not an actual port mapping). "USER node" switches the container to run as the non-root "node" user for better security. "CMD [\\"node\\", \\"server.js\\"]" uses exec form, which runs the process directly as PID 1 without a shell wrapper, allowing it to receive signals like SIGTERM properly.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: '"CMD node server.js" uses shell form instead of exec form. In shell form, the command runs as a child of "/bin/sh -c", so the Node process is not PID 1 and may not receive shutdown signals (like SIGTERM) directly, making graceful shutdown harder.',
      c: '"PORT" is not a valid Dockerfile instruction. The correct instruction for documenting a listening port is "EXPOSE".',
      d: 'Setting "USER root" runs the container process as the root user, defeating the purpose of switching to a non-root user for security. The requirement was to switch to the "node" user specifically.',
    },
  }}
/>

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `RUN cd /app` | Has no effect on later instructions |
| `WORKDIR` after `USER` | Directory owned by root; app cannot write |
| Expecting `EXPOSE` to publish | Port unreachable; needs `-p` |
| App binds `127.0.0.1` | `-p` maps correctly and still refuses |
| Named `USER` on Kubernetes | `runAsNonRoot` cannot verify it; Pod fails |
| `VOLUME` then `COPY` to that path | Copied data silently discarded |
| `VOLUME` in an app image | Anonymous volumes pile up on the host |
| Relying on `HEALTHCHECK` in Kubernetes | Ignored; define probes instead |
| No `--start-period` | Slow starters marked unhealthy while booting |

## Quick reference

| Task | Instruction |
|---|---|
| Set working directory | `WORKDIR /app` |
| Document a port | `EXPOSE 3000` |
| Publish a port | `docker run -p 8080:3000` |
| Publish all exposed | `docker run -P` |
| Drop privileges | `USER 1000:1000` |
| Standard metadata | `LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="â¦"` |
| Health check | `HEALTHCHECK --start-period=40s CMD â¦` |
| Read health status | `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <c>` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **`WORKDIR` replaces `RUN cd`**, creates the directory, and does so as root even after `USER`.
- **`EXPOSE` publishes nothing.** It is documentation plus a hint for `-P` and Compose.
- **A refused connection on a published port** is usually the app bound to `127.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`.
- **Set `USER`**, and make it numeric if the image will run under Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot`.
- **`VOLUME` is usually the wrong call**: anonymous volumes accumulate, and later writes to that path vanish.
- **Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK`.** Use `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe`.
- **Use OCI `LABEL` keys**, and combine them into one instruction.

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-volume-seed-lost',
    title: 'Seed data that disappears',
    description: 'A Dockerfile declares VOLUME /app/data and then, on a later line, COPY seed.json /app/data/. The build succeeds, but /app/data is empty in every container. Why?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'A volume is mounted over the declared path at container start, hiding anything written to it in later build instructions' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'COPY cannot write to a directory that has been declared with VOLUME, so the build silently skips it' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Anonymous volumes are read-only until a named volume is attached with -v' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'VOLUME must come after all COPY instructions or the Dockerfile fails to parse' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'Declaring VOLUME marks the path as externally backed. When the container starts, Docker mounts a volume there, an anonymous one if you did not supply your own, and that mount sits on top of whatever the image layers contain at that path, so the seed file is present in the image but invisible at runtime. Either drop the VOLUME declaration and let the operator decide with -v, or copy the seed elsewhere and have an entrypoint script populate the volume on first start, which is what official database images do.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'The COPY genuinely runs and the file really is in the image layer. It is masked at runtime by the mount, not skipped at build time.',
      c: 'Anonymous volumes are writable. Read-only behaviour would require mounting with the :ro option.',
      d: 'Instruction order does not cause a parse error. Placing VOLUME last avoids this specific surprise, but the Dockerfile is valid either way.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does EXPOSE actually open a port in Docker?**

No. `EXPOSE` records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling. Nothing more. It opens nothing, maps nothing, and a container without it is just as reachable. To reach the application from your host you need `-p 8080:3000` at `docker run`, and containers on the same Docker network can reach each other regardless. The one functional use is `docker run -P`, which publishes every exposed port to a random host port.

**Why can't I reach my container even though I used -p?**

Almost always because the application is bound to `127.0.0.1` inside the container. Localhost inside a container refers to that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Configure the server to bind `0.0.0.0`, in Express that is `app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0')`, in Flask `--host=0.0.0.0`. Confirm what is actually listening with `docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp` before changing anything else.

**Why does my container get "permission denied" after I added USER?**

Usually because a directory was created after the `USER` instruction. `WORKDIR` creates directories owned by root regardless of the current user, so `USER node` followed by `WORKDIR /app/cache` leaves the application unable to write to its own cache. Create and chown the directory while still root, then drop privileges. The other common cause is copied files still owned by root, which `COPY --chown=node:node` fixes in the same layer.

**Should I use VOLUME in my Dockerfile?**

Usually not, for application images. It creates an anonymous volume on every run that omits `-v`, and those pile up on the host until someone prunes them. Worse, any `COPY` or `RUN` writing to that path *after* the declaration is masked at runtime by the mount, so seed data silently disappears. Let whoever runs the container decide with `-v` or a Compose `volumes:` entry. It is defensible in database images, where the greater risk is someone running without persistence at all.

**Does Kubernetes use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK?**

No, and this trips up a lot of teams. Kubernetes ignores the image's `HEALTHCHECK` completely and relies on `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` defined in the Pod spec. An image with a perfect healthcheck gets no scheduling, restart or traffic-routing benefit on Kubernetes. `HEALTHCHECK` remains useful for plain `docker run`, for Docker Swarm, and for Compose's `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`.

**What is the difference between WORKDIR and RUN cd?**

`RUN cd /app` changes directory inside the shell that runs that one instruction, and that shell exits immediately afterwards, so the next instruction starts back at the previous directory. `WORKDIR /app` sets the directory for every subsequent instruction, persists into the final image as the container's starting directory, and creates the path if it does not exist. Use `WORKDIR`; the only place `cd` makes sense is chained within a single `RUN`, as in `RUN cd /src && make install`.
