dockerfile-env-arg.subtitle: Learn the difference between ENV and ARG in a Dockerfile, how ARG scoping works, why neither is safe for secrets, and how ARG affects the build cache.
verifiedFacts: Production workloads utilizing Dockerfile ENV vs ARG must follow least-privilege security boundaries and declarative state.
Verified against standard cloud-native specifications and official Docker documentation.
Hands-on commands can be executed immediately in our Docker in-browser playground.

keyConcepts.explanation: Learn the difference between ENV and ARG in a Dockerfile, how ARG scoping works, why neither is safe for secrets, and how ARG affects the build cache.
Ensure declarative state, idempotent changes, and version control when deploying Docker.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn the difference between ENV and ARG in a Dockerfile, how ARG scoping works, why neither is safe for secrets, and how ARG affects the build cache.

Both define variables, but they live in different phases of the image's life. ARG exists only while the image is being built. ENV is baked into the image and present in every container started from it.
Getting them backwards produces one of two outcomes: a variable your application cannot see at runtime, or a secret permanently readable by anyone who pulls the image.

sections.title: The core difference
paragraphs: That fourth row is the one people miss. ARG is gone at runtime, which feels private, but the value it was given is written into the image's build metadata regardless.

sections.title: ENV: runtime configuration
paragraphs: One instruction for several variables, because each ENV is its own layer. The older space-separated form (ENV NODE_ENV production) still parses but is deprecated and cannot set multiple values. Use =.
Values are visible to every RUN that follows, to the container's main process, and to any later docker exec session:
ENV sets a default, and -e overrides it without a rebuild:

That is the point of it: the image ships sensible defaults, the deployment overrides what differs. Precedence runs docker run -e → Compose environment: → Compose env_file: → Dockerfile ENV, with the leftmost winning.
ENV also expands earlier variables, which is how you extend PATH:
Good uses: default ports and log levels, PATH-style variables, tool configuration such as PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 or PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1.
Never: API tokens, passwords, connection strings with credentials. Those come from the orchestrator at runtime.

codeBlock.code:
ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    PORT=3000 \
    LOG_LEVEL=info

sections.title: ARG: build-time parameters
paragraphs: With no default and no --build-arg, the value is simply empty. The build does not fail. That silent emptiness is worth guarding when the value matters:

codeBlock.code:
ARG APP_VERSION=1.0.0
ARG GIT_COMMIT

RUN echo "Building $APP_VERSION from $GIT_COMMIT"

sections.title: Scoping is where ARG surprises people
paragraphs: ARG is the only instruction allowed before FROM, which is how you parameterise the base image:
Omit that second declaration and $NODE_VERSION expands to nothing, with no warning:
The same rule applies to every stage of a multi-stage build:

codeBlock.code:
ARG NODE_VERSION=22
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine

# The pre-FROM ARG is out of scope here, re-declare to use it
ARG NODE_VERSION
RUN echo "Running on Node $NODE_VERSION"

sections.title: Promoting ARG to ENV
paragraphs: The standard pattern when a build-time value must also exist at runtime:

Do this only for things that are safe to publish: a version string, a build date, a commit SHA. Promoting a token to ENV takes something already in the build history and makes it visible in docker inspect too.

You want to build an image tagged myapp:3.0.0, passing a build argument APP_VERSION=3.0.0 (which the Dockerfile promotes from ARG to ENV). Then you want to run the container and print the value of APP_VERSION from inside it. Which sequence of commands is correct?

codeBlock.code:
ARG APP_VERSION=1.0.0
ENV APP_VERSION=${APP_VERSION}

sections.title: Why ARG is not safe for secrets
paragraphs: This looks careful. The file is deleted in the same layer:
But the value was passed as a build argument, and build arguments are recorded:
Anyone who can pull the image can read that. Rotating the token is the only remedy once an image has shipped.
The fix is a BuildKit secret mount, which makes the value available to one instruction and writes it to no layer:

codeBlock.code:
ARG NPM_TOKEN
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc \
 && npm ci \
 && rm .npmrc

sections.title: ARG and the build cache
paragraphs: An ARG invalidates the cache from the point it is first used, not from where it is declared. Declaring ten build args and using one changes nothing about the other nine.
That makes it a precise cache-busting tool:
Everything above that line stays cached; everything from it rebuilds.

codeBlock.code:
ARG CACHE_BUST=1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y

sections.title: Predefined build arguments
paragraphs: Some args exist without being declared. The platform ones are what make cross-compilation work:
The build stage runs natively on the builder and cross-compiles to the target, which avoids emulation entirely and is what stops an arm64 build producing an exec format error on amd64 servers.
HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are also predefined and, usefully, are excluded from docker history.

codeBlock.code:
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.23 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/server .

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile declares ARG NODE_VERSION=22 before FROM, uses it successfully in the FROM line, then RUN echo "Node $NODE_VERSION" prints "Node" with no number. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between ARG and ENV in a Dockerfile?

ARG defines a variable that exists only while docker build runs and is gone once the image is finished. Nothing inside a running container can see it. ENV writes a variable into the image so it is present during the remainder of the build and in every container started from that image. Use ARG for things that shape how the image is built, such as a base image version or a commit SHA, and ENV for configuration the application reads at runtime, such as a port or log level.
Is it safe to pass a secret with --build-arg?

No. The value is recorded in the image's build metadata and docker history --no-trunc prints it back, even if the file you wrote it to was deleted in the same RUN. Anyone who can pull the image can recover it, and rotating the credential is the only fix after the fact. Use a BuildKit secret mount instead, RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token … with docker build --secret id=token,env=TOKEN, which exposes the value to a single instruction and writes it to no layer.
Why is my ARG empty after FROM?

Because the region before the first FROM is a separate scope, and build stages do not inherit from it. That scope exists so the base image itself can be parameterised. Add a bare ARG NODE_VERSION after FROM to bring the value into that stage, and repeat it in every stage of a multi-stage build that needs it. Docker gives no warning. An out-of-scope variable simply expands to an empty string.
How do I override an environment variable at runtime?

docker run -e LOG_LEVEL=debug myapp overrides whatever the Dockerfile's ENV set, with no rebuild. In Compose, use environment: for inline values or env_file: for a file. Precedence runs from most to least specific: docker run -e beats Compose environment:, which beats env_file:, which beats the Dockerfile's ENV. Treat ENV as the image's default rather than a fixed value.
Why does changing --build-arg rebuild my whole image?

It does not rebuild the whole image. It invalidates the cache from the point the argument is first used, and everything above stays cached. If that feels like everything, the ARG is probably referenced earlier than it needs to be, often in a FROM line or an early RUN. Moving its first use further down keeps the expensive install layers cached. The same behaviour is useful deliberately: ARG CACHE_BUST placed just above an apt-get upgrade forces exactly that step to re-run.
Should I use ENV or a .env file for configuration?

Different tools for different jobs. Dockerfile ENV bakes a default into the image, which is right for values that are part of the image itself: a PATH addition, PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, a default port. A .env file is read by Docker Compose on your machine and never enters the image, which makes it right for per-environment values and for anything you would not publish. In production the orchestrator supplies the values, typically from a Kubernetes Secret or a parameter store, and the image's ENV defaults just fill the gaps.

dockerfile-env-arg.markdown:
A Dockerfile is a script of instructions for building an image. Each instruction produces a layer, and understanding that one fact explains most of what makes a Dockerfile fast or slow, large or small.

## A complete example

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies first. This layer is cached until package files change
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Source last. Changes here do not invalidate the install above
COPY . .

ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000

USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 myapp:1.0
```

That trailing `.` is the **build context**. The directory sent to the Docker daemon before the build starts. It is not the Dockerfile location, which is why a large context slows builds even when nothing is copied.

## The instructions

| Instruction | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `FROM` | The base image. Always first (after any `ARG`) |
| `WORKDIR` | Sets and creates the working directory |
| `COPY` | Copies files from the build context into the image |
| `ADD` | Like COPY, plus URL fetching and auto-extraction |
| `RUN` | Executes a command at **build** time, creating a layer |
| `CMD` | Default command at **run** time |
| `ENTRYPOINT` | Fixed executable at run time |
| `ENV` | Environment variable, persisted into the image |
| `ARG` | Build-time variable, **not** present at runtime |
| `EXPOSE` | Documents a port. Publishes nothing |
| `USER` | Switches the user for subsequent instructions and runtime |
| `VOLUME` | Declares a mount point |
| `HEALTHCHECK` | How Docker tests container health |

### FROM

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
FROM node:22-alpine AS build        # named stage, for multi-stage
FROM node@sha256:abc123...          # pinned by digest, fully reproducible
```

Pin a specific version. `FROM node` means `node:latest`, which changes without warning and makes your build non-reproducible.

### COPY vs ADD

**Use COPY.** It does exactly one thing: copy files from the context.

`ADD` additionally fetches URLs and auto-extracts local tar archives. Both behaviours are surprising. The auto-extraction in particular has caused real bugs when a `.tar.gz` was meant to be copied verbatim. Use `COPY`, and `RUN curl` when you genuinely need to download something.

```dockerfile
COPY package*.json ./        # explicit and predictable
COPY --chown=node:node . .   # set ownership while copying
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist   # from another stage
```

### RUN and the layer problem

Each `RUN` is a layer, and **layers are additive**. A file created in one and deleted in a later one still ships in the image:

```dockerfile
# Wrong. The apt cache is in the image forever
RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Right. One layer, cleaned up inside it
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
```

`--no-install-recommends` alone often removes tens of megabytes.

### ENV vs ARG

```dockerfile
ARG NODE_VERSION=22          # build time only, gone at runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production      # persists into the running container
```

`ARG` values are passed with `--build-arg` and are **not secret**. They appear in `docker history`. Never pass a token or password as a build arg. Use BuildKit secrets instead:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npmtoken) npm ci
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npmtoken,src=./token.txt -t myapp .
```

### EXPOSE publishes nothing

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 3000
```

This is **documentation**. It records which port the application listens on for humans and tooling; it does not open or publish anything. Publishing happens at run time with `-p 3000:3000`.

### USER

```dockerfile
USER node
```

Containers run as **root by default**, which is unnecessary for almost every application and a real risk if the container is compromised. Most official images provide a non-root user. Place `USER` after any instruction needing root, such as package installation.

## Layer caching is the whole game

Docker reuses cached layers up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. **Order instructions from least to most frequently changing:**

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine          # changes rarely
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./        # changes when dependencies change
RUN npm ci --omit=dev        # expensive. Keep it cached
COPY . .                     # changes on every commit
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Putting `COPY . .` before `RUN npm ci` means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile mistake and costs minutes on each build.

For `RUN` instructions, the cache key is the **command string**, not what it produces. `RUN apt-get update` stays cached indefinitely even as upstream packages change, which is why it must be chained with the `install` in the same instruction.

## .dockerignore

Without one, `COPY . .` pulls in `node_modules`, `.git`, local `.env` files and build output:

```
node_modules
.git
.env
dist
*.log
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
```

This reduces image size, speeds up the build by shrinking the context, and, importantly, stops local secrets being baked into the image.

## Multi-stage builds

Build in one stage, ship from another. Tooling never reaches the final image:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a `scratch` image is a few megabytes against a 900 MB build image.

```bash
docker build --target build -t myapp:debug .   # stop at a named stage
```

## HEALTHCHECK

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
```

`docker ps` then shows `healthy` or `unhealthy`. `--start-period` is the one that matters, without enough of it, a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `COPY . .` before dependency install | Every build reinstalls everything |
| Cleaning up in a separate `RUN` | Deleted files still ship in the earlier layer |
| Using `ADD` for local files | Surprising auto-extraction |
| No `.dockerignore` | Bloated context, secrets in the image |
| Secrets in `ARG` | Visible in `docker history` |
| No `USER` | Container runs as root |
| `FROM node` with no tag | Non-reproducible builds |
| Shell-form `CMD` | Application never receives `SIGTERM` |

## Quick reference

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Build | `docker build -t <name>:<tag> .` |
| Build a specific stage | `docker build --target <stage> -t <name> .` |
| Build with an argument | `docker build --build-arg KEY=value .` |
| Build with a secret | `docker build --secret id=<n>,src=<file> .` |
| Different Dockerfile | `docker build -f path/to/Dockerfile .` |
| No cache | `docker build --no-cache .` |
| Inspect layers | `docker history <image>` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **Every instruction is a layer**, and order determines what stays cached.
- **Copy dependency manifests before source code**: the single biggest build-speed win.
- **Clean up inside the same `RUN`**; a later deletion does not shrink the image.
- **Use `COPY`, not `ADD`**: auto-extraction and URL fetching are surprising.
- **`EXPOSE` documents a port and publishes nothing.** Use `-p` at run time.
- **`ARG` values appear in `docker history`**: never pass secrets that way.
- **Set `USER`.** Containers run as root by default.
- **Always pin the base image tag**, and prefer exec-form `CMD`.

---

/>

    wrongExplanations: {

    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?**

`COPY` copies files and directories from the build context into the image, and does nothing else. `ADD` does the same but additionally fetches remote URLs and automatically extracts local tar archives. Both extras are surprising in practice. A `.tar.gz` you meant to copy verbatim gets unpacked instead. Use `COPY` for local files and `RUN curl` when you genuinely need to download something, which also lets you verify a checksum in the same layer.

**Why is my Docker build slow every time?**

Almost certainly instruction order. Docker caches layers up to the first instruction whose inputs changed and rebuilds everything after it, so `COPY . .` placed before your dependency install means every source edit reinstalls all dependencies. Copy the package manifest and lockfile first, run the install, then copy the source. A missing `.dockerignore` compounds it by sending `node_modules` and `.git` into the build context on every build.

**What does EXPOSE actually do?**

Only documentation. It records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling such as `docker run -P`, which publishes all exposed ports to random host ports. It does not open a port, publish one, or affect networking in any way. Reaching the application from the host requires `-p 3000:3000` at run time, and the container is reachable by other containers on the same network whether or not `EXPOSE` is present.

**What is the difference between ENV and ARG?**

`ARG` defines a build-time variable available only while the image is being built, and it is gone at runtime. `ENV` sets an environment variable baked into the image and present in every container started from it. A critical caveat: `ARG` values appear in `docker history`, so they must never carry secrets. Use BuildKit secret mounts, which make a value available during a single `RUN` without recording it in any layer.

**Should I use a multi-stage build?**

Almost always, for anything with a build step. Compilers, development dependencies and source code stay in the build stage and never reach the shipped image, which usually cuts size dramatically. A Go binary in a `scratch` image is a few megabytes against a 900 MB build environment. It also reduces attack surface, since a compiler in a production image is a tool an attacker can use. The cost is a few extra lines.

**Why does my container run as root and how do I change it?**

Because that is the default when no `USER` instruction is given, and most base images do not set one. It is unnecessary for nearly every application and increases the damage a compromise can do, particularly combined with a mounted host path. Add `USER node`, or whichever non-root user your base image provides, after any instructions that need root, such as package installation. On Kubernetes you can additionally enforce it with `runAsNonRoot: true`, which turns a root image into a visible startup failure rather than a silent risk.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Does EXPOSE actually open a port in Docker?

No. EXPOSE records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling. Nothing more. It opens nothing, maps nothing, and a container without it is just as reachable. To reach the application from your host you need -p 8080:3000 at docker run, and containers on the same Docker network can reach each other regardless. The one functional use is docker run -P, which publishes every exposed port to a random host port.
Why can't I reach my container even though I used -p?

Almost always because the application is bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container. Localhost inside a container refers to that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Configure the server to bind 0.0.0.0, in Express that is app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0'), in Flask --host=0.0.0.0. Confirm what is actually listening with docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp before changing anything else.
Why does my container get "permission denied" after I added USER?

Usually because a directory was created after the USER instruction. WORKDIR creates directories owned by root regardless of the current user, so USER node followed by WORKDIR /app/cache leaves the application unable to write to its own cache. Create and chown the directory while still root, then drop privileges. The other common cause is copied files still owned by root, which COPY --chown=node:node fixes in the same layer.
Should I use VOLUME in my Dockerfile?

Usually not, for application images. It creates an anonymous volume on every run that omits -v, and those pile up on the host until someone prunes them. Worse, any COPY or RUN writing to that path after the declaration is masked at runtime by the mount, so seed data silently disappears. Let whoever runs the container decide with -v or a Compose volumes: entry. It is defensible in database images, where the greater risk is someone running without persistence at all.
Does Kubernetes use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK?

No, and this trips up a lot of teams. Kubernetes ignores the image's HEALTHCHECK completely and relies on livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe defined in the Pod spec. An image with a perfect healthcheck gets no scheduling, restart or traffic-routing benefit on Kubernetes. HEALTHCHECK remains useful for plain docker run, for Docker Swarm, and for Compose's depends_on with condition: service_healthy.
What is the difference between WORKDIR and RUN cd?

RUN cd /app changes directory inside the shell that runs that one instruction, and that shell exits immediately afterwards, so the next instruction starts back at the previous directory. WORKDIR /app sets the directory for every subsequent instruction, persists into the final image as the container's starting directory, and creates the path if it does not exist. Use WORKDIR; the only place cd makes sense is chained within a single RUN, as in RUN cd /src && make install.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
dockerfile-workdir-expose.markdown:
These are the instructions that turn a Dockerfile that builds into one you would put in production. Two of them do considerably less than their names suggest, which is where most of the confusion lives.

## WORKDIR

`WORKDIR` sets the directory for every `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`, `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` that follows, and it is where you land when you `docker exec` into the container.

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json .        # â /app/package.json
RUN npm ci                 # runs in /app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]  # runs /app/server.js
```

It **creates the directory** if it does not exist, so `RUN mkdir -p /app` before it is redundant.

### Never use RUN cd

```dockerfile
RUN cd /app && npm ci      # the cd dies with the shell
WORKDIR /app               # persists for every later instruction
RUN npm ci
```

Each `RUN` starts a fresh shell, so a `cd` inside one has no effect on the next. This is a common source of files landing in `/` when the author was certain they were in `/app`.

### Always use an absolute path

```dockerfile
WORKDIR /app        # unambiguous
WORKDIR app         # relative to whatever WORKDIR came before
```

Relative `WORKDIR` stacks, which works until someone inserts a `WORKDIR` above it.

### The permission gotcha

`WORKDIR` creates directories owned by **root**, even when a `USER` instruction came earlier:

```dockerfile
USER node
WORKDIR /app/cache     # created as root, and node cannot write to it
```

```
Error: EACCES: permission denied, mkdir '/app/cache/tmp'
```

Create and chown the directory before dropping privileges:

```dockerfile
RUN mkdir -p /app/cache && chown node:node /app/cache
USER node
WORKDIR /app
```

## EXPOSE publishes nothing

This is the single most misunderstood instruction in Docker.

```dockerfile
EXPOSE 3000          # TCP by default
EXPOSE 8080/tcp
EXPOSE 53/udp
EXPOSE 80 443
```

`EXPOSE` is **metadata**. It opens no port, maps nothing, and changes no networking behaviour. A container with `EXPOSE 3000` is not reachable from your host:

```bash
docker run myapp
curl localhost:3000
```

```
curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 3000: Connection refused
```

Publishing is a runtime decision:

```bash
docker run -p 8080:3000 myapp     # host 8080 â container 3000
```

Equally: a container **without** `EXPOSE` is still reachable by other containers on the same Docker network, and still publishable with `-p`. The instruction genuinely changes nothing about connectivity.

So why write it? Three real reasons: it documents the interface for whoever runs the image, `docker run -P` uses it to auto-publish every exposed port to a random host port, and Compose and other tooling read it when wiring services.

If a published port still refuses connections, the usual cause is the application binding to `127.0.0.1` inside the container rather than `0.0.0.0`. Localhost inside a container is that container alone.

## USER

Containers run as **root** by default. That is unnecessary for nearly every application and materially worse when combined with a mounted host path.

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .

USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Many official images already ship a non-root user: `node`, `nginx`, `postgres`. For your own:

```dockerfile
# Alpine
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

# Debian / Ubuntu
RUN groupadd -r appgroup && useradd -r -g appgroup appuser
USER appuser
```

Place `USER` after anything that needs root, and step back up briefly when you must:

```dockerfile
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini
USER appuser
```

### Use a numeric UID if you deploy to Kubernetes

```dockerfile
USER 1000
```

Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot: true` check runs before the image's user database is consulted, so a *named* user cannot be verified and the Pod fails to start:

```
Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image has non-numeric user (appuser),
cannot verify user is non-root
```

A numeric `USER` avoids it. `USER 1000:1000` sets the group too.

## LABEL

Key-value metadata, visible in `docker inspect` and filterable with `docker images --filter`.

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
```

Use the OCI standard keys rather than inventing your own. Tooling reads them, and `org.opencontainers.image.source` in particular is what makes GitHub link a published package back to its repository automatically.

Combine labels into one instruction; each `LABEL` is a layer.

```bash
docker inspect myapp --format='{{json .Config.Labels}}'
```

## VOLUME is usually a mistake

```dockerfile
VOLUME /app/data
```

This declares that a path should be backed by a volume, and Docker creates an **anonymous volume** for it whenever the container starts without an explicit `-v`.

That sounds helpful and mostly is not:

- **Anonymous volumes accumulate.** Every `docker run` without `-v` leaves another one behind after the container is removed, quietly filling the disk until someone runs `docker volume prune`.
- **The path becomes effectively frozen.** Any `COPY` or `RUN` that writes to a declared `VOLUME` path in a *later* instruction is discarded, because the volume is mounted over it at container start. Seeding a database image with data this way silently does nothing.
- **The decision is not the image's to make.** Whoever runs the container knows whether they want a named volume, a bind mount or nothing at all.

Declare the path in your documentation and let `docker run -v` or a Compose `volumes:` entry do the work. `VOLUME` earns its place mainly in database images, where accidentally running without persistence is the worse failure.

## HEALTHCHECK

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
```

| Option | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `--interval` | 30s | How often the check runs |
| `--timeout` | 30s | Check is a failure if it exceeds this |
| `--start-period` | 0s | Failures here do not count toward `--retries` |
| `--retries` | 3 | Consecutive failures before `unhealthy` |

`--start-period` is the one that matters most. Without enough of it, a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

```bash
docker ps
```

```
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS
9f2c1a4b7e3d   myapp:1.0   Up 2 minutes (healthy)
```

### Kubernetes ignores this entirely

Worth being blunt about, because it is widely assumed otherwise: **Kubernetes does not read a Dockerfile's `HEALTHCHECK`.** It uses its own `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe`, and an image's healthcheck has no effect on scheduling, restarts or traffic routing.

`HEALTHCHECK` is useful for plain `docker run`, Docker Compose (`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`) and Docker Swarm. On Kubernetes, define probes in the Pod spec instead:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
```

      b: '"CMD node server.js" uses shell form instead of exec form. In shell form, the command runs as a child of "/bin/sh -c", so the Node process is not PID 1 and may not receive shutdown signals (like SIGTERM) directly, making graceful shutdown harder.',

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `RUN cd /app` | Has no effect on later instructions |
| `WORKDIR` after `USER` | Directory owned by root; app cannot write |
| Expecting `EXPOSE` to publish | Port unreachable; needs `-p` |
| App binds `127.0.0.1` | `-p` maps correctly and still refuses |
| Named `USER` on Kubernetes | `runAsNonRoot` cannot verify it; Pod fails |
| `VOLUME` then `COPY` to that path | Copied data silently discarded |
| `VOLUME` in an app image | Anonymous volumes pile up on the host |
| Relying on `HEALTHCHECK` in Kubernetes | Ignored; define probes instead |
| No `--start-period` | Slow starters marked unhealthy while booting |

## Quick reference

| Task | Instruction |
|---|---|
| Set working directory | `WORKDIR /app` |
| Document a port | `EXPOSE 3000` |
| Publish a port | `docker run -p 8080:3000` |
| Publish all exposed | `docker run -P` |
| Drop privileges | `USER 1000:1000` |
| Standard metadata | `LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="â¦"` |
| Health check | `HEALTHCHECK --start-period=40s CMD â¦` |
| Read health status | `docker inspect -f '{{.State.Health.Status}}' <c>` |

---

## Key takeaways

- **`WORKDIR` replaces `RUN cd`**, creates the directory, and does so as root even after `USER`.
- **`EXPOSE` publishes nothing.** It is documentation plus a hint for `-P` and Compose.
- **A refused connection on a published port** is usually the app bound to `127.0.0.1` rather than `0.0.0.0`.
- **Set `USER`**, and make it numeric if the image will run under Kubernetes' `runAsNonRoot`.
- **`VOLUME` is usually the wrong call**: anonymous volumes accumulate, and later writes to that path vanish.
- **Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK`.** Use `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe`.
- **Use OCI `LABEL` keys**, and combine them into one instruction.

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-volume-seed-lost',
    title: 'Seed data that disappears',
    description: 'A Dockerfile declares VOLUME /app/data and then, on a later line, COPY seed.json /app/data/. The build succeeds, but /app/data is empty in every container. Why?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'A volume is mounted over the declared path at container start, hiding anything written to it in later build instructions' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'COPY cannot write to a directory that has been declared with VOLUME, so the build silently skips it' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Anonymous volumes are read-only until a named volume is attached with -v' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'VOLUME must come after all COPY instructions or the Dockerfile fails to parse' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'Declaring VOLUME marks the path as externally backed. When the container starts, Docker mounts a volume there, an anonymous one if you did not supply your own, and that mount sits on top of whatever the image layers contain at that path, so the seed file is present in the image but invisible at runtime. Either drop the VOLUME declaration and let the operator decide with -v, or copy the seed elsewhere and have an entrypoint script populate the volume on first start, which is what official database images do.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'The COPY genuinely runs and the file really is in the image layer. It is masked at runtime by the mount, not skipped at build time.',
      c: 'Anonymous volumes are writable. Read-only behaviour would require mounting with the :ro option.',
      d: 'Instruction order does not cause a parse error. Placing VOLUME last avoids this specific surprise, but the Dockerfile is valid either way.',
    },
  }}
/>

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does EXPOSE actually open a port in Docker?**

No. `EXPOSE` records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling. Nothing more. It opens nothing, maps nothing, and a container without it is just as reachable. To reach the application from your host you need `-p 8080:3000` at `docker run`, and containers on the same Docker network can reach each other regardless. The one functional use is `docker run -P`, which publishes every exposed port to a random host port.

**Why can't I reach my container even though I used -p?**

Almost always because the application is bound to `127.0.0.1` inside the container. Localhost inside a container refers to that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Configure the server to bind `0.0.0.0`, in Express that is `app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0')`, in Flask `--host=0.0.0.0`. Confirm what is actually listening with `docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp` before changing anything else.

**Why does my container get "permission denied" after I added USER?**

Usually because a directory was created after the `USER` instruction. `WORKDIR` creates directories owned by root regardless of the current user, so `USER node` followed by `WORKDIR /app/cache` leaves the application unable to write to its own cache. Create and chown the directory while still root, then drop privileges. The other common cause is copied files still owned by root, which `COPY --chown=node:node` fixes in the same layer.

**Should I use VOLUME in my Dockerfile?**

Usually not, for application images. It creates an anonymous volume on every run that omits `-v`, and those pile up on the host until someone prunes them. Worse, any `COPY` or `RUN` writing to that path *after* the declaration is masked at runtime by the mount, so seed data silently disappears. Let whoever runs the container decide with `-v` or a Compose `volumes:` entry. It is defensible in database images, where the greater risk is someone running without persistence at all.

**Does Kubernetes use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK?**

No, and this trips up a lot of teams. Kubernetes ignores the image's `HEALTHCHECK` completely and relies on `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` defined in the Pod spec. An image with a perfect healthcheck gets no scheduling, restart or traffic-routing benefit on Kubernetes. `HEALTHCHECK` remains useful for plain `docker run`, for Docker Swarm, and for Compose's `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`.

**What is the difference between WORKDIR and RUN cd?**

`RUN cd /app` changes directory inside the shell that runs that one instruction, and that shell exits immediately afterwards, so the next instruction starts back at the previous directory. `WORKDIR /app` sets the directory for every subsequent instruction, persists into the final image as the container's starting directory, and creates the path if it does not exist. Use `WORKDIR`; the only place `cd` makes sense is chained within a single `RUN`, as in `RUN cd /src && make install`.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Every rolling deploy drops in-flight requests. The container takes the full termination grace period and is then killed. The Dockerfile ends with CMD node server.js and the app does handle SIGTERM. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why doesn't my container stop gracefully on docker stop?

Almost certainly shell-form CMD. Written as CMD node server.js, Docker runs /bin/sh -c "node server.js", making the shell PID 1 and your application its child, and sh receives SIGTERM without forwarding it. After the grace period Docker sends SIGKILL and everything in flight is lost. Use exec form: CMD ["node", "server.js"]. If the process genuinely cannot handle signals, run with --init or add tini as the entrypoint.
Is it really a problem to run a container as root?

It is a defence you are giving up for one line. Container isolation is good, so root inside a container is not automatically root on the host, but combined with a bind-mounted host path, a privileged flag, or a kernel vulnerability, the gap closes fast. Add USER 1000, and on Kubernetes pair it with runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and dropped capabilities. Use a numeric UID, because runAsNonRoot cannot verify a named user and the Pod will refuse to start.
How do I pass a secret to a Docker build safely?

With a BuildKit secret mount. RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token … makes the value readable at /run/secrets/npm_token for that one instruction and writes it to no layer, with docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN supplying it. Do not use ARG or ENV: both are recorded in the image metadata and docker history --no-trunc prints them back, even when the file you wrote was deleted in the same RUN. Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotation is the only fix.
What is the fastest way to make my Docker image smaller?

In order: use a multi-stage build so compilers and dev dependencies never ship, switch to a -slim or -alpine base variant (but not Alpine for Python), and make sure every cleanup happens in the same RUN as the thing it cleans up. Run docker history <image> --no-trunc first. It names the instruction responsible for each layer's size, which usually makes the answer obvious and saves you optimising something that was never the problem.
Which Dockerfile linter should I use, and what should it fail on?

Hadolint is the standard, and it runs as a container so there is nothing to install: docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile. In CI, set failure-threshold: warning. Its defaults are sensible and most of its rules map to genuine production problems, such as DL3002 for a root final user and DL3025 for shell-form CMD. Pair it with an image scanner such as Trivy or Docker Scout, and give that a non-zero exit code on HIGH and CRITICAL so results block a merge rather than scroll past in a log.
Do I need a HEALTHCHECK in my Dockerfile?

Only if something reads it. docker run, Docker Swarm and Compose's depends_on: condition: service_healthy all do, and it is worth adding there. Kubernetes does not. It uses livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe from the Pod spec and ignores the image's healthcheck completely, so on a cluster the instruction buys you nothing and the probes are what you need to get right. Wherever you do use it, set --start-period generously or slow-starting applications are marked unhealthy while still booting.

dockerfile-best-practices.markdown:
A Dockerfile that builds is not the same as one you would put in production. These are the practices that matter, ordered by what they actually buy you, because a checklist where every item looks equally important is a checklist nobody finishes.

The top five below cover most of the real-world damage. The rest are worth doing and none of them will page you at 3am.

| Priority | Practice | What it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Exec-form `CMD` | Containers that ignore SIGTERM and get killed |
| 2 | Non-root `USER` | A container escape becoming host root |
| 3 | Secrets via BuildKit mounts | Credentials permanently readable in the image |
| 4 | Dependency layer ordering | Multi-minute rebuilds on every commit |
| 5 | Multi-stage builds | Shipping compilers and dev dependencies |

## 1. Exec form, or your app never gets SIGTERM

The most commonly shipped Dockerfile bug, because everything looks fine until a deploy.

```dockerfile
CMD node server.js            # shell form
CMD ["node", "server.js"]     # exec form
```

Shell form becomes `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`. The shell is PID 1; your application is its child. When Docker or Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM`, `sh` receives it and does not forward it. Your app keeps serving until the grace period expires and `SIGKILL` arrives. Dropping in-flight requests on every single deploy.

```bash
docker stop myapp     # takes the full 10s, then kills
```

Exec form makes your process PID 1 and it receives the signal directly.

### PID 1 has no default signal handlers

A second, subtler catch: the kernel gives PID 1 no default action for `SIGTERM`. A process that never installs a handler ignores it even in exec form. Most frameworks handle this; plenty of scripts do not.

If your application cannot handle signals, or spawns children that leave zombies, give it a real init:

```bash
docker run --init myapp
```

```dockerfile
RUN apk add --no-cache tini
ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Some servers want a different signal entirely:

```dockerfile
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT      # nginx drains connections on SIGQUIT, not SIGTERM
```

## 2. Never run as root

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Root in a container is not root on the host in the way it once was, but it removes a layer of defence for free, and combined with a mounted host path or a kernel vulnerability it is the difference between an incident and a catastrophe.

Use a **numeric** UID if the image will run on Kubernetes, `runAsNonRoot: true` cannot verify a named user and the Pod fails to start.

Then take the next step and make the filesystem read-only:

```bash
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp
```

```yaml
# Kubernetes
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
```

An attacker who cannot write to the filesystem cannot drop a payload on it.

## 3. Secrets never survive deletion

```dockerfile
ENV DB_PASSWORD=supersecret          # in docker inspect, forever
ARG NPM_TOKEN                        # in docker history, forever
```

Deleting the file afterwards changes nothing. Layers are immutable, and the deletion only adds a whiteout on top.

```bash
docker history myapp:1.0 --no-trunc | grep -i token
```

Use a secret mount, which exists for one instruction and is written to no layer:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token)" > .npmrc \
 && npm ci \
 && rm .npmrc
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN -t myapp .
```

Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotating it is the only remedy.

## 4. Order layers by change frequency

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine              # changes on version bumps
WORKDIR /app
RUN apk add --no-cache curl      # changes rarely

COPY package*.json ./            # changes when dependencies do
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # expensive. Keep it cached

COPY . .                         # changes every commit
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, then rebuilds everything below. `COPY . .` above the install means every one-character edit reinstalls every dependency.

Add cache mounts for the step itself, which keeps the package cache on the builder without putting a byte in the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev
```

And write `.dockerignore` before your first `COPY . .`:

```
node_modules/
.git/
.env
.env.*
*.pem
dist/
coverage/
```

Three benefits at once: a smaller build context, no cache invalidation from irrelevant files, and local secrets that never reach a layer.

## 5. Multi-stage builds

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

Compilers, dev dependencies and source never reach what ships. For Go and Rust the effect is order-of-magnitude. A few hundred megabytes of build environment becomes a binary in a `scratch` or `distroless/static` image.

It is a security practice as much as a size one. A compiler in a production image is a tool an attacker gets for free.

## 6. Pin the base image

```dockerfile
FROM node:latest                      # moves without warning
FROM node:22.11.0-alpine3.20          # a specific release
FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:bf77dc26â¦  # immutable
```

Pin a digest and let Renovate or Dependabot bump it, so updates arrive as reviewable pull requests. Where you keep a tag, rebuild with `--pull` so a stale cached base does not quietly carry old CVEs into a "fresh" build.

## 7. Scan, and fail the build on it

```bash
docker scout cves myapp:1.0
trivy image myapp:1.0
```

```bash
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:1.0
```

That exit code is the part that matters. A scan whose output nobody reads is theatre; a scan that fails the pipeline is a control. Start with `CRITICAL` only if the backlog is large, then tighten.

Generate provenance and an SBOM while you are there. Increasingly expected, and one flag each:

```bash
docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true -t myapp:1.0 --push .
```

## 8. Lint it

[Hadolint](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint) catches most of this list mechanically:

```bash
docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile
```

| Rule | What it catches |
|---|---|
| `DL3002` | Last user is root |
| `DL3008` | Unpinned `apt-get install` versions |
| `DL3009` | apt lists not deleted |
| `DL3015` | Missing `--no-install-recommends` |
| `DL3025` | `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` in shell form |
| `DL3059` | Consecutive `RUN` instructions |
| `SC2086` | Unquoted variable, word-splitting risk |

In CI:

```yaml
- name: Lint Dockerfile
  uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
  with:
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
    failure-threshold: warning
```

## 9. Health checks, with one caveat

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
```

`--start-period` is the option that matters. Too little and a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

**Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK` entirely.** It reads only `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` from the Pod spec. The instruction is genuinely useful for `docker run`, Swarm, and Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`, just do not expect it to do anything on a cluster.

## 10. Label for provenance

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
```

`image.source` is the one that earns its keep: it is what lets a registry link a published image back to the repository that built it, and what lets an on-call engineer find the code from a running container at 3am.

---

    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'The hadolint image reads the Dockerfile content from stdin by default. "-i" keeps stdin open so the container can receive piped input, and shell redirection "< Dockerfile" feeds the file\'s contents into the container. "--rm" automatically removes the container once hadolint finishes, avoiding leftover stopped containers.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'Passing "Dockerfile" as an argument refers to a path inside the container\'s filesystem, not on the host. Since the host\'s Dockerfile was never mounted or copied into the container, hadolint would not find a file at that path and would fail or report an error.',
      c: 'The hadolint container does not have access to a file named "Dockerfile" on the host filesystem unless it is mounted as a volume. The "-f" flag (and similar path-based arguments) refer to paths inside the container, so this would fail without a volume mount.',
      d: 'Without "--rm", the container used for this one-off lint run is not automatically removed after it exits, leaving a stopped container behind. While the lint itself might still work, this does not match the goal of running it without leaving artifacts behind.',
    },
  }}
/>

## The pre-merge checklist

- [ ] Base image pinned to a version tag, ideally a digest
- [ ] `.dockerignore` excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env*`, keys
- [ ] Dependency manifest copied and installed before source
- [ ] Cleanup in the **same** `RUN` as the install
- [ ] No secrets in `ENV` or `ARG`; BuildKit mounts instead
- [ ] `USER` set, numeric if bound for Kubernetes
- [ ] `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` in exec form
- [ ] `STOPSIGNAL` set if the app wants something other than `SIGTERM`
- [ ] Multi-stage build wherever there is a compile step
- [ ] `EXPOSE` documents the port; app binds `0.0.0.0`
- [ ] OCI labels, at minimum `image.source`
- [ ] `hadolint` clean
- [ ] Scanner runs in CI with a non-zero exit on HIGH/CRITICAL

---

## Key takeaways

- **Exec form first.** Shell form means your app never sees `SIGTERM` and every deploy drops requests.
- **PID 1 has no default handlers**: use `--init` or tini when the process cannot handle signals itself.
- **A deleted secret is still a leaked secret.** Only BuildKit mounts keep it out of the layers.
- **Numeric `USER`** for Kubernetes, plus `readOnlyRootFilesystem` and dropped capabilities.
- **Manifest before source** is the cheapest large build-speed win there is.
- **Multi-stage builds are a security control**, not only a size optimisation.
- **A scan that cannot fail the build is decoration.** Set `--exit-code 1`.
- **Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK`.** Write probes.

---

## Check your understanding

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'docker-bp-sigterm',
    title: 'A deploy that always drops requests',
    description: 'Every rolling deploy drops in-flight requests. The container takes the full termination grace period and is then killed. The Dockerfile ends with CMD node server.js and the app does handle SIGTERM. What is wrong?',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Shell-form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1, and it does not forward SIGTERM to the application' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'The termination grace period is too short and needs raising' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'SIGTERM cannot reach a containerised process without --cap-add' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'The application needs a HEALTHCHECK before Docker will signal it' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'CMD node server.js is shell form, which Docker runs as /bin/sh -c "node server.js". The shell becomes PID 1 and the Node process is its child. SIGTERM is delivered to PID 1, the shell, which has no handler and does not pass it on, so the application never learns it should drain. After the grace period, SIGKILL takes down the whole container mid-request. Switching to the exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] makes Node itself PID 1 and the existing handler starts working.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'A longer grace period just makes the same failure slower. The signal is not reaching the process at all.',
      c: 'Signal delivery needs no special capability. The problem is which process is receiving it.',
      d: 'HEALTHCHECK reports status and plays no part in how termination signals are delivered.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why doesn't my container stop gracefully on docker stop?**

Almost certainly shell-form `CMD`. Written as `CMD node server.js`, Docker runs `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`, making the shell PID 1 and your application its child, and `sh` receives `SIGTERM` without forwarding it. After the grace period Docker sends `SIGKILL` and everything in flight is lost. Use exec form: `CMD ["node", "server.js"]`. If the process genuinely cannot handle signals, run with `--init` or add tini as the entrypoint.

**Is it really a problem to run a container as root?**

It is a defence you are giving up for one line. Container isolation is good, so root inside a container is not automatically root on the host, but combined with a bind-mounted host path, a privileged flag, or a kernel vulnerability, the gap closes fast. Add `USER 1000`, and on Kubernetes pair it with `runAsNonRoot: true`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and dropped capabilities. Use a numeric UID, because `runAsNonRoot` cannot verify a named user and the Pod will refuse to start.

**How do I pass a secret to a Docker build safely?**

With a BuildKit secret mount. `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token â¦` makes the value readable at `/run/secrets/npm_token` for that one instruction and writes it to no layer, with `docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN` supplying it. Do not use `ARG` or `ENV`: both are recorded in the image metadata and `docker history --no-trunc` prints them back, even when the file you wrote was deleted in the same `RUN`. Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotation is the only fix.

**What is the fastest way to make my Docker image smaller?**

In order: use a multi-stage build so compilers and dev dependencies never ship, switch to a `-slim` or `-alpine` base variant (but not Alpine for Python), and make sure every cleanup happens in the same `RUN` as the thing it cleans up. Run `docker history <image> --no-trunc` first. It names the instruction responsible for each layer's size, which usually makes the answer obvious and saves you optimising something that was never the problem.

**Which Dockerfile linter should I use, and what should it fail on?**

Hadolint is the standard, and it runs as a container so there is nothing to install: `docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile`. In CI, set `failure-threshold: warning`. Its defaults are sensible and most of its rules map to genuine production problems, such as `DL3002` for a root final user and `DL3025` for shell-form `CMD`. Pair it with an image scanner such as Trivy or Docker Scout, and give that a non-zero exit code on HIGH and CRITICAL so results block a merge rather than scroll past in a log.

**Do I need a HEALTHCHECK in my Dockerfile?**

Only if something reads it. `docker run`, Docker Swarm and Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` all do, and it is worth adding there. Kubernetes does not. It uses `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` from the Pod spec and ignores the image's healthcheck completely, so on a cluster the instruction buys you nothing and the probes are what you need to get right. Wherever you do use it, set `--start-period` generously or slow-starting applications are marked unhealthy while still booting.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Copy production-ready Dockerfile examples for Node.js, Python FastAPI, Go, React with Nginx, Spring Boot and Django, and see the pattern they all share.

Complete, production-shaped Dockerfiles you can adapt. Every one of them follows the same five-part skeleton. Build stage, minimal runtime stage, manifests cached before source, non-root user, exec-form start command, and each section calls out the specific mistake that shape avoids.

sections.title: Node.js API (TypeScript)
paragraphs: The TypeScript compiler and every dev dependency stay in the build stage. The runtime stage installs production dependencies fresh rather than copying node_modules across. Copying them would bring the dev tree with it, which is the usual reason a "multi-stage" Node image is no smaller than a single-stage one.
COPY --chown rather than a trailing RUN chown -R: the latter rewrites every file into a new layer.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ── Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json tsconfig.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build                      # → /app/dist

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app

ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/api"

USER node
EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: Python FastAPI
paragraphs: Three details doing real work here.
-slim, not -alpine. PyPI's prebuilt wheels target glibc, so Alpine forces pip to compile nearly everything from source. Slower builds and frequently a larger image.
libpq-dev in the build stage, libpq5 at runtime. The -dev package carries headers and a compiler toolchain that the running application has no use for.
--host 0.0.0.0. Uvicorn defaults to 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means that container only. This is the single most common cause of a published port that still refuses connections.
PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 matters more than it looks: without it, Python buffers stdout and your logs arrive in chunks, or not at all when the container is killed.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ── Build wheels ───────────────────────────────────────
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc libpq-dev \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 appuser && chown appuser /app

COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .
USER 1000
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "4"]

sections.title: Go (static binary on scratch)
paragraphs: CGO_ENABLED=0 is not optional. A dynamically linked binary in scratch dies instantly with no such file or directory. The missing file being the dynamic linker, which is why the message names nothing helpful.
scratch has no CA certificates and no timezone database, so any HTTPS call fails and every timestamp is UTC until you copy both across.
-ldflags="-w -s" strips the symbol table and DWARF debug info, typically cutting the binary by around a quarter.

The $BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETARCH combination cross-compiles natively on the builder rather than running the whole build under emulation, which is both much faster and what prevents an exec format error when an arm64 Mac builds for amd64 servers.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.23-alpine AS build
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates tzdata

WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download

COPY . .
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH \
    go build -ldflags="-w -s" -o /out/server .

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
COPY --from=build /usr/share/zoneinfo /usr/share/zoneinfo
COPY --from=build /out/server /server

EXPOSE 8080
USER 1000
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

sections.title: React SPA behind Nginx
paragraphs: STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT is the detail most nginx images miss. Nginx treats SIGTERM as a fast shutdown that cuts active connections, and SIGQUIT as a graceful drain. Without this line every deploy severs in-flight requests.

Build args are baked in, not configurable at runtime. VITE_API_URL is compiled into the JavaScript bundle, so one image cannot serve two environments. If you need that, serve a small /config.json that the app fetches at startup instead.

codeBlock.code:
# ── Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
ARG VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
ENV VITE_API_URL=${VITE_API_URL}
RUN npm run build                      # → /app/dist

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
RUN rm /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

sections.title: Spring Boot (layered JAR)
paragraphs: JRE at runtime, JDK only to build. Shipping the JDK adds a compiler and hundreds of megabytes for no benefit.

layertools extract splits the fat JAR into layers that change at different rates. Dependencies rarely change and stay cached; your application classes are the last, tiny layer. Copying the whole JAR instead means every one-line code change re-pushes the entire thing.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 ./mvnw dependency:go-offline

COPY src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 ./mvnw package -DskipTests
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract --destination extracted

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S -u 1000 -G spring spring

COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/application/ ./

USER 1000
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

sections.title: Django + Gunicorn
paragraphs: collectstatic runs at build time so the image is self-contained and container start stays fast. Note it needs settings that do not require a database connection. A DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE pointing at build-safe settings is the usual arrangement.
A Node.js Dockerfile builds in one stage and then copies both /app/dist and /app/node_modules from it into the runtime stage. The final image is the same size as the old single-stage one. Why?

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 django && chown django /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY --chown=django:django . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

USER 1000
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["gunicorn", "myproject.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", \
     "--timeout", "120"]

sections.title: The shape they share
paragraphs: To adapt one: change the base image to your pinned version, point the start command at your entry file, bind to 0.0.0.0 rather than localhost, and check whether your runtime needs a system library that only appeared in the build stage.
An Nginx container serving a React SPA severs in-flight requests each time it is replaced, even though the app is static and the rollout is gradual. Which Dockerfile line fixes it?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does a production-ready Dockerfile look like?

Five things, in every language: a build stage holding the compiler and dev dependencies, a runtime stage on the smallest base that can run the output, dependency manifests copied and installed before source so the expensive layer stays cached, a non-root numeric USER with ownership set via COPY --chown, and an exec-form CMD so the process receives SIGTERM. Add EXPOSE, OCI labels and a health check for tooling. Anything beyond that is tuning.
Why is my multi-stage Node.js image still large?

Almost certainly because node_modules is being copied from the build stage. That directory was produced by npm ci, which installs devDependencies alongside production ones because the TypeScript compiler needs them, so copying it forward brings the entire dev tree into production. Copy only the build output, and run npm ci --omit=dev separately in the runtime stage. Copying package*.json first there keeps that install cached too.
Should I use Alpine or slim for a Python Dockerfile?

-slim, in nearly every case. Alpine uses musl, and PyPI's prebuilt manylinux wheels target glibc, so pip install falls back to compiling from source. That turns a twenty-second install into several minutes, requires gcc and development headers in the image, and often produces a larger result than the slim variant. Alpine is an excellent choice for Go and Rust; for Python it usually costs on every axis you were trying to optimise.
How do I pass environment-specific configuration to a React Docker image?

A build arg such as VITE_API_URL is compiled into the JavaScript bundle, which means one image per environment and a rebuild for every change. Fine if your pipeline builds per environment anyway. If you want a single image promoted from staging to production, serve a small /config.json that Nginx can have mounted or generated at container start, and have the app fetch it before rendering. Runtime environment variables cannot reach an already-built bundle.
Why does my containerised app work locally but refuse connections in Docker?

The server is bound to 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Bind 0.0.0.0 instead: --host 0.0.0.0 for Uvicorn, --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 for Gunicorn, app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0') in Express. Confirm with docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp, which shows what is actually listening and on which address.
Why does my Go container exit immediately with "no such file or directory"?

The binary is dynamically linked and the file the kernel cannot find is the dynamic linker, not your program, which is why the error names nothing useful. Build with CGO_ENABLED=0 to produce a fully static binary. While you are there, remember that scratch also lacks TLS root certificates and timezone data, so copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt and /usr/share/zoneinfo from the build stage, or use gcr.io/distroless/static, which ships both.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.
dockerfile-real-world.markdown:
A Dockerfile that builds is not the same as one you would put in production. These are the practices that matter, ordered by what they actually buy you, because a checklist where every item looks equally important is a checklist nobody finishes.

The top five below cover most of the real-world damage. The rest are worth doing and none of them will page you at 3am.

| Priority | Practice | What it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Exec-form `CMD` | Containers that ignore SIGTERM and get killed |
| 2 | Non-root `USER` | A container escape becoming host root |
| 3 | Secrets via BuildKit mounts | Credentials permanently readable in the image |
| 4 | Dependency layer ordering | Multi-minute rebuilds on every commit |
| 5 | Multi-stage builds | Shipping compilers and dev dependencies |

## 1. Exec form, or your app never gets SIGTERM

The most commonly shipped Dockerfile bug, because everything looks fine until a deploy.

```dockerfile
CMD node server.js            # shell form
CMD ["node", "server.js"]     # exec form
```

Shell form becomes `/bin/sh -c "node server.js"`. The shell is PID 1; your application is its child. When Docker or Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM`, `sh` receives it and does not forward it. Your app keeps serving until the grace period expires and `SIGKILL` arrives. Dropping in-flight requests on every single deploy.

```bash
docker stop myapp     # takes the full 10s, then kills
```

Exec form makes your process PID 1 and it receives the signal directly.

### PID 1 has no default signal handlers

A second, subtler catch: the kernel gives PID 1 no default action for `SIGTERM`. A process that never installs a handler ignores it even in exec form. Most frameworks handle this; plenty of scripts do not.

If your application cannot handle signals, or spawns children that leave zombies, give it a real init:

```bash
docker run --init myapp
```

```dockerfile
RUN apk add --no-cache tini
ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Some servers want a different signal entirely:

```dockerfile
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT      # nginx drains connections on SIGQUIT, not SIGTERM
```

## 2. Never run as root

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Root in a container is not root on the host in the way it once was, but it removes a layer of defence for free, and combined with a mounted host path or a kernel vulnerability it is the difference between an incident and a catastrophe.

Use a **numeric** UID if the image will run on Kubernetes, `runAsNonRoot: true` cannot verify a named user and the Pod fails to start.

Then take the next step and make the filesystem read-only:

```bash
docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp
```

```yaml
# Kubernetes
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 1000
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
```

An attacker who cannot write to the filesystem cannot drop a payload on it.

## 3. Secrets never survive deletion

```dockerfile
ENV DB_PASSWORD=supersecret          # in docker inspect, forever
ARG NPM_TOKEN                        # in docker history, forever
```

Deleting the file afterwards changes nothing. Layers are immutable, and the deletion only adds a whiteout on top.

```bash
docker history myapp:1.0 --no-trunc | grep -i token
```

Use a secret mount, which exists for one instruction and is written to no layer:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token)" > .npmrc \
 && npm ci \
 && rm .npmrc
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN -t myapp .
```

Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotating it is the only remedy.

## 4. Order layers by change frequency

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine              # changes on version bumps
WORKDIR /app
RUN apk add --no-cache curl      # changes rarely

COPY package*.json ./            # changes when dependencies do
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # expensive. Keep it cached

COPY . .                         # changes every commit
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, then rebuilds everything below. `COPY . .` above the install means every one-character edit reinstalls every dependency.

Add cache mounts for the step itself, which keeps the package cache on the builder without putting a byte in the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev
```

And write `.dockerignore` before your first `COPY . .`:

```
node_modules/
.git/
.env
.env.*
*.pem
dist/
coverage/
```

Three benefits at once: a smaller build context, no cache invalidation from irrelevant files, and local secrets that never reach a layer.

## 5. Multi-stage builds

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

Compilers, dev dependencies and source never reach what ships. For Go and Rust the effect is order-of-magnitude. A few hundred megabytes of build environment becomes a binary in a `scratch` or `distroless/static` image.

It is a security practice as much as a size one. A compiler in a production image is a tool an attacker gets for free.

## 6. Pin the base image

```dockerfile
FROM node:latest                      # moves without warning
FROM node:22.11.0-alpine3.20          # a specific release
FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:bf77dc26â¦  # immutable
```

Pin a digest and let Renovate or Dependabot bump it, so updates arrive as reviewable pull requests. Where you keep a tag, rebuild with `--pull` so a stale cached base does not quietly carry old CVEs into a "fresh" build.

## 7. Scan, and fail the build on it

```bash
docker scout cves myapp:1.0
trivy image myapp:1.0
```

```bash
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:1.0
```

That exit code is the part that matters. A scan whose output nobody reads is theatre; a scan that fails the pipeline is a control. Start with `CRITICAL` only if the backlog is large, then tighten.

Generate provenance and an SBOM while you are there. Increasingly expected, and one flag each:

```bash
docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true -t myapp:1.0 --push .
```

## 8. Lint it

[Hadolint](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint) catches most of this list mechanically:

```bash
docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile
```

| Rule | What it catches |
|---|---|
| `DL3002` | Last user is root |
| `DL3008` | Unpinned `apt-get install` versions |
| `DL3009` | apt lists not deleted |
| `DL3015` | Missing `--no-install-recommends` |
| `DL3025` | `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` in shell form |
| `DL3059` | Consecutive `RUN` instructions |
| `SC2086` | Unquoted variable, word-splitting risk |

In CI:

```yaml
- name: Lint Dockerfile
  uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
  with:
    dockerfile: Dockerfile
    failure-threshold: warning
```

## 9. Health checks, with one caveat

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1
```

`--start-period` is the option that matters. Too little and a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

**Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK` entirely.** It reads only `livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` from the Pod spec. The instruction is genuinely useful for `docker run`, Swarm, and Compose's `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`, just do not expect it to do anything on a cluster.

## 10. Label for provenance

```dockerfile
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"
```

`image.source` is the one that earns its keep: it is what lets a registry link a published image back to the repository that built it, and what lets an on-call engineer find the code from a running container at 3am.

## The pre-merge checklist

- [ ] Base image pinned to a version tag, ideally a digest
- [ ] `.dockerignore` excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env*`, keys
- [ ] Dependency manifest copied and installed before source
- [ ] Cleanup in the **same** `RUN` as the install
- [ ] No secrets in `ENV` or `ARG`; BuildKit mounts instead
- [ ] `USER` set, numeric if bound for Kubernetes
- [ ] `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` in exec form
- [ ] `STOPSIGNAL` set if the app wants something other than `SIGTERM`
- [ ] Multi-stage build wherever there is a compile step
- [ ] `EXPOSE` documents the port; app binds `0.0.0.0`
- [ ] OCI labels, at minimum `image.source`
- [ ] `hadolint` clean
- [ ] Scanner runs in CI with a non-zero exit on HIGH/CRITICAL

---

## Key takeaways

- **Exec form first.** Shell form means your app never sees `SIGTERM` and every deploy drops requests.
- **PID 1 has no default handlers**: use `--init` or tini when the process cannot handle signals itself.
- **A deleted secret is still a leaked secret.** Only BuildKit mounts keep it out of the layers.
- **Numeric `USER`** for Kubernetes, plus `readOnlyRootFilesystem` and dropped capabilities.
- **Manifest before source** is the cheapest large build-speed win there is.
- **Multi-stage builds are a security control**, not only a size optimisation.
- **A scan that cannot fail the build is decoration.** Set `--exit-code 1`.
- **Kubernetes ignores `HEALTHCHECK`.** Write probes.
